Name: Sarah McTighe
CommentOriginal: I strongly object to this development going ahead due to the following reasons  The area around the development is a haven for wildlife and is used by large numbers of dog walkers and families for recreational activities. We are already living in a world where obesity is becoming even more of an issue and yet green space where children can play safely is being swallowed up with houses. The wildlife and trees will gradually die due to the work and development and Blaby will lose such a valuable asset. It will be very sad to see that happen. My teenagers have grown up with this beautiful place and I wanted their children to have the same great place to play.   The entry and exit to the development is on a road which is already congested. This is to all intents and purposes a country lane which would not stand up to in excess of 200 more cars using it on a daily basis. During peak times it can take me 10 minutes to get off my drive already and the cars from the new development will be coming onto my road. The doctors, schools and dentists are already over stretched so to introduce 200 + more families will make matters worse. Blaby has exceeded its new build quota now and needs to retain its identity as a village. This is all to do with money and no one is listening to what the residents want. With regard to the drop off/pick up point for the school this will be totally unworkable as it is not staggered start times and parents all turn up at the same time. Parking is already a problem at start and end of school day and some parents can not walk the short distance therefore causing a hazard by the way they park. This will not change with an increase in numbers and no amount of measures will make any difference.   This development should not be allowed to go ahead just to ease Leicestershire County Council's budget problems.

CommentOriginal: Application Reference: S62A/2014/0001/Hospital Lane Blaby I strongly object to this application.  Blaby does not have the infrastructure for this development, nor can it possibly be built for it, our village is already at bursting point & we find ourselves practically joined with Countesthorpe & Whetstone.  Our surgeries, schools and roads are already overloaded and pollution and noise are far too high.  The traffic is already horrendous along Hospital Lane & Welford Road/Sycamore Streets, with volume & speeding cars a terrible issue & the number of accidents on the increase.  Blaby cannot possibly support what could be another 1000+ people & 500 cars.  I have researched this and Blaby has already fulfilled the housing need in our village with over 72 new houses/flats recently built and another 130+ currently being built (scout hut land) and the villages that "join us" have over 170+ new houses being built (& I see another 290+ approved).  Not only have Blaby village met their quota but Blaby District has also more than met their quota especially with well over 2500 houses in one location already approved.  We have had 2 consultation meetings about this proposed development, one several years ago and one in 2013 and at BOTH there was overwhelming widespread public opposition to the plans. NO-ONE who LIVES in Blaby wants this.  We also have the support of local councillors, the Parish Council and our member of parliament on this matter!  Add to all of that the fact that the area in question is the last "open space" of green land that Blaby has left.  As a dog-owner we use these footpaths, fields and woodland EVERY day, as do MANY of the village. We have seen muntjac deer, foxes, an amazing array of birdlife including green woodpeckers all who live in these fields and woodland.  As someone who has previously lived on a housing estate I can guarantee that all the wildlife will disappear if this development goes ahead.  We will have nothing left.  According to my research "local communities will be able to earmark for special consideration local 'green space' land - whether its value is in its natural beauty, its historic resonances, its recreational value, its tranquillity or its importance as wildlife habitat." "Environment Secretary Caroline Spelman said: Giving communities the power to protect green spaces in towns and cities important to their local environment will benefit the wellbeing of people and wildlife.  The natural environment matters to all of us, we have an interest in protecting it and making it better.  Working together we can be the first generation to leave the environment in a better state than we found it." "The Government attaches great important to Green Belts.  The fundamental aim of Green Belt policy is to prevent urban sprawl by keeping land permanently open; the essential characteristics of Green Belts are their openness and their permanence."  If this goes ahead it will fundamentally damage our village and its future irrevocably.  Please do not let this happen, please let the voices of the people who live in this community be heard over the people with power and money.  Thank you.

Name: Michael Norman
CommentOriginal: This application seeks to build up to 220 dwellings on green belt land which boarders a conservation area and up to the boundary of an important archaeological site, which is the undisturbed site of the old medieval village of Blaby. -The visual impact of this development would destroy the current rural aspect of 'old' Blaby village, Blaby Hall and Bouskell park and bury them behind this new development. - The proposed development will completely effect the character of the village. The current environment would be ruined by new buildings occupying medieval farm land right up to the edge of a beautiful historic,important, unspoiled park which contains the remains of the old medieval village.  - This development is completely out of scale to the site, occupying all the land available. I believe that no development should be permitted, However if any development is allowed, it should be limited to a small number of homes and be restricted to the field which fronts on to Hospital Lane only. Thereby stopping the detrimental effect on the conservation area and ancient park and leaving a 'green buffer' of land between the development and the current village boundary. - The proposed development will clearly have an adverse effect on the conservation area, it will ruin one of the few historic rural village views left in this District. As you approach the village from the east It will also impact on the view of Blaby Hall, which I understand is a Grade 2 listed Building. The same applies to Blaby Parish Church, which stands next to the hall. -The development will significantly impact on the the safety and convenience of road users. It will substantially increase rush hour traffic on Hospital Lane. Currently traffic on Hospital lane can queue back for long distances and struggle to exit out onto Countesthorpe Road and on to Winchester Road.  - Within a short distance from the proposed development large housing developments have been started, particularly on the site of the old scout hut on Winchester Road and on Countesthorpe Road, Countesthorpe. These developments alone will substantially add to peak hour road congestion.  - I know that during severe weather the drains can not copy with current levels of demand. I have seen man hole covers blow off and foul water flow across Sycamore Street. This proposed development can only have a further negative impact on a drainage system which is struggling to cope with continued over development in the area. - This is green belt land which should not be developed. The current use of this area, which is mainly dog walking and leisure, will be adversely effected by this development which is not in the interest of the community.  With the current new developments already underway locally in Blaby and Countesthorpe  (not to mention the 4500 homes to be built nearby at Enderby) this additional housing is not required to support housing needs in the District.  Thank you.

Name: Pam Hunt
CommentOriginal: I am a long standing resident of the Blaby area, I regularly walk my dogs along the bridle path through long walk and onto Bouskell Park as do many, many others.  This is one of the few truly green picturesque areas of Blaby.  They are already building on the old scout site and on the field adjoining the golf course as well as the development in Countesthorpe.  Are they intending to build and staff an extra school and GP surgery to cater for all these extra people?  Are they intending to rehome all the wildlife who will be having their homes destroyed?  Are they going to ensure adequate drainage as there will be a vast reduction in the amount of natural green land for surplus water to soak into?  How do they propose that the problem of already congested roads be dealt with?  There are plenty of disused factory units that could be used for housing without the need to destroy existing green land.  Please do not deny my children and future children the fun of being in a natural and relaxing area.

Name: Les Edkins
CommentOriginal: Dear Sir or Madam  I wish to object to major planning application S62A/2014/0001 on the following grounds:  1) Infrastructure  A development of this size will place a heavy burden on existing public transport, road and drainage/foul water systems.  Although considered as part of the would-be developer's proposal I do not consider that these aspects have been fully addressed.  2) Loss of amenity  Bouskell Park and the surrounding area is a valuable recreational amenity which will be overshadowed by the development should it go ahead, further eroding the "green space" between Blaby and nearby built-up areas  3) Local services  Insufficient account has been taken of the effect of such a major development on local health and education services.  Although the proposal states that local GP surgeries are "accepting patients" this does not guarantee that the surgeries have the necessary resources to cope with such an influx of patients.  In summary, a development of this size is wholly unsuited to the proposed location, both for the reasons outlined above and on the grounds that "old Blaby" (immediately adjacent to the site) is of historic importance.  I trust that the above comments will be considered as part of the decision-making process and await the outcome in due course.  Yours faithfully  Les Edkins

CommentOriginal: I am a Glen Parva parish councillor and a local resident for many years. The Blaby Hall farm land is a major amenity shared by not only Blaby residents, but also Glen Parva residents. The area adjacent to Bouskell Park, especially "The long walk" should be protected by a Land for life (FIT) deed.  Also the Cemetery in Mill lane will also be affected by this development, restricting any future expansion. Additionally the traffic along Hospital lane, which is excessive now, will have additional vehicle movements affecting the Winchester road junction. This junction is already very difficult for the small children attending the local school here.  Additionally there is no requirement of more housing within Blaby district due to the approval of the 4250 house development at Lubbesthorpe (SUE).  I formally object on the grounds of loosing this amenity.

CommentOriginal: As the development's "next door neighbours"- we are the next house on the same side in an easterly direction, I can say we are horrified at the amount of traffic that would be going past our gate if this goes ahead. At the moment, we risk our lives trying to turn out of our gateway as cars are travelling in excess of 50 mph on both sides of the road and if you dare to pull out, the cars are behind you in a minute hooting. We always slow down to 30mph at Oakfield Park but again cars are right up your boot as they don't want to slow down (recent police "stings" have caught many speeding drivers here) despite the school crossing. The footpath along Hospital Lane stops abruptly at the old hospital so walkers, joggers and cyclists are forced to walk along this very busy lane taking their lives in their hands. There have been several car accidents just after this point including one fatality. Lodge Farm cross their cows for milking across the road twice a day and although there are flashing signs warning of this, drivers do not want to wait a minute. There are many people walking, jogging or cycling along this country lane. The thought of another 220/440 odd cars on this country lane is awful. The highways aspect of this development will impact on Hospital Lane and only can be to the detriment of residents at this end of it. If this development goes ahead, please could the footpath be continued along the length of Hospital Lane so that people using it not in cars are safe? Also reducing the speed limit to 40mph would help.

Name: Sandra and Gordon Woollatt
CommentOriginal: There is already an extensive building programme in Blaby district and we understand that Blaby is already exceeding its target.  Currently, the proposed development area is much used by local people and visitors to Blaby.  The Long Walk provides continuous green space between Bouskell Park and Oak Woods.  The development would isolate the woods turning it into a barren environment for nature.   This unnecessary housing development would irreversibly destroy this much loved and well used recreational facility.  If the development goes ahead, an opportunity would be missed to improve the quality of life for people living in Leicestershire by providing continuous park land between Countesthorpe and Blaby.

Name: Raymond Watson
CommentOriginal: Neither I nor those whom have made their objections known to me are opposed to the development of new housing which we realise is much required.  There are other alternative sites within this small area which could have been used such as the land used by a travelling circus a few times a year and at no other time I have witnessed. I travel that road every day and speak as a proven fact. It abutts a main road so traffic would not be unduly affected and also places a greater amount of the required facilities with easy reach. Being aware of those facts this is my objection which others also support. Besides personally, the whole of our small community are applalled that this is yet another land grabbing excercise by developers to remove the pleasure we derive from having an easily available, much used  green and open area that is within easy reach for all local residents including the elderly and disabled with mobility problems. The development will also increase traffic levels within this area which already has significant traffic problems during rush hours, add to the heavily subscribed Doctors, Dentists Health care and  Schools. There is no common sense or logical reason for this development within that particular area of natural beauty. WHY must we go through this repeated application time and again? Our objections will not change.

Name: Caroline Allen
CommentOriginal: The area being considered for development is heavily used by walkers, dog walkers, cyclists and horse riders.  The long walk is an area of natural beauty and a haven for wild life.  The proposed development will see houses backing on to the Long Walk and this is likely to become a corridor/alley spoiling the area completely.  The ice house is of a great deal of historical interest and the entire area surrounding Bouskell Park is believed to be the original settlement of Blaby.   Finally the road infrastructure around Hospital Lane, Welford Road and Roads leading to the motorway and Leicester city will not cope with the additional traffic and are currently heavily congested during peak periods.   I live on Welford Road and much of the traffic already ignores speed limits.  I have seen the bollard outside of my house already knocked down by speeding cars on 2 occasions and a further speeding car veer of the road opposite the park in the last 24 months alone. This road is heavily used by children attending the local schools and colleges of Blaby and Countesthorpe and in the last 12 months I am aware of 3 accidents along this stretch of road - 2 of which involved local school children.    So far none of these accidents have caused fatalities - however an additional 220 dwellings will increase the potential for traffic and with no traffic calming in place it is only a matter of time before a fatality will occur.   Blaby and Countesthorpe are already seeing a considerable amount of development in the area - including Winchester Road and the large RedRow estate in Countesthorpe.   The majority of additional traffic created will need to go through Blaby village in order to reach the main commuter roads using an already busy, fast travelling and congested road system.  Bouskell Park is enjoyed by the residents of Blaby and surrounding villages and the car park is frequently full of people who enjoy this area for its natural beauty and are likely to go elsewhere should this unnecessary, unwanted and unrequired development be allowed to go ahead.

CommentOriginal: Dear Laura OUTLINE PLANNING APPLCIATION WITH ACCESS ONLY. PROPOSED CONSTRUCTION OF UP TO 220 NEW DWELLINGS (USE CLASS C3) AND SCHOOL DROP OFF/PICK UP ZONE, WITH ACCESS AND ASSOCIATED INFRASTRUCTURE. LAND TO THE NORTH OF HOSPITAL LANE, TO THE SOUTH OF MILL LANE AND TO THE EAST OF BOUSKELL PARK, BLABY, LEICESTERSHIRE. Thank you for referring the above application which was received on 24 April 2014. Although an outline application, there are no details of the sizing or capacity of the culverts crossing the site, and notwithstanding the easements and proposed restriction of run-off to greenfield rates, we do not have confidence to condition the application without further investigation being undertaken. We require clarification of the sizing and capacity of the culverts to ascertain whether they pose a flood risk to the site and whether the suggested mitigation is appropriate to safeguard the development against flood risk. The development proposes to connect surface water flows into the culverted system and we would advise that the system is fully modelled and its entire function and capacity ascertained, prior to adding additional flows into the system. Although the 2 culvert systems are not afforded broad scale flood mapping due to the small size of the catchment area, we have concerns that without further investigation of the capacity of the system, the additional flows from the development may create or exacerbate an existing flood risk, if the culverts are shown to have insufficient capacity. With further investigation, if their is insufficient capacity within the culverts, additional storage would be required on site - up to climate change for the drainage and additional storage for surcharge events for the 1 in 30 up to the fluvial climate change event. It may also influence the indicative layout by placing SUDs features outside of areas of flood risk. The efficiency of the land drainage and groundwater of the area should also be maintained post-development. Environment Agency position In the absence of sufficient information contained within the Flood Risk Assessment (FRA) we object to the grant of planning permission and recommend refusal on this basis for the following reasons: Reason The FRA submitted with this application does not comply with the requirements set out in paragraph 30 of the National Planning Practice Guidance. The submitted FRA does not therefore, provide a suitable basis for assessment to be made of the flood risks arising from the proposed development. In particular, the submitted FRA does not: Consider the capacity of the culverts crossing the site, nor give an indication of capacity. Therefore, additional flows may overwhelm the system and lead to increased flood risk. Overcoming our objection You can overcome our objection by submitting a FRA which covers the deficiencies highlighted above and demonstrates that the development will not increase risk elsewhere and where possible reduces flood risk overall. If this cannot be achieved we are likely to maintain our objection to the application. We ask to be re-consulted with the results of the FRA. We will provide you with bespoke comments within 21 days of receiving formal reconsultation. Our objection will be maintained until an adequate FRA has been submitted.

Name: English Heritage
CommentOriginal: Dear Ms O'Brien LAND TO THE NORTH OF HOSPITAL LANE, TO THE SOUTH OF MILL LANE AND TO THE EAST OF BOUSKELL PARK, BLABY, LEICESTERSHIRE Thank you for consulting English Heritage on the above outline planning application. We understand this application has been accepted for consideration by the Planning Inspectorate , who also provided pre-application advice, fo r which a copy has been made available on your website (refer: S62A/PRE-APP/2013 /001).  Whilst we were not engaged at pre application stage , we welcome the opportun ity to advise now. We understand this application will be determined by the Inspector on behalf of the Secretary of State. Summary The outline planning application is for a residential development of up to 220 residentia l units with associated infrastructure and access , amenity open space including new parkland, improved access through Long Walk Woodland and two vehicular access points off Hospital Lane. All other matters are reserved. The site is 17.37 hectares of land predominantly in agricultural use with woodland known as Long Walk running through the site.  The site is defined by Mill Lane and Cemetery to the north/north east, agricultural land and estab lishing woodland to the east, Hospital Lane to the south and Thistley Meadow Primary School and Bouskell Park to the west.  The Blaby conservation area borders the north and west of the site and includes a number of listed buildings; the Grade I listed Church of All Saints, the Grade II listed Blaby Hall, icehouse , hall farmhouse , Blaby Hall mews, and other statutory listings.  The scheduled Motte and Hut circle at Glen Parva is situated approx . 300m north east of the application site. Our advice is given in line with the relevant legislation , the NPPF, the Planning EAST MIDLANDS OFFICE Practice Guidance and the PPS5 Practice Guide which remains live. We also refer to our published guidance document The Setting of Heritage Assets, 2011.  We believe this outline application is harmful to the significance of numerous designated heritage assets.  This harm is assessed as less than substantial; any level of harm requires a clear and convincing justification, less than substantial harm does not equate to acceptable harm.  We do not believe clear and convincing justification has been made and do not consider the harm has been outweighed by public benefits.  Therefore we do not support this application and recommend refusal. In the event that a hearing is deemed appropriate we would be happy to attend if the Inspector would find that beneficial. English Heritage Advice We are the Government's principal advisers on the historic environment and in giving this advice we will set out the possible impacts this development has on the significance of the heritage assets.........

CommentOriginal: I wish to object to the proposed "Hospital Lane" housing development in Blaby. This development will encroach upon undeveloped countryside adjacent to a conservation area covering the medieval village centre of Blaby and the highly valued Bouskell park. Name: John Seaman
CommentOriginal: I wish to register my objection to this proposed development of rural agricultural land.  The grounds for my objection are as follows:  LOSS OF AGRICULTURAL LAND: These are fertile green fields which are needed to provide food and agricultural produce.  Farmland lost to development is gone forever. It is worth noting that the Government's own Food 2030 Strategy states:  'We need to increase food production to feed a growing world population ' there'll be another 2-3 billion people in 40 years. This food will need to be produced in a way that protects the natural resources on which food production depends - soil and water - and on which we rely for drinking water, to regulate our climate, stem flood waters and filter pollution.  We want UK agriculture to produce as much food as possible, as long as it's what people want, and it's done sustainably.'   LOSS OF WILDLIFE HABITAT: The fields are an important part of the rural ecology of the area, and their loss will have a devastating effect on its rich wildlife, including bats, ground nesting birds and insects such as bees, all the more important because of its location on the edge of the built up area. Open ditches and the brook are important breeding grounds for water creatures and amphibians. Other wildlife higher up in the food chain will be badly affected, and the vital wildlife corridors between open countryside, the Sence Valley and Bouskell Park will be virtually blocked off.   LOSS OF AMENITY FOR LOCAL PEOPLE: the peace and beauty of this rural area is highly valued by people of Blaby and Glen Parva because of its accessibility as the only area of unspoilt countryside within reasonable walking distance. The much loved footpaths and bridleways will become litter strewn back alleys when surrounded by new buildings. The area is particularly popular with young people, but a generation of pupils at Thistly Meadow School will witness the destruction of the beautiful countryside around them if permission is granted.  OVERDEVELOPMENT: The area is already undergoing multiple new developments on green fields and former sports and amenity sites, in particular the former Scouts playing field off Winchester Road and the farmland opposite, as well as the former cricket ground adjacent to the Dog and Gun public house. Further development of the Leyslands site and of farmland at Leicester Road, Countesthorpe is also proceeding. The argument that this development is needed because of shortage of accommodation locally does not apply.  TRAFFIC PROBLEMS: Hospital Lane is an extremely fast and busy road used as an unofficial bypass by commuters and others. It is normal to find up to half a mile of stationary traffic towards Countesthorpe at busy periods.  The additional traffic generated by a large housing development will make this much worse, not least because of all the other major developments going on in Blaby and Countesthorpe.  OTHER COMMENTS: By far the best thing for the Bouskell Park and the village in general would be for the County Council to reinstate the farm and bring agriculture back to the heart of Blaby, restoring the irreplaceable village atmosphere and using the land profitably and sustainably to produce food. The Councillors and Officers should remember that it is not their land, it is owned  and much valued by the people of Blaby district, whose wishes should not lightly be ignored.

Name: Paul Madine
CommentOriginal: 'We are certainly not opposed to all new development in principle.  The government have decided to devolve more power over planning decisions to local communities (Localism Bill & NPPF). I think this proposal is a singularly inappropriate and unwelcome development which has wide ranging negative implications for the environment and residents of the District (survey and petition evidence is available). 'The proposed site is not just another area of green space / countryside on the 'edge of town' ' it is a particularly valuable area with high amenity value to the local community and to a wider community in the region.  It is also described as important to the form and character of the landscape and it has high heritage potential.  'Local infrastructure is not capable of supporting a development of this size and in this location. I do not think the proposed development is properly sustainable.  The size of the proposed residential development significantly exceeds the residual housing requirement for Blaby as defined by the Local Plan, CS5, Housing distribution. 'Hospital Lane is already severely congested during peak periods especially at the junction with Leicester Road / Countesthorpe Road to the east of Blaby. Welford Road in Blaby is also now congested at busy times and can be difficult for pedestrians to cross. The proposed development would make the situation a great deal worse in Blaby, Whetstone, Glen Parva, Countesthorpe and South Wigston. ''Bouskell Park, the historic Long Walk and the green spaces that surround it form Blaby's breathing space, its green 'Jewel in the Crown,' arguably Blaby's finest asset ' it should be preserved to protect the quality of life of local residents and provide a haven for wildlife.  Its loss would be a tragedy for Blaby on several levels.' ''Bouskell Park is one of the Council's strategic green spaces and we strive to keep improving it.' ' Blaby District Green Space Strategy 2012.  I think it is undeniable that this proposed development will harm Bouskell Park. 'This outline planning application is opposed by the overwhelming majority of the community, many local Councillors and the Parish Council. ''This is not a NIMBY protest ' the community want to have a say in shaping their local environment and want to protect this vital green infrastructure as a key part of the settlement of Blaby.' 'Bouskell Park is a beautiful public park on the site of a 10th century medieval village (the original settlement of Blaby) with a pond and a Victorian Ice House (a Grade II Listed building).  Interpretative panels give visitors the history of the area and the wildlife to be seen.  If the park was to be 'hemmed-in' by housing it would loose much of its amenity value to residents and it would be too small and isolated to be the valuable habitat for wildlife it is at present. 'If the wooded Long Walk with its very popular permissive path were to be surrounded with an estate of over 200 houses it would result in a considerable reduction in the amenity value of the Long Walk area to local residents and is very strongly opposed by the community. 'If the proposed development went ahead it would isolate Long Walk from the surrounding countryside and it is then likely that it would become unpopular with many users who use it extensively at present. The government have decided to devolve more power over planning decisions to local communities (Localism Bill and NPPF). I think this proposal is a singularly inappropriate and unwelcome development which has wide ranging negative implications for the environment and residents of the District (survey and petition evidence is available).  The proposed site is not just another area of green space / countryside on the edge of town it is a particularly valuable area with high amenity value to the local community and to a wider community in the region.  It is also described as important to the form and character of the landscape and it has high heritage potential.  Local infrastructure is not capable of supporting a development of this size and in this location. I do not think the proposed development is properly sustainable.  The size of the proposed residential development significantly exceeds the residual housing requirement for Blaby as defined by the Local Plan, CS5, Housing distribution.  Hospital Lane is already severely congested during peak periods especially at the junction with Leicester Road / Countesthorpe Road to the east of Blaby. Welford Road in Blaby is also now congested at busy times and can be difficult for pedestrians to cross. The proposed development would make the situation a great deal worse in Blaby, Whetstone, Glen Parva, Countesthorpe and South Wigston. Bouskell Park, the historic Long Walk and the green spaces that surround it form Blaby's breathing space, its green - Jewel in the Crown - arguably Blaby's finest asset - it should be preserved to protect the quality of life of local residents and provide a haven for wildlife.  Its loss would be a tragedy for Blaby on several levels.  Bouskell Park is one of the Council's strategic green spaces and we strive to keep improving it. Blaby District Green Space Strategy 2012.  I think it is undeniable that this proposed development will harm Bouskell Park.  This outline planning application is opposed by the overwhelming majority of the community, many local Councillors and the Parish Council. This is not a NIMBY protest-  the community want to have a say in shaping their local environment and want to protect this vital green infrastructure as a key part of the settlement of Blaby.   Bouskell Park is a beautiful public park on the site of a 10th century medieval village (the original settlement of Blaby) with a pond and a Victorian Ice House (a Grade II Listed building).  Interpretative panels give visitors the history of the area and the wildlife to be seen.  If the park was to be hemmed-in by housing it would loose much of its amenity value to residents and it would be too small and isolated to be the valuable habitat for wildlife it is at present. If the proposed development went ahead it would isolate Long Walk from the surrounding countryside and it is then likely that it would become unpopular with many users who use it extensively at present. CommentOriginal: I hereby include the reasons for my objection to the plans to turn the green open space into a housing estate.  As residents in the Blaby and Glen Parva area for the last 45 years my family has enjoyed the opportunity to walk and horse ride through the area and enjoy the countryside aspect, despite being so near to Blaby.  Whilst I appreciate the need for housing - care must be taken to balance the area in order to give all residents ready access to green, relatively unstructured open space in order to promote well being in an area that is already oversupplied with housing and lacking in green space to meet needs.  It links into green routes to Countesthorpe and beyond.  It is also a vital space for people living in areas all around Blaby who travel to this lovely green space.  I live in Glen Parva now and regularly walk 'the long way round'  to the shops in order to enjoy this area.   Localism Bill & NPPF  ·	The government have decided to devolve more power over planning decisions to local communities). The community think this proposal is a singularly inappropriate and unwelcome development which has wide ranging negative implications for the environment and residents of the District (survey and petition evidence is available).  ·	Bouskell Park, the historic Long Walk and the green spaces that surround it form Blaby's breathing space, its green 'Jewel in the Crown,' arguably Blaby's finest asset ' it should be preserved to protect the quality of life of local residents and provide a haven for wildlife.  Its loss would be a tragedy for Blaby on several levels.  Bouskell Park is one of the Council's strategic green spaces and it is undeniable that this proposed development will harm Bouskell Park.  ·	This outline planning application is opposed by the overwhelming majority of the community, many local Councillors and the Parish Council.  	Policy on Open Spaces, Sport and Recreation (CS15) seeks to ensure that all residents have access to sufficient, high quality, accessible open space, sport and recreation facilities.  It states that existing open space, sport and recreation facilities will be protected, and where possible enhanced. Where development is proposed on existing open space, sport and recreation facilities, land should not be released, either in total or in part unless it can be demonstrated that it is surplus to requirements for its current play and open space function. The Local Plan CS (Issues, problems and challenges facing the District) para. 4.3 states that, 'A recent survey of play and open spaces has indicated that the District is broadly lacking in these facilities.' This site is of high quality and valuable open space that is not at all surplus to requirements.  Planning Policy on Countryside & the Requirement for New Housing (CS18) (CS5) (LSCA) (NPPF) Blaby District Council already have a 5 year supply of deliverable housing sites (as defined by the NPPF) to meet the District's requirements for new housing, so it is not necessary to support development proposals that do not align with planning policy.   The proposal runs counter to the recommendations of the Blaby District Landscape and Settlement Character Assessment (LSCA) which has an important role in assessing the effect a development would have on the countryside's landscape.  A development of this size (over 200 dwellings) in this location is not justified by the outstanding housing requirement numbers for Blaby defined in Policy CS5, Housing Distribution  The site is designated as Countryside and this development proposal is not supported by planning policy on Countryside (CS18), which states that  'Within areas designated as Countryside, planning permission will not be granted for built development, or other development which would have a significantly adverse effect on the appearance or character of the landscape.  2. Policy on Historic Environment and Culture, Conservation and Heritage (CS20) (CS2) (SHLAA) The proposed site is next to the Blaby Conservation Area which is also designated an 'open area of importance to the form and character of the built environment.'  The proposed development is so close to the Conservation Area it would have a very adverse impact on the area and would be against policy on Historic Environment and Culture (CS20) which seeks to preserve and enhance the cultural heritage of the District and states that proposed development should avoid harm to the significance of historic sites, buildings or areas, including their setting.  Blaby's Bouskell Park which is part of the Conservation Area and just a few metres from the proposed housing site is regarded as the best historical site in the District. Heritage potential  Leicestershire County Council has classified the heritage potential of the proposed site as High (Grade 1). It is immediately adjacent to the site of a medieval village ' the original settlement of Blaby.  The Victorian Ice House (Grade II listed) and pond in Bouskell Park will loose all sense of place and context if they are just a few metres from a modern housing estate.  No amount of interpretative panels and new infrastructure would be able to compensate for this fundamental and irretrievable loss of setting and context.  Change of character.  If the proposed development went ahead it would isolate Long Walk from the surrounding countryside and it is then likely that it would become unpopular with many users who use it extensively at present.  It could easily become an unattractive wooded 'back ally' in the centre of a housing estate which could attract fly tipping and anti-social behaviour.   NPPF Para 118.  When determining planning applications, local planning authorities should aim to conserve and enhance biodiversity by applying the following principles:  If significant harm resulting from a development cannot be avoided (through locating on an alternative site with less harmful impacts), adequately mitigated, or, as a last resort, compensated for, then planning permission should be refused.  The estate provides corridors for wildlife that we think play an important role in the wider wildlife context of the area. (see 2008 Phase 1 Habitat Survey for details) The area is quite special and possibly unique in this region to the south of Leicester which is relatively poor in good habitat compared with many other parts of the county.   Please count my letter as TWO objections.

Name: Dean Lang
CommentOriginal: The proposed site is designated as countryside and the development is not supported by the planning policy on countryside. (CS18) This development will have a significant adverse effect on the landscape and neighbouring conservation area and Bouskell Park. This development would constitute a loss of valuable green space. Blaby residents have a right to access to local open spaces as this contributes to their quality of life. The site is crossed by footpaths, Long Walk, a cycle way and bridle way and is extensively used by local people for recreation activities including walking, running, dog walking etc. The proposal runs counter to the recommendations of the Blaby District Landscape Assessment. Blaby District already have a 5 year supply of deliverable housing sites to meet the district's requirement for new housing. A development of this size and in this proposed location is not justified by the outstanding housing requirement numbers for Blaby as defined in Policy CS5 (Housing distribution). The development will have an adverse effect on local wildlife and the proposed site is home to both badgers and bats which are both protected species. The local plan core strategy does not support this development. This could impact on future strategies within Blaby. This development will increase the risk of flooding locally and possibly beyond. There are areas within the local area which are already prone to flooding. The additional traffic on Hospital Lane will be unacceptable. `the traffic at peak times in this area is already too heavy and it can take several minutes to cross the road at busy times. An increase in traffic will also have an effect on the air quality. The local infrastructure cannot adequately support the additional residents. People including my family moved to Blaby specifically because of the immediate access to the countryside and this particular area is used by us on a daily basis and this development would constitute a deterioration in our quality of life. Name: Mr Roger Barnett
CommentOriginal: I wish to object to this planning application Application Reference S62A/2014/0001/Hospital Lane Blaby  I think the attractive area behind Bouskell Park with the beautiful Long Walk woodland walk and very well used network of paths should be protected and not turned into a large housing estate.  I think it is clear that this proposal will have a significantly adverse effect on the landscape, in particular the appearance and setting of the Blaby Conservation Area, especially Bouskell Park which has an essentially rural parkland character with a strong perceived connection with the wider countryside.  This proposed development would severely degrade Bouskell Park's rural character and its perceived connection to the wider countryside.                                                                      The proposal runs counter to the recommendations of the Blaby District Landscape and Settlement Character Assessment (LSCA) which has an important role in assessing the effect a development would have on the countryside's landscape.                                                        Blaby District Council already have a 5 year supply of deliverable housing sites (as defined by the NPPF) to meet the District's requirements for new housing, so it is not necessary to support development proposals that do not align with planning policy.                                                       A development of this size (over 200 dwellings) in this location is not justified by the outstanding housing requirement numbers for Blaby defined in Policy CS5, Housing Distribution.  The proposed development is so close to the Conservation Area it would have a very adverse impact on the area and would be against policy on Historic Environment and Culture (CS20) which seeks to preserve and enhance the cultural heritage of the District and states that proposed development should avoid harm to the significance of historic sites, buildings or areas, including their setting.                                                                                    The proposed development would have a significant negative impact on existing wildlife corridors and the wildlife habitat in and around Bouskell Park which is part of the Conservation Area.  The Strategic Housing Land Availability Assessment (SHLAA) also emphasises the importance of considering the impact any proposed development would have on the Conservation area.                                                                                       Blaby's Bouskell Park which is part of the Conservation Area and just a few metres from the proposed housing site is regarded as the best historical site in the District.                             The Victorian Ice House (Grade II listed) and pond in Bouskell Park will loose all sense of place and context if they are just a few metres from a modern housing estate.    The proposed development on this site is not consistent with policy on Green Infrastructure (CS14). The site is crossed by a popular wooded permissive path (Long Walk), footpaths, a bridleway and a National Cycle Route (Guthlaxton Trail). It is an area loved and enjoyed by many local residents.   The government have decided to protect 'green space of special importance to local communities,' now called Local Green Spaces (LGS).  This popular and very attractive area falls into this category and meets all the LGS selection criteria defined in the NPPF.  LGS status for the Long Walk area has the overwhelming backing of the community.                                                                             Blaby District Green Space Strategy:- refers to the NPPF 'Existing green spaces should not be built on unless they are surplus to requirements and losses are replaced with equivalent or better provision in terms of quantity and quality '  The application proposes a substantial development on this site that will have a significant impact on the future development of Blaby.  If an outline planning application is approved prior to adoption of the Delivery DPD and the Neighbourhood Plan it could prejudice the DPD by predetermining decisions about the scale and location of new development which are being addressed in the DPD.  In view of this, this application is considered to be premature and potentially prejudicial to emerging plans.   Impact on local flooding risk:' the Hall Farm site is close to a floodplain and historically Blaby has had a problem with repeated flooding. It is not unusual for flooding of the River Sence and its tributaries to affect the road connections to Leicester, especially at Crow Mills at South Wigston and the A426 between Blaby and Glen Parva, resulting in severe road congestion in and around Whetstone, Blaby and Wigston as motorists attempt to find alternative routes. An extra 200 plus houses to the east of Blaby off Hospital Lane would make the situation worse, firstly because of the extra traffic that would discharge into Hospital Lane and secondly increased water run-off rate from the site following extreme weather could increase the severity and frequency of flooding.

Name: Kathryn Trudi Smith
CommentOriginal: I absolutely object to the planning proposals for the area behind Bouskell Park. There are many reasons why I believe this attractive area with the beautiful Long Walk woodland walk and very well used network of paths should be protected and not turned into a large housing estate.  This application is totally misplaced.  The number of houses that need to be built in Blaby by 2026 has already been exceeded by 26. A development of 220 houses in this location would exceed the calculated housing requirement of 420, by 40%. Here are the reasons for my objection: 1. Planning Policy on Countryside & the Requirement for New Housing (CS18) (CS5) (LSCA) (NPPF) '	The site is designated as Countryside and this development proposal is not supported by planning policy on Countryside (CS18), which states that  'Within areas designated as Countryside, planning permission will not be granted for built development, or other development which would have a significantly adverse effect on the appearance or character of the landscape.' '	I think it is clear that this proposal will have a significantly adverse effect on the landscape, in particular the appearance and setting of the Blaby Conservation Area, especially Bouskell Park which has an essentially rural parkland character with a strong perceived connection with the wider countryside.  This proposed development would severely degrade Bouskell Park's rural character and its perceived connection to the wider countryside. '	 The proposal runs counter to the recommendations of the Blaby District Landscape and Settlement Character Assessment (LSCA) which has an important role in assessing the effect a development would have on the countryside's landscape. '	Blaby District Council already have a 5 year supply of deliverable housing sites (as defined by the NPPF) to meet the District's requirements for new housing, so it is not necessary to support development proposals that do not align with planning policy. '	A development of this size (over 200 dwellings) in this location is not justified by the outstanding housing requirement numbers for Blaby defined in Policy CS5, Housing Distribution. 2. Policy on Historic Environment and Culture, Conservation and Heritage (CS20) (CS2) (SHLAA) '	The proposed site is next to the Blaby Conservation Area which is also designated an 'open area of importance to the form and character of the built environment.'  The proposed development is so close to the Conservation Area it would have a very adverse impact on the area and would be against policy on Historic Environment and Culture (CS20) which seeks to preserve and enhance the cultural heritage of the District and states that proposed development should avoid harm to the significance of historic sites, buildings or areas, including their setting. '	Policy CS2 ' Design of New Development has as one of its objectives 'to protect the important areas of the District's natural environment (species and habitats), landscape and geology and to improve biodiversity, wildlife habitats and corridors through the design of new developments''.  The proposed development would have a significant negative impact on existing wildlife corridors and the wildlife habitat in and around Bouskell Park which is part of the Conservation Area.  The Strategic Housing Land Availability Assessment (SHLAA) also emphasises the importance of considering the impact any proposed development would have on the Conservation Area. '	The following three objection points relate directly to these planning policies. 1.	Blaby's Bouskell Park which is part of the Conservation Area and just a few metres from the proposed housing site is regarded as the best historical site in the District. 2.	Leicestershire County Council has classified the heritage potential of the proposed site as High (Grade 1). It is immediately adjacent to the site of a medieval village ' the original settlement of Blaby. 3.	 The Victorian Ice House (Grade II listed) and pond in Bouskell Park will loose all sense of place and context if they are just a few metres from a modern housing estate.  We believe that no amount of interpretative panels and new infrastructure would be able to compensate for this fundamental and irretrievable loss of setting and context. 3. Loss of Valuable Green Space & Infrastructure (CS14) (CS15) '	The proposed development on this site is not consistent with policy on Green Infrastructure (CS14). The site is crossed by a popular wooded permissive path (Long Walk), footpaths, a bridleway and a National Cycle Route (Guthlaxton Trail). It is an area loved and enjoyed by many local residents. In addition visitors travel from across the District and in some cases from across the Country to enjoy the area and explore the District's heritage. The government have decided to protect 'green space of special importance to local communities,' now called Local Green Spaces (LGS) in the NPPF (para. 76 ' 77).  This popular and very attractive area falls into this category and meets all the LGS selection criteria defined in the NPPF.  LGS status for the Long Walk area has the overwhelming backing of the community. '	Policy on Open Spaces, Sport and Recreation (CS15) seeks to ensure that all residents have access to sufficient, high quality, accessible open space, sport and recreation facilities.  It states that existing open space, sport and recreation facilities will be protected, and where possible enhanced. Where development is proposed on existing open space, sport and recreation facilities, land should not be released, either in total or in part unless it can be demonstrated that it is surplus to requirements for its current play and open space function. The Local Plan CS (Issues, problems and challenges facing the District) para. 4.3 states that, 'A recent survey of play and open spaces has indicated that the District is broadly lacking in these facilities.' We believe that this site is clearly a very high quality and valuable open space that is not at all surplus to requirements. '	Blaby District Green Space Strategy:- refers to the NPPF 'Existing green spaces should not be built on unless they are surplus to requirements and losses are replaced with equivalent or better provision in terms of quantity and quality (NPPF, paragraph 74).' Policy CS14 Green Infrastructure 6.19.  Policy CS2 is also relevant.  4. Prematurity of this Application with regard to Local Green Space Designation '	This application as premature as it could prejudice emerging plans.  The adopted Local Plan Core Strategy does not support a housing development on this site.  Moreover, especially relevant to this application is that there is widespread support for designating the area around Long Walk as a Local Green Space (LGS) as defined in the NPPF. '	The call for LGS designation of this site is supported by local residents, the L&R Wildlife Trust, the RSPB, walking groups, the Leicestershire Footpaths Association, Natural England, local Parish Councils and many District / County Councillors. '	Site specific planning issues such as LGS designation are covered by the emerging Local Plan Delivery DPD (previously called the Allocations, Designations and Development Management DPD) and also the Neighbourhood Plan being prepared by Blaby Parish Council.  Blaby Parish Council have indicated that they seek to protect this special Green Space in the Neighbourhood Plan. In view of this, this application is considered to be premature and potentially prejudicial to emerging plans.  5. Flood Risk & Climate Change '	Impact on local flooding risk:' the Hall Farm site is close to a floodplain and historically Blaby has had a problem with repeated flooding. We are told that because of climate changes we are to expect more frequent extreme weather events that could lead to localised flooding. Large scale building on the site could compromise flood prevention and mitigation measures and result in increased local flooding risk on the site and more importantly elsewhere. Policy on Climate Change (CS21) and the NPPF refer to the importance of good site selection for new development. '	It is not unusual for flooding of the River Sence and its tributaries to affect the road connections to Leicester, especially at Crow Mills at South Wigston and the A426 between Blaby and Glen Parva, resulting in severe road congestion in and around Whetstone, Blaby and Wigston as motorists attempt to find alternative routes. CommentOriginal: Dear Sir, I wish to object in the strongest terms to the proposed development at Hospital Lane,  Blaby. The people of Blaby make great use of the park and paths around - especially the paths through the woods where wildlife exists to be seen in abundance. To remove this facility would be detrimental to the area and destroy the simple pleasures of a visit to the countryside enjoyed by walkers and families,  which are already on our doorstep. Concreting over more acres of countryside will add to the urban sprawl and  increase the risk of flooding,  as we are near to a flood plain. Blaby already has two building developments nearby,  has a new smaller, development in the centre and should not be subjected to further building.  There are enough houses here. Traffic congestion is bad already. The Hospital Lane is already congested by people going to and returning from work.  Further traffic would generate an impossible situation due to having too few roads to carry more traffic.  The A426 has been reduced in size by bus lanes and simply cannot take more cars thus adding to traffic backing up into Blaby.  The number of extra homes would also inflict great harm on the local schools.  A possible further 600 children on top of the existing and new developments would,  in my opinion, be catastrophic. I sincerely hope that common sense prevails and that this scheme is rejected. Yours faithfully, M.F. Nelson-Judd.

Name: Colin Dickson
CommentOriginal: The proposed development on this site is not consistent with policy on Green Infrastructure (CS14). The site is crossed by a popular wooded permissive path (Long Walk), footpaths, a bridleway and a National Cycle Route (Guthlaxton Trail). It is an area loved and enjoyed by many local residents. In addition visitors travel from across the District and in some cases from across the Country to enjoy the area and explore the District's heritage. The government have decided to protect 'green space of special importance to local communities,' now called Local Green Spaces (LGS) in the NPPF (para. 76 ' 77).  This popular and very attractive area falls into this category and meets all the LGS selection criteria defined in the NPPF.  LGS status for the Long Walk area has the overwhelming backing of the community. Policy on Open Spaces, Sport and Recreation (CS15) seeks to ensure that all residents have access to sufficient, high quality, accessible open space, sport and recreation facilities.  It states that existing open space, sport and recreation facilities will be protected, and where possible enhanced. Where development is proposed on existing open space, sport and recreation facilities, land should not be released, either in total or in part unless it can be demonstrated that it is surplus to requirements for its current play and open space function. The Local Plan CS (Issues, problems and challenges facing the District) para. 4.3 states that, 'A recent survey of play and open spaces has indicated that the District is broadly lacking in these facilities.' We believe that this site is clearly a very high quality and valuable open space that is not at all surplus to requirements. Blaby District Green Space Strategy:- refers to the NPPF 'Existing green spaces should not be built on unless they are surplus to requirements and losses are replaced with equivalent or better provision in terms of quantity and quality (NPPF, paragraph 74).' Policy CS14 Green Infrastructure 6.19.  Policy CS2 is also relevant.

Name: Sue Jordan
CommentOriginal: I am very upset about the proposal to build in the historic centre of Blaby.  This area is a lovely green area, which gives Blaby a feeling of being in the countryside.  The council has already agreed to allow a large scale development at Lubbesthorpe and smaller developments on nearly every field or open space in the area. We have sufficient new houses in the area (Blaby DC has a 5 year supply of new housing).  I walk my dog in the Long Walk/ Bouskell Park every day - it is the only suitable area nearby - several people from Countesthorpe also use the area as developments have been built on every green area in that village.   Being on the edge of the old part of Blaby and the edge of Blaby Conservation Area it gives an appreciation of what Blaby may have been like in the past - if it was surrounded by houses this would not be so. This sense of history would totally disappear if the area were surrounded by houses and we would never get it back.  It also allows one to get away from the hustle and bustle to somewhere peaceful without having to drive - this would be totally ruined if the area were surrounded by houses. This proposal runs counter to the Blaby District Landscape and Character Assessment.   I am also concerned that as every green space is being built on there will be a bigger problem with flooding - there is already a flooding problem at Crow Mills every time is rains heavily.  Building further houses so close and concreting over the fields can only make the problem worse.  Traffic congestion is already a problem in Blaby on Hospital Lane, Winchester Rd and also the roundabout by Northfield Park.  Also to drive into Leicester at peak times is horrendous at the moment - the houses under construction at the moment will only add to this.  A development of this size could only make it much worse.  There are no bus routes in that part of Blaby. I feel that if this development were allowed to go ahead it would totally ruin the feel of the village of Blaby and would destroy the only green space nearby, causing the destruction of the habitat for wildlife and birds such as badgers, bats and other species. I understand that the majority of the people in Blaby are against this development and would ask that the area that is loved by so many people is not destroyed by a development that is not needed in the area.

CommentOriginal: I am writing to object to this development on a number of reasons.  This piece of land is used by my family and hundreds of members of the local community on a regular basis as a piece of countryside and open land. Whether it is by people walking, cycling, horse riding or exploring the area for its nature value it would be desperately sad to lose this Local Green Space  / piece of natural countryside as any recreational resource which is put in its place would not enhance the experience for the users. We do not want a walk / bridleway that is left in situ but surrounded by houses. We want a walk in the local countryside that is on our doorstep with views of the local countryside.  Indeed in planning legislation it states: Planning Policy on Countryside & the Requirement for New Housing (CS18) (CS5) (LSCA) (NPPF) The site is designated as Countryside and this development proposal is not supported by planning policy on Countryside (CS18), which states that  'Within areas designated as Countryside, planning permission will not be granted for built development, or other development which would have a significantly adverse effect on the appearance or character of the landscape.' Indeed in the Planning Inspectorate's pre application letter it states: The site is well-used by the local community for recreational purposes. The cycle path, footpath and permissive paths provide a recreational resource. The attraction of this resource is influenced by the rural, undeveloped, setting providing the community with access to the countryside. The proposed development would undoubtedly have an impact on the setting of the routes and the experience of the users.  It also states in the Planning Inspectorate's pre planning letter: The proposal would provide for all the routes to be retained. Nevertheless the largely undeveloped character of the area will be eroded. The undeveloped character of the site is an intrinsic element of the recreation resource. The erosion of this would have an adverse effect on the appearance and character of the countryside when experienced from the footpaths. Therefore there would be harm to the recreational value of the site.  My main point of objection though is that it would significantly impact on the life of my physically and mentally disabled son. He is 7 years old and we as a family have used the bridleway since he was aged approximately 4 years old as a way for him to be able to access the countryside. The bridleway has a tarmac surface covering which enabled him to use his wheeled walking frame and be able to walk in the countryside on his doorstep. Other paths in the district are not tarmac but gravel or mud which cause problems for the wheels. Evidence for this is that I did contact Leicestershire County Council to get the Bridleway cleaned  up after a local farmer left it covered in mud a while ago - which they did.   Now that he has learnt how to walk he needs a completely flat surface or he falls over with the slightest bump in the surface. He loves to look at the lovely open countryside and enjoys looking at the local plants, trees and wildlife in this lovely area. Due to the lack of traffic he can be allowed to walk freely and independently which enhances his enjoyment of the Local Green Space. We as a family find that this is a unique resource - we have found no other walk in the local area that offers this resource for our son and means that we as a family have a greater sense of health and well being as we can easily go out for walks together in the countryside.  Indeed Blaby District Council states: ' 'Our parks and open spaces provide visual breaks in the built environment and contribute to the health of the local residents by creating clean and attractive environments that provide opportunities for a wide range of formal and informal leisure, sport, recreational and play for all ages, as well as offering other social benefits such as community cohesion, learning and development.'   Also planning policy says:  Loss of Valuable Green Space & Infrastructure (CS14) (CS15) Blaby District Green Space Strategy:- refers to the NPPF 'Existing green spaces should not be built on unless they are surplus to requirements and losses are replaced with equivalent or better provision in terms of quantity and quality (NPPF, paragraph 74).' Policy CS14 Green Infrastructure 6.19.  Policy CS2 is also relevant.  Additionally I am against the location of this housing development as Blaby District Council has already exceeded the provision of housing needed for their 5 year plan.  I hope that you will take note of my points and agree that the development should be stopped and the mental and physical well being of the local people should take priority.

Name: Sharon Marriott
CommentOriginal: The following objection is for planning application number S62A/2014/0001 Hospital Lane Blaby.  The number of houses that need to be built in Blaby by 2026 has already been exceeded by 26. A further development of 220 houses in this location would exceed that calculated housing requirement by40%. Blaby district council has already demonstrated a 5 year land supply to meet the districts requirements for new housing. It is therefore unnecessary to support a devlopment that is unsustainable. and does not align with the local and national palnning policies. The development would border on the conservation area and the victorian ice house (grade 11listed) and the pond in Bouskell will loose all sense of context if they are a few metres away from a housing estate. According to the strategic land housing availability assessment Leicestershire County Council has classified the heritage potential of this site as high (grade 1). The development will cause major transport problems with in the area. Hospital Lane is already congested through out the day. This will place children at huge risk that attend Thistley Meadow school. Hospital Lane and the surrounding roads do not have the capicity to accomadate any extra cars that will be in the area if this development goes ahead. The development will create a flood risk. As the north of Hall farm estate site is very close to a floodpalin and other parts of the site are at risk of surface water flooding.

Name: Jane Toon
CommentOriginal: My family and I strongly object to this residential development at Hospital Lane, Blaby.   This area is well used by many local residents of all age groups.  Such a development would significantly affect the appearance and setting of Bouskell Park, where there is also a Listed Victorian Ice House and pond, and which is also on the edge of the Blaby Conservation Area. The cemetery is in very close proximity, and currently a very peaceful and tranquil area, these areas would be ruined by such a development.  According to Blaby's policy a development of 220 houses in this location would exceed the calculated housing requirement by 40%. They have already demonstrated a 5 year Land Supply for new housing, therefore such a development is unsustainable and does not accord with the Local and National Planning policies.    This development would also have an adverse effect on the current schools and doctors facilities in the area, where they are already struggling to cope with numbers.  This area of countryside is also home to many wildlife species. These species should be protected from development. A housing estate on this site would isolate these habitats and their natural environment.  Open countryside should be protected.  This area of road network already has a high volume of traffic and at peak travelling times is already severely congested along the main Lutterworth Road/Soar Valley Way and Enderby Road, Whetstone, with no capacity for the increased traffic that would be caused by a development of such a size.  Public transport in this area also have no links to any existing or planned employment areas within the District.  Development on this site should be strongly resisted!

Name: Mrs Kathleen Barnett
CommentOriginal: Application Reference S62A/2014/0001/Hospital Lane Blaby I wish to object to this planning application  I think the attractive area behind Bouskell Park with the beautiful Long Walk woodland walk and very well used network of paths should be protected and not turned into a large housing estate. The development is  close to the Conservation Area it would have a impact on the area.                                                                                       The proposed development would have a significant negative impact on existing wildlife corridors and the wildlife habitat in and around Bouskell Park which is part of the Conservation Area.                                                                                     Blaby's Bouskell Park which is part of the Conservation Area and just a few metres from the proposed housing site is regarded as the best historical site in the District.                             The Victorian Ice House (Grade II listed) and pond in Bouskell Park will loose all sense of place and context if they are just a few metres from a modern housing estate.  The site is crossed by a popular wooded permissive path (Long Walk), footpaths, a bridleway and a National Cycle Route (Guthlaxton Trail). It is an area loved and enjoyed by many local residents.  The government have decided to protect 'green space of special importance to local communities,'  This popular and very attractive area falls into this category, the Long Walk area has the overwhelming backing of the community.                                                                                                                                The application proposes a substantial development on this site that will have a significant impact on the future development of Blaby.  If an outline planning application is approved prior to adoption of the Delivery DPD and the Neighbourhood Plan it could prejudice the DPD by predetermining decisions about the scale and location of new development which are being addressed in the DPD.  In view of this, this application is considered to be premature and potentially prejudicial to emerging plans.  Impact on local flooding risk:' the Hall Farm site is close to a floodplain and historically Blaby has had a problem with repeated flooding. It is not unusual for flooding of the River Sence and its tributaries to affect the road connections to Leicester, especially at Crow Mills at South Wigston and the A426 between Blaby and Glen Parva, resulting in severe road congestion in and around Whetstone, Blaby and Wigston as motorists attempt to find alternative routes. An extra 200 plus houses to the east of Blaby off Hospital Lane would make the situation worse, firstly because of the extra traffic that would discharge into Hospital Lane and secondly increased water run-off rate from the site following extreme weather could increase the severity and frequency of flooding. I think it is clear that this proposal will have a significantly adverse effect on the landscape, in particular the appearance and setting of the Blaby Conservation Area, especially Bouskell Park which has an essentially rural parkland character with a strong perceived connection with the wider countryside.  This proposed development would severely degrade Bouskell Park's rural character and its perceived connection to the wider countryside.                                                                            Blaby District Council already have a 5 year supply of deliverable housing sites (as defined by the NPPF) to meet the District's requirements for new housing, so it is not necessary to support development proposals that do not align with planning policy.                                                       A development of this size (over 200 dwellings) in this location is not justified by the outstanding housing requirement numbers for Blaby

Name: Rebecca James
CommentOriginal: I am writing regarding the proposed housing development on Hospital Lane, Blaby.  I have been a resident of Blaby for 18 years and the green spaces around Mill Lane, Bouskell Park and the Long Walk were a major factor in our decision to move here.  During this time I have seen that these spaces are extremely well-used and popular.  To build on this site would have a detrimental affect on all three of the areas mentioned.  As such the development cannot be consistent with policy on valuable green space and infrastructure (CS14 and CS15).  Green space of special importance to local communities (LGS) is, say the government, to be protected and this well-loved area meets the criteria for LGS status.  Whilst helping at Thistly Meadow Primary School's 'Into the Woods' experiences I saw the enormous, positive impact of the woodland environment on a diverse range of children.  Their faces as they watched sparrowhawk chicks fed in their nest (through a telescope) were wonderful.  As a protected species the sparrowhawks' immediate environment would be radically altered by these proposals.   Furthermore, the site is designated as Countryside and the proposed development is not supported by planning policy on Countryside (CS18) which states that "With-in areas designated as Countryside, planning permission will not be granted for built development... which would have a significantly adverse effect on the appearance or character of the landscape."  Although Mill Lane and Long Walk and the little wood behind Thistly Meadow would still be there if this development were to go ahead their "appearance and character" would certainly be very adversely affected.  The tree-and-sky horizon that surrounds the children of Thistly Meadow Primary School and the many frequent users of this wonderful green space would be lost.    It is difficult to talk of the value of the existing environment as it is not objective or measurable.  However, it is real.  The area is well used and irreplaceably valuable to the mental and physical health and well-being of the people of Blaby.  I strongly support LGS status for Long Walk, Bouskell Park and the surrounding areas to protect them for future generations.    As such, I respectfully state my strong objections to building on this very precious pocket of Countryside.    Yours faithfully, Rebecca James
