Name: Miss Sophie Bevin
CommentOriginal: Dear Sir or Madam,  Re: S62A/2014/0001/Hospital Lane Blaby  I write in response to Gladman Developments Ltd's planning application as above and oppose it on the following grounds:  1.  Traffic Problems  (a) Local congestion  Surrounding roads already suffer considerable congestion at peak times.  In particular, the mini-roundabout at the west end of Hospital Lane and the T-junction at the east end of Hospital Lane are already troublesome to navigate at peak times.  (b) Neighbouring congestion  The increased population would have a 'knock-on' effect on the surrounding routes, further congesting the roads out of Blaby towards Leicester and South Wigston and towards Countesthorpe and Cosby.  (c) Width of Hospital Lane  Hospital Lane is a narrow road and struggles with its existing burden.  Construction traffic would cause flow problems for the duration of the construction, particularly if large vehicles struggle to access the site.  (d) Health  Increased traffic fumes, brick dust and other construction debris will detract from the health of (i) local residents and (ii) primary school children and staff who attend Thistly Meadow Primary School nearby.  (e) Safety  Increased construction and thereafter traffic will pose a threat to the school children's safety.  Visibility (pedestrians Vs vehicles) is also an issue on Hospital Lane.  2.  Existing sufficient commitment to house building in Blaby  (a) Blaby District Council (BDC) has committed to building 26 more houses than is required by 2026, so a development of 220 houses exceeds the predicted housing requirement by 40%, rendering this development excessive.  (b) BDC has demonstrated a 5 year land supply to meet the district's requirement for housing, so will be able to meet its targets without this development.  3.  Policy conflict ' 'Green Space, Landscape and Setting'  (a) BDC's core strategy CS14 seeks to 'protect existing'networks of multi-functional green spaces' which describes this area which is well used by local residents.  (b) Policy CS15 states 'existing open space, sport and recreation facilities will be protected'.  A large housing development located so close to the Long Walk pathway and Bouskell Park does not protect open space, it changes it comprehensively and adversely.  For us, it's like someone building apartments surrounding Nelson's Column and claiming 'it's still visible, we haven't harmed it'.  (c) Policy CS18 details how the Blaby District Landscape and Settlement Character Assessment states 'development on this site should be resisted'  (d) Policy CS15 also notes the area has been widely nominated as 'Local Green Space' in the Development Plan Document.  (e) Policy CS19 aims to 'protect the important areas of the District's natural environment (species and habitats), landscape and geology'.  Development would cause total disruption to local wildlife such as birds, voles, bats and an array of hedgerow-dwelling species, already in decline due to urbanisation, such as bees and butterflies, adversely impacting on the local ecosystem.  (f) BDC's core strategy also states 'The Council will seek to maintain networks of natural habitats'by avoiding or repairing the fragmentation and isolation of natural habitats.  These networks should be protected from development.'  Noise and light pollution from a housing development would continue to deter wildlife once completed and even more so during construction.  4.  Policy conflict ' 'Historic Environment and Culture'  (a) BDC's core strategy aims to 'preserve and enhance the cultural heritage of the District'.  The proposed development is too close to the conservation area, including the Grade II listed Victorian Ice House and pond.  Building right up to the edges of these features makes a mockery of claiming to protect and preserve them.  (b) Leicester City Council's Strategic Land Housing Availability Assessment classifies the heritage potential of this site as 'High (Grade 1)'  5.  Increased risk of flooding  (CS21 (Core strategy on Climate Change) and the NPPF note the importance of sound development site selection regarding flood minimization.  The north of the Hall Farm site is very close to a floodplain and other parts of the site are at high risk of surface water flooding.  Reducing the available surface area of land for rainwater absorption by building on it will increase the risk of flooding. Hospital Lane has been a frequently flooded road in the past.  6.  Health and wellbeing  Walking is one of the simplest and cheapest ways to reduce the likelihood of developing obesity, high blood pressure and diabetes.  Developing this area and permanently reducing the natural habitat and open space of the area will deter people from using Long Walk and gaining all the physical and psychological benefits from 'a walk in the countryside', which can currently be done for local residents without the need of a car and burning precious fuel.  7.  Permanency   If Hall Farm is built on, the open space is lost forever and the natural habitat will never have the chance to recover.  There are brown sites and derelict sites nearby and it should be absolutely essential to prioritise 'already built on' sites for housing development before unused land is considered.   I hope you will give these points due consideration.  Please note I would like to be informed of the date, location and time of any hearing proceedings, should they occur.  Yours faithfully,  Miss Sophie Bevin BSc (Hons) Ost Med

Name: Katherine Staples
CommentOriginal: The objections for this planning proposal on green belt land in Blaby are endless. I have yet to realise or be told of a single positive for this development. This is green belt land. It is land that is enjoyed by masses of people all day long. It allows locals to have a quality of life by enjoying the countryside, the wildlife and the tranquillity of the area. Blaby has already been built on from every other side, there is a bypass along one side and commuters already use Blaby as a rat run. This green belt land is all that is left before Blaby becomes a concrete suburb rather than a green village. The people of Blaby are not making up these objections, they are true. If this planning were to go ahead it will dramatically alter the quality of life that Blaby currently offers to such a detrimental effect. Please listen to the people of Blaby who ACTUALLY LIVE IN THE AREA. The list begins: Blaby District Council has addressed its 5 year land supply of new housing sufficiently in alignment with the local and national planning policies. Blaby has already exceeded its housing requirements until 2026 by 22 houses. This development will exceed the required housing by 40%. Blaby will lose its only remaining green space that is used by people of all ages. This space is not surplus to requirements, it is all that we have. People walk themselves, their children, their dogs, ride horses, bikes, it is used ALL DAY LONG as a recreation green space. A conservation area surrounds this planning application. 220 houses will dramatically affect the conservation area and the setting that it sits. The area is so important for wildlife and geology of the area including owls, bats, woodpeckers, badgers, ducks, rabbits squirrels, deer, pheasants, the list is endless. A housing estate will destroy the natural habitat of the wildlife, noise and light pollution will deter the wildlife.  Bouskell Park borders and leads onto the proposed area. The Ice House is on the park, this Is a listed building with a pond with ducks, squirrels, rabbits, woodpeckers and owls. The noise and destruction from a building site which would be right next to the ice house and pond would scare away the existing wildlife. The area needs to be cherished and preserved not destroyed. The strategic land housing availability assessment from Leicestershire County Council has classified the heritage potential of this area as high. Blaby is a bottle neck at peak times. It is becoming incredibly hard to cross the local roads safely due to the speed and amount of cars already bypassing or driving through Blaby. It is unimaginable to think what an extra 220 houses and their cars would add to the local traffic.  Has anybody from the developers considered how this housing estate will affect Blaby re congestion, schooling places, doctors surgeries, dentists?  There are no public transport links to the proposed site which means that the majority of potential occupants will use their cars to go everywhere. Blaby has always flooded with exception of the several years when England was drier than normal. In the last 2 years it has flooded many times. This proposed site is right next to the flood plain. By concreting this area it will force water to drain away from the estate and cause additional flood problems on the flood plain. When it does flood in Blaby  it floods the roads including the main road into Blaby and South Wigston and Whetstone. As I'm sure you don't know the area, the 3 main points of flooding are the only 3 main roads in and out of Blaby. Blaby becomes gridlocked and believe me any additional water that isn't allowed to drain into the ground will flow directly to the flood plain. The flood plain is only a single lanes width away from one of the boundaries of this planning application.  Another boundary of this application sits alongside the cemetery. My husband and myself had the horrendous decision of where to bury our young son. We chose close to the Long Walk and the woods because that is where our son spent most of his life playing, walking and cycling. To have a housing estate overlooking his grave is completely unthinkable. This application does not affect you as you do not live in Blaby, it affects everybody who lives in Blaby. There are so many other suitable sites for building on, this is not one of them. This development is all about money to Leicestershire County Council and the deveolpers. Money cannot buy wildlife and natural green space. Once the green space is destroyed it can never be claimed back. Please consider all of the objections to this planning application very carefully as you will be making decisions that affect Blaby forever. I would like a response from somebody in answer to all of these objections. I would like somebody to tell me why it is beneficial for this development to go ahead. Please listen to the people of Blaby who ACTUALLY LIVE THERE. Thank you.

Name: Nicola Wilson
CommentOriginal: I have lived in the village of Blaby for many years and we chose to live here because of the village atmosphere.   This is due to the fact that the village is not just a continuation of Leicester city, which now strectches 5 miles from the centre to Glen Parva, but has an area of green surrounding it. Another objection I have is that the village is surrounded by small artery roads - Hospital Lane, Welford Road, Blaby Road Whetstone, Winchester Road and during the 6 months of the year that The bridge at Crow Mills, South Wigston and the bridge at the end of the Blaby bypass flood regularly, there is back log and congestion throughout Blaby, Countesthorpe, South Wigston and Whetstone causing chaios and extremely lengthy delays for drivers and dangerous pavements and places to cross for pedestrians.  Earlier this year, when Crow Mills flooded, the traffic queued from Countesthorpe, all the way down Winchester Road and into Leicester - I have photographic proof.  The area does not have the road capacity, the amenities or the  facilities suitable for such growth and a new 'park' or larger school will not help.  Our village cannot cope with extra traffic.  We have  3 developments in the village already.  The Lubbesthorpe Development in the district means that the districts quota has been met until 2028!  It is the wrong site for housing.  It is a resource used by the whole of South Leicester for recreation, dog walking and regular festivals and fates and it's loss will be a travesty. Also on a less personal level and on a factual level I would like to say that   The Core Strategy states that it seeks to 'protect existing...networks of multi-functional green spaces'.  The site is extremely well used by locals and by those further afield of all ages.  Core Strategy says - existing open space, sport and recreational facilities will be protected'  This open space is unique and not surplus to requirement. The site is designated as Countryside and this development proposal is not supported by planning policy on Countryside (CS18), which states that  'Within areas designated as Countryside, planning permission will not be granted for built development, or other development which would have a significantly adverse effect on the appearance or character of the landscape.' We think it is clear that this proposal will have a significantly adverse effect on the landscape, in particular the appearance and setting of the Blaby Conservation Area, especially Bouskell Park which has an essentially rural parkland character with a strong perceived connection with the wider countryside.  This proposed development would severely degrade Bouskell Park's rural character and its perceived connection to the wider countryside.  The proposal runs counter to the recommendations of the Blaby District Landscape and Settlement Character Assessment (LSCA) which has an important role in assessing the effect a development would have on the countryside's landscape. Blaby District Council already have a 5 year supply of deliverable housing sites (as defined by the NPPF) to meet the District's requirements for new housing, so it is not necessary to support development proposals that do not align with planning policy. A development of this size (over 200 dwellings) in this location is not justified by the outstanding housing requirement numbers for Blaby defined in Policy CS5, Housing Distribution.   The proposed site is next to the Blaby Conservation Area which is also designated an 'open area of importance to the form and character of the built environment.'  The proposed development is so close to the Conservation Area it would have a very adverse impact on the area and would be against policy on Historic Environment and Culture (CS20) which seeks to preserve and enhance the cultural heritage of the District and states that proposed development should avoid harm to the significance of historic sites, buildings or areas, including their setting. Policy CS2 ' Design of New Development has as one of its objectives 'to protect the important areas of the District's natural environment (species and habitats), landscape and geology and to improve biodiversity, wildlife habitats and corridors through the design of new developments''.  The proposed development would have a significant negative impact on existing wildlife corridors and the wildlife habitat in and around Bouskell Park which is part of the Conservation Area.  The Strategic Housing Land Availability Assessment (SHLAA) also emphasises the importance of considering the impact any proposed development would have on the Conservation Area. The following three objection points relate directly to these planning policies. Blaby's Bouskell Park which is part of the Conservation Area and just a few metres from the proposed housing site is regarded as the best historical site in the District. Leicestershire County Council has classified the heritage potential of the proposed site as High (Grade 1). It is immediately adjacent to the site of a medieval village ' the original settlement of Blaby.  The Victorian Ice House (Grade II listed) and pond in Bouskell Park will loose all sense of place and context if they are just a few metres from a modern housing estate.  We believe that no amount of interpretative panels and new infrastructure would be able to compensate for this fundamental and irretrievable loss of setting and context. The proposed development on this site is not consistent with policy on Green Infrastructure (CS14). The site is crossed by a popular wooded permissive path (Long Walk), footpaths, a bridleway and a National Cycle Route (Guthlaxton Trail). It is an area loved and enjoyed by many local residents. In addition visitors travel from across the District and in some cases from across the Country to enjoy the area and explore the District's heritage. The government have decided to protect 'green space of special importance to local communities,' now called Local Green Spaces (LGS) in the NPPF (para. 76 ' 77).  This popular and very attractive area falls into this category and meets all the LGS selection criteria defined in the NPPF.  LGS status for the Long Walk area has the overwhelming backing of the community. Policy on Open Spaces, Sport and Recreation (CS15) seeks to ensure that all residents have access to sufficient, high quality, accessible open space, sport and recreation facilities.  It states that existing open space, sport and recreation facilities will be protected, and where possible enhanced. Where development is proposed on existing open space, sport and recreation facilities, land should not be released, either in total or in part unless it can be demonstrated that it is surplus to requirements for its current play and open space function. The Local Plan CS (Issues, problems and challenges facing the District) para. 4.3 states that, 'A recent survey of play and open spaces has indicated that the District is broadly lacking in these facilities.' We believe that this site is clearly a very high quality and valuable open space that is not at all surplus to requirements. Blaby District Green Space Strategy:- refers to the NPPF 'Existing green spaces should not be built on unless they are surplus to requirements and losses are replaced with equivalent or better provision in terms of quantity and quality (NPPF, paragraph 74).' Policy CS14 Green Infrastructure 6.19.  Policy CS2 is also relevant. We regard this application as premature as it could prejudice emerging plans.  The adopted Local Plan Core Strategy does not support a housing development on this site.  Moreover, especially relevant to this application is that there is widespread support for designating the area around Long Walk as a Local Green Space (LGS) as defined in the NPPF. The call for LGS designation of this site is supported by local residents, the L&R Wildlife Trust, the RSPB, walking groups, the Leicestershire Footpaths Association, Natural England, local Parish Councils and many District / County Councillors. Site specific planning issues such as LGS designation are covered by the emerging Local Plan Delivery DPD (previously called the Allocations, Designations and Development Management DPD) and also the Neighbourhood Plan being prepared by Blaby Parish Council.  Blaby Parish Council have indicated that they seek to protect this special Green Space in the Neighbourhood Plan. The application proposes a substantial development on this site that will have a significant impact on the future development of Blaby.  If an outline planning application is approved prior to adoption of the Delivery DPD and the Neighbourhood Plan it could prejudice the DPD by predetermining decisions about the scale and location of new development which are being addressed in the DPD.  In view of this, this application is considered to be premature and potentially prejudicial to emerging plans. Impact on local flooding risk:' the Hall Farm site is close to a floodplain and historically Blaby has had a problem with repeated flooding. We are told that because of climate changes we are to expect more frequent extreme weather events that could lead to localised flooding. Large scale building on the site could compromise flood prevention and mitigation measures and result in increased local flooding risk on the site and more importantly elsewhere. Policy on Climate Change (CS21) and the NPPF refer to the importance of good site selection for new development. It is not unusual for flooding of the River Sence and its tributaries to affect the road connections to Leicester, especially at Crow Mills at South Wigston and the A426 between Blaby and Glen Parva, resulting in severe road congestion in and around Whetstone, Blaby and Wigston as motorists attempt to find alternative routes. An extra 200 plus houses to the east of Blaby off Hospital Lane would make the situation worse, firstly because of the extra traffic that would discharge into Hospital Lane and secondly increased water run-off rate from the site following extreme weather could increase the severity and frequency of flooding.  We are certainly not opposed to all new development in principle.  The government have decided to devolve more power over planning decisions to local communities (Localism Bill & NPPF). The community think this proposal is a singularly inappropriate and unwelcome development which has wide ranging negative implications for the environment and residents of the District (survey and petition evidence is available). The proposed site is not just another area of green space / countryside on the 'edge of town' ' it is a particularly valuable area with high amenity value to the local community and to a wider community in the region.  It is also described as important to the form and character of the landscape and it has high heritage potential. 'Bouskell Park, the historic Long Walk and the green spaces that surround it form Blaby's breathing space, its green 'Jewel in the Crown,' arguably Blaby's finest asset ' it should be preserved to protect the quality of life of local residents and provide a haven for wildlife.  Its loss would be a tragedy for Blaby on several levels.' 'Bouskell Park is one of the Council's strategic green spaces and we strive to keep improving it.' ' Blaby District Green Space Strategy 2012.  We think it is undeniable that this proposed development will harm Bouskell Park. This outline planning application is opposed by the overwhelming majority of the community, many local Councillors and the Parish Council. This is not a NIMBY protest ' the community want to have a say in shaping their local environment and want to protect this vital green infrastructure as a key part of the settlement of Blaby.' Bouskell Park is a beautiful public park on the site of a 10th century medieval village (the original settlement of Blaby) with a pond and a Victorian Ice House (a Grade II Listed building).  Interpretative panels give visitors the history of the area and the wildlife to be seen.  If the park was to be 'hemmed-in' by housing it would loose much of its amenity value to residents and it would be too small and isolated to be the valuable habitat for wildlife it is at present. If the wooded Long Walk with its very popular permissive path were to be surrounded with an estate of over 200 houses it would result in a considerable reduction in the amenity value of the Long Walk area to local residents and is very strongly opposed by the community. If the proposed development went ahead it would isolate Long Walk from the surrounding countryside and it is then likely that it would become unpopular with many users who use it extensively at present.  It could easily become an unattractive wooded 'back ally' in the centre of a housing estate which could attract fly tipping and anti-social behaviour. Badgers are known to live in the area and the site provides them with good quality foraging habitat and cover (see WYG Blaby District Council: Phase 1 Habitat Survey 2008 ' LDF evidence base). Badgers and their setts are protected under the Protection of Badgers Act 1992. Bats are known to roost close by (possibly the old Hall Farm buildings) and Long Walk is a very important wildlife corridor that provides both feeding habitat and links between other important feeding sites. The Bouskell Park area is used for local 'bat walks' organised by Blaby District Council. 'Bats are poorly catered for in planning development.  Bat boxes are a very poor substitute for the habitat loss which bats often suffer and there is a low occupancy rate. The real issue is usually the loss of bats' feeding areas. They need a large area over which to forage. The loss of the included farmland would be a real loss to the many bats that live and feed on the Hall Farm estate land.  All British bat species and their roosts are legally protected under the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981.' ' a member of the local bat group. There is potential for white-clawed crayfish and possibly water voles in the small brook running parallel to Hospital Lane and further survey work should be performed to assess the potential loss of habitat.  Sometimes the water flow is low, but in recent years it has rarely run dry and 'deeper pools may sustain wildlife during drought.' See the WYG 2008 Phase 1 Habitat Survey reference above.     3. Health and Wellbeing     BDC state on their website that 'Our parks and open spaces provide visual breaks in the built environment and contribute to the health of the local residents by creating clean and attractive environments that provide opportunities for a wide range of formal and informal leisure, sport, recreational and play for all ages, as well as offering other social benefits such as community cohesion, learning and development.'  We agree completely with this statement and believe that a large scale building development on this site would substantially degrade Bouskell Park and the surrounding open spaces that make it a very special and valuable place. 'This a very important area for recreation, sport, leisure and social cohesion within the community. It is regularly used by people from many different parts of the District and further afield (we have survey evidence). Please don't allow it to be spoilt, to do so would be a disgrace to the District and the County of Leicestershire. Instead please give it protection from inappropriate development by making it a special 'Local Green Space' in line with the NPPF' (NPPF para 76 ' 77 refers). The area is used as part of the Blaby Health Walks programme organised by Blaby District Sports Alliance and Blaby District Council aimed at encouraging local people of all ages to take more exercise. 'Blaby Buggy Walks', organised by Blaby District Council use Bouskell Park.  Parents with young children frequently use Long Walk as a safe and healthy way of accessing the countryside. The network of paths which has Bouskell Park and Long Walk at its heart is used by orienteering, walking and running groups and clubs, including Leicestershire & Rutland Walking Group. The proposed development would seriously compromise this centre of health and wellbeing. Blaby scores highly in Quality of Life surveys ' see for example BDC Contact spring 2010 issue ' good access to high quality countryside is an important factor. Many residents have based their decision to move to and live in the district largely because of the easily accessible green spaces. Long Walk behind Bouskell Park is at the heart of this special local green infrastructure. If a housing development of the type and scale proposed was to go ahead, a very likely consequence of the degradation of this green space would be that residents who have the option would get in their cars and drive to more distant areas to enjoy the countryside. Those without that option would loose a valuable opportunity for outdoor exercise and would be severely disadvantaged.     4. Inadequate Local Infrastructure     Local infrastructure is not capable of supporting a development of this size and in this location. We do not think the proposed development is properly sustainable.  The size of the proposed residential development significantly exceeds the residual housing requirement for Blaby as defined by the Local Plan, CS5, Housing distribution. Hospital Lane is already severely congested during peak periods especially at the junction with Leicester Road / Countesthorpe Road to the east of Blaby. Welford Road in Blaby is also now congested at busy times and can be difficult for pedestrians to cross. The proposed development would make the situation a great deal worse in Blaby, Whetstone, Glen Parva, Countesthorpe and South Wigston.     5. Ecology     The unusually wide range of habitats in a relatively small area encourages a rich variety of wildlife. Over 50 species of birds have been reported using Bouskell Park and the surrounding area. We have a list of recent wildlife sightings in and around the park and Long Walk add hyperlink. The different closely connected elements in the area creates an interesting and diverse habitat that encourages a variety of wildlife. On Hall Farm estate itself habitats include, mixed woodland, hedgerows, small areas of young trees and bushes, small areas of scrub, small brooks and a well vegetated pond plus the included farmed estate land which is often used for grass. There is excellent hunting habitat for birds of prey such as owls and kestrels. The immediately adjacent park land of Bouskell contains a pond (next to the Icehouse and less than 30m from the proposed housing development), the Black Spinney and several magnificent protected specimen trees. There is a larger pond close by on private land. Take one part of the habitat mix away and the whole environmental infrastructure would be degraded and could collapse and disappear. The Leicestershire & Rutland Wildlife Trust and the RSPB have recognised the importance of wildlife corridors on the site and the role these play in sustaining a variety of wildlife in the area and increasing the value of the area to visitors. NPPF Para 118. When determining planning applications, local planning authorities should aim to conserve and enhance biodiversity by applying the following principles:  If significant harm resulting from a development cannot be avoided (through locating on an alternative site with less harmful impacts), adequately mitigated, or, as a last resort, compensated for, then planning permission should be refused. The estate provides corridors for wildlife that we think play an important role in the wider wildlife context of the area. (see 2008 Phase 1 Habitat Survey for details) We think that the area is quite special and possibly unique in this region to the south of Leicester which is relatively poor in good habitat compared with many other parts of the county. Policy CS19 Bio-diversity and geo-diversity (page 86) In terms of species protection, the Council will protect those species which do not receive statutory protection under a range of legislative provisions, but have been identified as requiring conservation action as a species of principal importance for the conservation of biodiversity nationally. Any development proposals should ensure that these species and their habitats are protected from the adverse effects of development through the use of appropriate mitigation measures. Policy CS19 Bio-diversity and geo-diversity (page 86) The Council will seek to maintain / extend networks of natural habitats to link sites of biodiversity importance by avoiding or repairing the fragmentation and isolation of natural habitats. These networks should be protected from development.    I would appreciate if if you look very carefully at the proposed application.  Your decision may not affect you, but to me and my family the effects will be profound and once done, cannot ever be undone.  Our quality of life, and the whole landscape and the villages feel and quality will be diminished.   I teach at the local Primary School, our class sizes are at a maximum capacity and have been for years.  We do not have space for more children. Please make the right decision, and the right decision is NO.

CommentOriginal: 1. Planning Policy on Countryside & the Requirement for New Housing (CS18) (CS5) (LSCA) (NPPF)  The site is designated as Countryside and this development proposal is not supported by planning policy on Countryside (CS18), which states that  'Within areas designated as Countryside, planning permission will not be granted for built development, or other development which would have a significantly adverse effect on the appearance or character of the landscape.'   It is clear that this proposal will have a significantly adverse effect on the landscape, in particular the appearance and setting of the Blaby Conservation Area, especially Bouskell Park which has an essentially rural parkland character with a strong perceived connection with the wider countryside.  This proposed development would severely degrade Bouskell Park's rural character and its perceived connection to the wider countryside.  The proposal runs counter to the recommendations of the Blaby District Landscape and Settlement Character Assessment (LSCA) which has an important role in assessing the effect a development would have on the countryside's landscape.  Blaby District Council already have a 5 year supply of deliverable housing sites (as defined by the NPPF) to meet the District's requirements for new housing, so it is not necessary to support development proposals that do not align with planning policy.  A development of this size (over 200 dwellings) in this location is not justified by the outstanding housing requirement numbers for Blaby defined in Policy CS5, Housing Distribution.  2. Policy on Historic Environment and Culture, Conservation and Heritage (CS20) (CS2) (SHLAA)  The proposed site is next to the Blaby Conservation Area which is also designated an 'open area of importance to the form and character of the built environment.'  The proposed development is so close to the Conservation Area it would have a very adverse impact on the area and would be against policy on Historic Environment and Culture (CS20) which seeks to preserve and enhance the cultural heritage of the District and states that proposed development should avoid harm to the significance of historic sites, buildings or areas, including their setting.  Policy CS2 ' Design of New Development has as one of its objectives 'to protect the important areas of the District's natural environment (species and habitats), landscape and geology and to improve biodiversity, wildlife habitats and corridors through the design of new developments''.  The proposed development would have a significant negative impact on existing wildlife corridors and the wildlife habitat in and around Bouskell Park which is part of the Conservation Area.  The Strategic Housing Land Availability Assessment (SHLAA) also emphasises the importance of considering the impact any proposed development would have on the Conservation Area.  Blaby's Bouskell Park which is part of the Conservation Area and just a few metres from the proposed housing site is regarded as the best historical site in the District.  Leicestershire County Council has classified the heritage potential of the proposed site as High (Grade 1). It is immediately adjacent to the site of a medieval village ' the original settlement of Blaby.  The Victorian Ice House (Grade II listed) and pond in Bouskell Park will loose all sense of place and context if they are just a few metres from a modern housing estate.  We believe that no amount of interpretative panels and new infrastructure would be able to compensate for this fundamental and irretrievable loss of setting and context.  3. Loss of Valuable Green Space & Infrastructure (CS14) (CS15)  The proposed development on this site is not consistent with policy on Green Infrastructure (CS14). The site is crossed by a popular wooded permissive path (Long Walk), footpaths, a bridleway and a National Cycle Route (Guthlaxton Trail). It is an area loved and enjoyed by many local residents. In addition visitors travel from across the District and in some cases from across the Country to enjoy the area and explore the District's heritage. The government have decided to protect 'green space of special importance to local communities,' now called Local Green Spaces (LGS) in the NPPF (para. 76 ' 77).  This popular and very attractive area falls into this category and meets all the LGS selection criteria defined in the NPPF.  LGS status for the Long Walk area has the overwhelming backing of the community.  Policy on Open Spaces, Sport and Recreation (CS15) seeks to ensure that all residents have access to sufficient, high quality, accessible open space, sport and recreation facilities.  It states that existing open space, sport and recreation facilities will be protected, and where possible enhanced. Where development is proposed on existing open space, sport and recreation facilities, land should not be released, either in total or in part unless it can be demonstrated that it is surplus to requirements for its current play and open space function. The Local Plan CS (Issues, problems and challenges facing the District) para. 4.3 states that, 'A recent survey of play and open spaces has indicated that the District is broadly lacking in these facilities.' We believe that this site is clearly a very high quality and valuable open space that is not at all surplus to requirements.  Blaby District Green Space Strategy:- refers to the NPPF 'Existing green spaces should not be built on unless they are surplus to requirements and losses are replaced with equivalent or better provision in terms of quantity and quality (NPPF, paragraph 74).' Policy CS14 Green Infrastructure 6.19.  Policy CS2 is also relevant  The lost of this green space will have a personal impact on the lives of those living and visiting Blaby, the area is a much loved area to relax and enjoying walking, cycling and horse riding, once this has gone we can never get it back.  Please reject this application.

The proposed development would have a significant negative impact on existing wildlife corridors and the wildlife habitat in and around Bouskell Park which is part of the Conservation Area.  The Strategic Housing Land Availability Assessment (SHLAA) also emphasises the importance of considering the impact any proposed development would have on the Conservation Area.  Blaby's Bouskell Park which is part of the Conservation Area and just a few metres from the proposed housing site is regarded as the best historical site in the District. Leicestershire County Council has classified the heritage potential of the proposed site as High (Grade 1). It is immediately adjacent to the site of a medieval village  the original settlement of Blaby.  The Victorian Ice House (Grade II listed) and pond in Bouskell Park will lose all sense of place and context if they are just a few metres from a modern housing estate.  I believe that no amount of interpretative panels and new infrastructure would be able to compensate for this fundamental and irretrievable loss of setting and context.  The proposed development on this site is not consistent with policy on Green Infrastructure (CS14). The site is crossed by a popular wooded permissive path (Long Walk), footpaths, a bridleway and a National Cycle Route (Guthlaxton Trail). It is an area loved and enjoyed by myself, my children and many local residents. In addition visitors travel from across the District and in some cases from across the Country to enjoy the area and explore the District's heritage. The government have decided to protect 'green space of special importance to local communities,' now called Local Green Spaces (LGS) in the NPPF (para. 76  77).  This popular and very attractive area falls into this category and meets all the LGS selection criteria defined in the NPPF.  LGS status for the Long Walk area has the overwhelming backing of the community. Policy on Open Spaces, Sport and Recreation (CS15) seeks to ensure that all residents have access to sufficient, high quality, accessible open space, sport and recreation facilities.  It states that existing open space, sport and recreation facilities will be protected, and where possible enhanced. Where development is proposed on existing open space, sport and recreation facilities, land should not be released, either in total or in part unless it can be demonstrated that it is surplus to requirements for its current play and open space function. The Local Plan CS (Issues, problems and challenges facing the District) para. 4.3 states that, 'A recent survey of play and open spaces has indicated that the District is broadly lacking in these facilities.' I believe that this site is clearly a very high quality and valuable open space that is not at all surplus to requirements.  Bouskell Park is a beautiful public park on the site of a 10th century medieval village (the original settlement of Blaby) with a pond and a Victorian Ice House (a Grade II Listed building).  Interpretative panels give visitors the history of the area and the wildlife to be seen.  If the park was to be 'hemmed-in' by housing it would lose much of its amenity value to residents and it would be too small and isolated to be the valuable habitat for wildlife it is at present. If the wooded Long Walk with its very popular permissive path were to be surrounded with an estate of over 200 houses it would result in a considerable reduction in the amenity value of the Long Walk area to local residents and is very strongly opposed by the community. If the proposed development went ahead it would isolate Long Walk from the surrounding countryside and it is then likely that it would become unpopular with many users who use it extensively at present.  It could easily become an unattractive wooded 'back ally' in the centre of a housing estate which could attract fly tipping and anti-social behaviour.  Badgers are known to live in the area and the site provides them with good quality foraging habitat and cover (see WYG Blaby District Council: Phase 1 Habitat Survey 2008  LDF evidence base). Badgers and their setts are protected under the Protection of Badgers Act 1992. Bats are known to roost close by (possibly the old Hall Farm buildings) and Long Walk is a very important wildlife corridor that provides both feeding habitat and links between other important feeding sites. The Bouskell Park area is used for local 'bat walks' organised by Blaby District Council. Bats are poorly catered for in planning development.  Bat boxes are a very poor substitute for the habitat loss which bats often suffer and there is a low occupancy rate. The real issue is usually the loss of bats' feeding areas. They need a large area over which to forage. The loss of the included farmland would be a real loss to the many bats that live and feed on the Hall Farm estate land.  All British bat species and their roosts are legally protected under the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981. a member of the local bat group. There is potential for white-clawed crayfish and possibly water voles in the small brook running parallel to Hospital Lane and further survey work should be performed to assess the potential loss of habitat.  Sometimes the water flow is low, but in recent years it has rarely run dry and 'deeper pools may sustain wildlife during drought.' See the WYG 2008 Phase 1 Habitat Survey reference above.  Blaby District Council state on their website that 'Our parks and open spaces provide visual breaks in the built environment and contribute to the health of the local residents by creating clean and attractive environments that provide opportunities for a wide range of formal and informal leisure, sport, recreational and play for all ages, as well as offering other social benefits such as community cohesion, learning and development.'  I strongly believe that a large scale building development on this site would substantially degrade Bouskell Park and the surrounding open spaces that make it a very special and valuable place.  The area is used as part of the Blaby Health Walks programme organised by Blaby District Sports Alliance and Blaby District Council aimed at encouraging local people of all ages to take more exercise. 'Blaby Buggy Walks', organised by Blaby District Council use Bouskell Park.  As a parent of young children I frequently use Long Walk as a safe and healthy way of accessing the countryside. The network of paths which has Bouskell Park and Long Walk at its heart is used by orienteering, walking and running groups and clubs, including Leicestershire & Rutland Walking Group. The proposed development would seriously compromise this centre of health and wellbeing. Blaby scores highly in Quality of Life surveys - see for example BDC Contact spring 2010 issue - good access to high quality countryside is an important factor.  Hospital Lane is already severely congested during peak periods especially at the junction with Leicester Road / Countesthorpe Road to the east of Blaby. Welford Road in Blaby is also now congested at busy times and can be difficult for pedestrians to cross. The proposed development would make the situation a great deal worse in Blaby, Whetstone, Glen Parva, Countesthorpe and South Wigston. Local infrastructure is not capable of supporting a development of this size and in this location. The proposed development is not properly sustainable.  The size of the proposed residential development significantly exceeds the residual housing requirement for Blaby as defined by the Local Plan, CS5, Housing distribution.  The Hall Farm site is close to a floodplain and historically Blaby has had a problem with repeated flooding. I understand that because of climate changes we are to expect more frequent extreme weather events that could lead to localised flooding. Large scale building on the site could compromise flood prevention and mitigation measures and result in increased local flooding risk on the site and more importantly elsewhere. Policy on Climate Change (CS21) and the NPPF refer to the importance of good site selection for new development. It is not unusual for flooding of the River Sence and its tributaries to affect the road connections to Leicester, especially at Crow Mills at South Wigston and the A426 between Blaby and Glen Parva, resulting in severe road congestion in and around Whetstone, Blaby and Wigston as motorists attempt to find alternative routes. An extra 200 plus houses to the east of Blaby off Hospital Lane would make the situation worse, firstly because of the extra traffic that would discharge into Hospital Lane and secondly increased water run-off rate from the site following extreme weather could increase the severity and frequency of flooding. The proposed development would make the situation a great deal worse in Blaby, Whetstone, Glen Parva, Countesthorpe and South Wigston.  I sincerely hope that the above points will be taken into account when considering this application.

CommentOriginal: I most strongly object to the proposed housing development at the above ref; I have been walking my dogs around Bouskell Park and the surrounding area for the past 14years, for me personally this loss would be a terrible, for the wildlife this is temination. I have actually seen, (in Long Walk) out of a old sqirrel dray nest, three fledgling Tawny Owls, for the people that would not know what they look like, if you can imagine three balls of cotton wool, each the size of a football, snoozing away perched high in the canopy, thats the image. Not very exciting for some, but for me, an absolute privilege, the last time that I'd seen a Tawny Owl chick is well over fifty years ago. The parent birds need the surrounding fields and countryside to find the food to feed the chicks. These birds are obviously just a very small part of the very big wildlife picture. There is much more at stake here than just people pleasure, We cannot keep stealing these poor creatures habitat, they have as much right, if not more than us, to have a chance of life. Enough is Enough, Stop the project.

Name: County Councillor Geoff Welsh
CommentOriginal: Sir,  I am the County Councillor for Blaby and Glen Parva, I am also a District Councillor at Blaby District Council.   I wish to object to this application. As councillors we have worked hard to ensure that Blaby has an adopted local plan.   We believe that this application is not in compliance with this adopted core strategy. The local community love that the village accesses open countryside at this side of Blaby and the plan reflects this community view. I believe that the point of a local plan is that it be allowed to run its course as long as the land supply figures are met and that each community delivers the housing number required. I submit that Blaby village has met this figure.  The land to the east of Blaby is very special in the hearts of local residents. It serves as a genuine green landscape to serve the residents of Glen Parva, Blaby and Countesthorpe.   All of these communities have seen significant development as required in the local plan. But this area stretching though to Oadby and Wigston BC has always been in place in the local plan to balance the development.  If the access point to this land is severed from the village the very special nature of the space is destroyed. The space is used by so very many people. A Sunday will see hundreds of people walking, cycling or even horse riding, along Mill Lane, through Long Walk, through the ancient park land. With footpaths and roads connecting it to the grand union canal conservation area, to Countesthorpe village through Blaby Oaks wood and through the new county park.  This special nature cannot be stressed enough. The plan recognises it and local councillors have allowed development of other land to ensure that this loved place is save.   Please recognise that the local community and their elected representatives wish to shape their community, allowing the housing development that is required but also saving that which is loved

Thorpe Meadows on the edge of  Countesthorpe, close to the eastern end of Hospital Lane is under construction. This will provide about 150 homes. Though in Countesthorpe, it is situated such that traffic will use Hospital Lane to reach Blaby. As there are few facilities in Countesthorpe and Hospital Lane is the most direct route to Blaby, this will increase traffic at all times of day.  2. Rapid Population increase when combined with other new development. The planning approvals already granted within Blaby, including  a number of smaller schemes not referenced, will increase the housing stock by approximately 300. This is expected to increase the population  by about 900. The addition of another 220 homes would bring that increase up to somewhere in the region of 1600, approximately 25% of the existing population.  Schools do not have excess capacity as claimed in the proposal. Some we know are working with more pupils than they were built for.  Despite the claims of the developer, there is no bus service along Hospital Lane. The nearest route is about half a mile away and provides a limited service. For full services from Blaby it is necessary to go approximately  ¾ mile to the village centre.  Parking in the village centre can already be difficult at busy times.  3. Blaby, Countesthorpe, Whetstone and Cosby are in danger of becoming part of the Leicester urban sprawl. Development on Winchester Road now effectively connects Blaby and Countesthorpe.  This proposal in conjunction with Thorpe Meadows significantly reduces the separation between the two villages along Hospital Lane/Leicester Road.  4. Congestion and Pollution. Hospital Lane has, over the last 10 years changed from being a relatively quiet lane to a commuter Rat Run. I understand that at times it can take in excess of 10 minutes to get from Hospital Lane to Lutterworth Road: a distance of less than half a mile. Stationary traffic, belching fumes outside a primary school is most undesirable.  The congestion is exacerbated during periods of heavy rain. The feeder road from South Wigston floods at Crow Mills as does the A426 Leicester Road under the railway bridge and the A5199 at Kilby Bridge. At these times the only route between Blaby and Leicester is via Enderby Road and Blaby becomes gridlocked.  5. Protected Species. Many wildlife species inhabit the area including up to 50 species of birds. Over the years we have observed badgers, foxes, squirrels and even a muntjac. Any displacement of these would have serious effects on the whole eco-structure.

CommentOriginal: S62A/2014/0001/Hospital Lane Blaby  I object in the strongest possible terms to Gladman Development's proposal for the building of 240 new homes on the land off Hospital Lane.  The proposed development is patently unsustainable and virtually all statements by Gladman in their Supporting Planning Statement (April 2014) are, at best, inaccurate and, at worst deliberate falsehoods.    In para 1.1.2 they make the entirely false statement that 'Blaby District Council cannot demonstrate a 5 year deliverable land supply'.  This is blatantly incorrect since the Council have a published and ratified sustainable Core Strategy and a 5 year land supply plan which, in actual fact, has exceeded the number of dwellings recommended!  The paragraph goes on to say that the application 'presents an excellent opportunity ' to assist the Council's immediate housing land shortfall'.  What immediate shortfall?  Publicly available data proves conclusively that Blaby District have already met their housing deliverance responsibilities and are well on track for 2026.  Gladman open their Planning Statement with the (unusually accurate and possibly first and last honest) statement 'The Site lies in the countryside'.  They then go on to try to explain how building 220 dwellings and changing the character of the area forever will be 'of benefit to the local community and surrounding area' and to present their provision of 'new green space' as a positive benefit.  How can developing (using their figures) 58% of an area of natural countryside provide new green space?  Simply repeating something does not make it so.  Gladman repeatedly state that their site is sustainable.  The facts suggest, however, that, not only is this not the case, but that the examples used to prove their case are flawed, inaccurate or simply false.  At para 1.1.4 it is stated: 'The Site is sustainable against the terms of the Frameworks 3 dimensions.  The presumption in favour of sustainable development must therefore apply'.  However, the three dimensions for sustainability laid out in the Policy are not met by the Gladman proposal ' despite their repeated statements that they are: Economic ' there is no requirement and no economic benefit in building surplus housing off Hospital Lane.  There is insufficient infrastructure in place within the community to support this (in terms of public transport, roads, medical, educational or employment availability); Social ' Gladman's own proposal states that 25% of the housing will be 'affordable'.  The other 75%, therefore, will, by definition, be less affordable and therefore, unlikely to benefit the young or local residents looking to enter the property market.  The residents, therefore are likely to be more affluent than the surrounding community and less likely to integrate socially.  Blaby is already a strong, vibrant and healthy community ' as evidenced by the overwhelming rejection of the Gladman proposal; Environmental ' the area is designated as countryside/farmland.  It is situated adjacent to a community park of great historical and local importance.  Slapping 220+ houses into this area, along with the commensurate traffic, population, waste, crime and pollution into this locale is going to have a serious and irreversible effect on the environment.  In their commissioned Environment Report, Gladman takes the findings that bats and other animals are happily catered for in the protected environs of Bouskell Park, therefore posing no impediment to the development site adjacent (para 4.4.2).  However, elsewhere in the proposal plans are suggested to incorporate Bouskell Park as a convenient thoroughfare to and from the village centre amenities.  This is unlikely to happen without the installation of lighting and better maintained pathways ' in short, the development and upheaval of the very same habitat identified as significant in the Environmental Report.  Furthermore, the supreme arrogance with which Gladman treat the communities which they purport to be benefiting is evident in that they have the audacity to suggest radical environmental changes to land to which they have no access or right of development in order the overcome fundamental errors in their plans.  Without thoroughfare through Bouskell Park there is no short, safe or practical pedestrian access to the centre of Blaby without considerable diversion through their own estate, out along busy roads or winding lanes with no footpaths.  Notwithstanding it's natural beauty and historic link to the medieval village of Blaby, the area surrounding the Long Walk, including the proposed development site, is designated as Local Green Space (LGS).  In relation to LGS the National Planning Policy Framework f para 76 says: 76.  Local communities through local and neighbourhood plans should be able to identify for special protection green areas of particular importance to them. By designating land as Local Green Space local communities will be able to rule out new development other than in very special circumstances. Identifying land as Local Green Space should therefore be consistent with the local planning of sustainable development and complement investment in sufficient homes, jobs and other essential services. Local Green Spaces should only be designated when a plan is prepared or reviewed, and be capable of enduring beyond the end of the plan period. 77.  The Local Green Space designation will not be appropriate for most green areas or open space. The designation should only be used: '  where the green space is in reasonably close proximity to the community it serves; '  where the green area is demonstrably special to a local community and holds a particular local significance, for example because of its beauty, historic significance, recreational value (including as a playing field), tranquillity or richness of its wildlife; and '  ''where the green area concerned is local in character and is not an extensive tract of land. The proposed site, it is wholeheartedly felt within the community of Blaby, falls squarely within the criteria of para 77.  Further examples regarding unsustainability and spin-doctoring include:  1.	 Gladmans state that there are sufficient school places within the catchment of the proposed development to accommodate the 240 new homes they intend to supply.  However, the County Council's own figures maintain that there would be a shortfall of over 50 places if the new population were taken into consideration.  What makes matters worse is that Gladmans were aware of the official figures before their final submission to the Planning Inspectorate since they form part of the Inspectorate's pre-application report to Gladmans yet, in their arrogance, decided to go to press with the inaccurate figures since they paint a rosier picture of the development.  2.	Gladmans state that there are bus stops within a short walking distance of the site with up to 6 buses an hour.  There are actually only 2 buses an hour (4 if you count both directions) at 3 bus stops.  The Gladman figures for the distance of these bus stops are considerably lower than the actual (proven) distance (in one case the distance is almost double, that cited in their report) which also makes mention of several bus stops which, although marked on some area maps, have not existed for several years.  3.	Their report claims that there are sufficient spaces for new patients at the medical and dental practices in Blaby.  Consultation with the practice managers and staff reveal that most are at full capacity at the time of writing.    In one report provided by Gladman a medical practice almost 2km from the site is described as being 'within comfortable cycling distance'.  How many patients are likely to cycle to see a doctor?  4.	In terms of local employment, the Gladman proposal cites a local business park as being within walking distance and potentially providing employment.  When actually called and spoken to, the businesses in the business park ' the majority of them being small, family firms employing less than 12 staff ' reported having just 6 vacancies.   5.	At 4.6.1 Gladman states it 'has sought to enter into constructive dialogue' with relevant Officers of Blaby District Council' in relation to its draft Section 106 agreement.  At the time of writing, the Planning Dept of Blaby District Council had seen no such document nor had record of any approach.  It is ironic that Gladman suggest that they have engaged in any dialogue, constructive or otherwise since they have steadfastly refused to engage with the local community and residents beyond the hastily executed 'Public Consultation' at Thistley Meadow School where they outlined their plans, arrogantly stated to more than one resident that planning permission 'would go through anyway', and then disappeared from sight ' refusing to attend Parish Council or public meetings apparently for fear that 'Land for Life would disrupt them'.  Instead they have chosen to compile their proposal remotely through desktop reconnaissance, outdated or fabricated data and selective reliance on third party reports (where it suits).  6.	 Development of two sites off Winchester Road, on the outskirts of Countesthorpe, less than 3km from Blaby, are well underway and, when complete, will place further strain on the traffic flow, transport and amenities of Blaby.  The bulk of the Leicester-bound traffic from Countesthorpe and the two sites will pass directly down Winchester Rd, past the junction with Hospital Lane (which is not light controlled), and onto a mini roundabout at the northern end of Blaby.  From there is will meet the bypass roundabout which is often congested during peak traffic times already.  The impact on 240 households' vehicles committed to trying to exit Hospital Lane at these times does not take much working out.  Taken in isolation, many of the throwaway comments and bluesky planning from Gladman may actually make sense (on paper) but, in the real world do not stack up to a sustainable benefit.     In summary Gladman Development's Planning Application S62A/2014/0001/Hospital Lane Blaby is inaccurate, unnecessary, unsustainable and ill-conceived.  It is a blatant money-making exercise by Leicester County Council placed into the hands of an unscrupulous development company with no community consideration or concept of impact.  Their proposal statement does not stand up to even the most casual scrutiny or research, consistent with their poor national reputation.  Faithfully yours,

CommentOriginal: Patricia Troake 64 Southway Blaby Leicester LE8 4BB  9th May 2014 Ref: S62A/2014/0001/Hospital Lane Blaby I wish to object most strongly to the proposed development on Hospital Lane and urge the Inspectorate to reject this application. Blaby has already exceeded the number of houses which need to be built by 2026, by 26, according to its policy. This development of 220 further houses would exceed the requirement by 40%. I feel that this figure is unacceptably high.  Blaby District Council has shown  a 5 year land supply to meet the its requirement for new housing.  Any more would be unsustainable and does not agree with local and national policies. This site is a well used green space enjoyed by residents of all ages.  (Core strategy policy CS14).  Whatever time or day you visit this site you always meet other residents enjoying this amenity. People walk, with or without dogs, cycle on the path that is part of the Sustrans route, children learn to ride bikes in a safe environment or ride horses.  Our visitors have often remarked how lucky we are to have this on our doorstep.  There isn't a surplus of green spaces in this area.  (CS15) This development would significantly alter the atmosphere of Bouskell Park.  The Blaby District Landscape and Settlement Character Assessment is totally against altering this site. (Policy CS18).  Residents often say that one of the reasons they chose Blaby to live was that the countryside comes into the centre of the village via this route and therefore maintains a rural feel.  As secretary of the local heritage group I feel appalled that we could lose the character of the village. This development would border the site where the mediaeval village of Blaby can still be seen and also has a Grade 11 listed Victorian ice house and pond. In fact Leicestershire County Council has classified the heritage potential of this site as Grade 1.  Please don't allow our history to be lost. The area is also an important ecological site for badgers, bats, owls and even deer have recently been seen. (CS19) The entrance to this development site is already extremely congested and as there are no public transport links in this part of Blaby the situation can only get worse.  Most houses will have one car, probably two.  Also we have yet to see what congestion will be added to this site from two more housing sites of several hundred houses that are presently being constructed.  The obvious route for these residents into Leicester and for all other major routes will pass close to the application site. Hall Farm is close to floodplain and more surface water will have an impact on flood risk. (CS21). Please listen to local residents and say no to this development that no-one supports.   Patricia Troake

CommentOriginal: 1. Planning Policy on Countryside & the Requirement for New Housing (CS18) (CS5) (LSCA) (NPPF)    The site is designated as Countryside and this development proposal is not supported by planning policy on Countryside (CS18), which states that  'Within areas designated as Countryside, planning permission will not be granted for built development, or other development which would have a significantly adverse effect on the appearance or character of the landscape.'  This proposal will have a significant adverse effect on the landscape, in particular the appearance and setting of the Blaby Conservation Area, especially Bouskell Park which has an essentially rural parkland character with a strong perceived connection with the wider countryside.  This proposed development would severely degrade Bouskell Park's rural character and its perceived connection to the wider countryside.  The proposal runs counter to the recommendations of the Blaby District Landscape and Settlement Character Assessment (LSCA) which has an important role in assessing the effect a development would have on the countryside's landscape. Blaby District Council already have a 5 year supply of deliverable housing sites (as defined by the NPPF) to meet the District's requirements for new housing, so it is not necessary to support development proposals that do not align with planning policy. A development of this size (over 200 dwellings) in this location is not justified by the outstanding housing requirement numbers for Blaby defined in Policy CS5, Housing Distribution.  2. Policy on Historic Environment and Culture, Conservation and Heritage (CS20) (CS2) (SHLAA)    The proposed site is next to the Blaby Conservation Area which is also designated an 'open area of importance to the form and character of the built environment.'  The proposed development is so close to the Conservation Area it would have a very adverse impact on the area and would be against policy on Historic Environment and Culture (CS20) which seeks to preserve and enhance the cultural heritage of the District and states that proposed development should avoid harm to the significance of historic sites, buildings or areas, including their setting. Policy CS2 ' Design of New Development has as one of its objectives 'to protect the important areas of the District's natural environment (species and habitats), landscape and geology and to improve biodiversity, wildlife habitats and corridors through the design of new developments''.  The proposed development would have a significant negative impact on existing wildlife corridors and the wildlife habitat in and around Bouskell Park which is part of the Conservation Area.  The Strategic Housing Land Availability Assessment (SHLAA) also emphasises the importance of considering the impact any proposed development would have on the Conservation Area. The following three objection points relate directly to these planning policies. Blaby's Bouskell Park which is part of the Conservation Area and just a few metres from the proposed housing site is regarded as the best historical site in the District. Leicestershire County Council has classified the heritage potential of the proposed site as High (Grade 1). It is immediately adjacent to the site of a medieval village ' the original settlement of Blaby.  The Victorian Ice House (Grade II listed) and pond in Bouskell Park will loose all sense of place and context if they are just a few metres from a modern housing estate.  We believe that no amount of interpretative panels and new infrastructure would be able to compensate for this fundamental and irretrievable loss of setting and context.  3. Loss of Valuable Green Space & Infrastructure (CS14) (CS15)     The proposed development on this site is not consistent with policy on Green Infrastructure (CS14). The site is crossed by a popular wooded permissive path (Long Walk), footpaths, a bridleway and a National Cycle Route (Guthlaxton Trail). It is an area loved and enjoyed by many local residents. In addition visitors travel from across the District and in some cases from across the Country to enjoy the area and explore the District's heritage. The government have decided to protect 'green space of special importance to local communities,' now called Local Green Spaces (LGS) in the NPPF (para. 76 ' 77).  This popular and very attractive area falls into this category and meets all the LGS selection criteria defined in the NPPF.  LGS status for the Long Walk area has the overwhelming backing of the community. Policy on Open Spaces, Sport and Recreation (CS15) seeks to ensure that all residents have access to sufficient, high quality, accessible open space, sport and recreation facilities.  It states that existing open space, sport and recreation facilities will be protected, and where possible enhanced. Where development is proposed on existing open space, sport and recreation facilities, land should not be released, either in total or in part unless it can be demonstrated that it is surplus to requirements for its current play and open space function. The Local Plan CS (Issues, problems and challenges facing the District) para. 4.3 states that, 'A recent survey of play and open spaces has indicated that the District is broadly lacking in these facilities.' We believe that this site is clearly a very high quality and valuable open space that is not at all surplus to requirements. Blaby District Green Space Strategy:- refers to the NPPF 'Existing green spaces should not be built on unless they are surplus to requirements and losses are replaced with equivalent or better provision in terms of quantity and quality (NPPF, paragraph 74).' Policy CS14 Green Infrastructure 6.19.  Policy CS2 is also relevant.  4. Prematurity of this Application with regard to Local Green Space Designation   We regard this application as premature as it could prejudice emerging plans.  The adopted Local Plan Core Strategy does not support a housing development on this site.  Moreover, especially relevant to this application is that there is widespread support for designating the area around Long Walk as a Local Green Space (LGS) as defined in the NPPF. The call for LGS designation of this site is supported by local residents, the L&R Wildlife Trust, the RSPB, walking groups, the Leicestershire Footpaths Association, Natural England, local Parish Councils and many District / County Councillors. Site specific planning issues such as LGS designation are covered by the emerging Local Plan Delivery DPD (previously called the Allocations, Designations and Development Management DPD) and also the Neighbourhood Plan being prepared by Blaby Parish Council.  Blaby Parish Council have indicated that they seek to protect this special Green Space in the Neighbourhood Plan. The application proposes a substantial development on this site that will have a significant impact on the future development of Blaby. And finally if the proposed development went ahead it would isolate Long Walk from the surrounding countryside and it is then likely that it would become unpopular with many users who use it extensively at present.  It could easily become an unattractive wooded 'back ally' in the centre of a housing estate which could attract fly tipping and anti-social behaviour. I believe this planning application to be flawed in law for several reasons:  The site is designated as Countryside and this development proposal is not supported by planning policy on Countryside (CS18), which states that 'Within areas designated as Countryside, planning permission will not be granted for built development, or other development which would have a significantly adverse effect on the appearance or character of the landscape.' I think it is clear that this proposal will have a significantly adverse effect on the landscape, in particular the appearance and setting of the Blaby Conservation Area, especially Bouskell Park which has an essentially rural parkland character with a strong perceived connection with the wider countryside.  This proposed development would severely degrade Bouskell Park's rural character and its perceived connection to the wider countryside.  Blaby District Council already has a 5 year supply of deliverable housing sites (as defined by the NPPF) to meet the District's requirements for new housing, so it is not necessary to support development proposals that do not align with planning policy.  A development of this size (over 200 dwellings) in this location is not justified by the outstanding housing requirement numbers for Blaby defined in Policy CS5, Housing Distribution.  The proposed development is so close to the Conservation Area it would have a very adverse impact on the area and would be against policy on Historic Environment and Culture (CS20) which seeks to preserve and enhance the cultural heritage of the District and states that proposed development should avoid harm to the significance of historic sites, buildings or areas, including their setting.  Therefore I object on the following points:  Blaby's Bouskell Park which is part of the Conservation Area and just a few metres from the proposed housing site is regarded as the best historical site in the District.  Leicestershire County Council has classified the heritage potential of the proposed site as High (Grade 1). It is immediately adjacent to the site of a medieval village  the original settlement of Blaby.  The Victorian Ice House (Grade II listed) and pond in Bouskell Park will lose all sense of place and context if they are just a few metres from a modern housing estate.  We believe that no amount of interpretative panels and new infrastructure would be able to compensate for this fundamental and irretrievable loss of setting and context.  The government have decided to protect 'green space of special importance to local communities,' now called Local Green Spaces (LGS) in the NPPF (para. 76  77).  This popular and very attractive area falls into this category and meets all the LGS selection criteria defined in the NPPF.  Blaby District Green Space Strategy refers to the NPPF  Existing green spaces should not be built on unless they are surplus to requirements and losses are replaced with equivalent or better provision in terms of quantity and quality (NPPF, paragraph 74.  Moreover, especially relevant to this application is that there is widespread support for designating the area around Long Walk as a Local Green Space (LGS) as defined in the NPPF. With all of this in mind I urge you to think carefully before you make a decision.  This green space is held in high regard by the local and wider community and there are many reasons why this development should not go ahead, I have merely highlighted a few of those which are dear to me personally.  Blaby Parish and District Councils are both opposed to this development, and they are the elected personnel working on behalf of the local people.  The Planning Officer who recently spoke at an open meeting also assured us that had the application been submitted through the usual channels (to Blaby District Council) then it would be NOT be passed on the very grounds that I and no doubt many other local residents are putting forward. PLEASE THINK CAREFULLY.

A development of this size (over 200 dwellings) in this location is not justified by the outstanding housing requirement numbers for Blaby defined in Policy CS5, Housing Distribution. Local infrastructure is not capable of supporting a development of this size and in this location. We do not think the proposed development is properly sustainable.  The size of the proposed residential development significantly exceeds the residual housing requirement for Blaby as defined by the Local Plan, CS5, Housing distribution. If the proposed development went ahead it would isolate Long Walk from the surrounding countryside and it is then likely that it would become unpopular with many users who use it extensively at present.  It could easily become an unattractive wooded 'back ally' in the centre of a housing estate which could attract fly tipping and anti-social behaviour.
