Name: Janet Feaver
CommentOriginal: I wish to object in the strongest terms to the Hospital Lane development S62A/2014/0001 Blaby District Council has already demonstrated a 5 year land supply to meet the district's requirements for new housing. A major development of 220 houses is not required and does not align with the local and national planning policies. The development would undoubtedly compromise the green spaces which the cores strategy states it seeks to "protect existing...networks of multi-functional green spaces"  This open space is unique and surely must be protected. The development would impact severely upon the appearance and character of the conservation area and the grade 11 listed Victorian ice house and pond in Bouskell Park, being several metres away from the proposed development and therefore losing all sense of context. I understand that the core strategy aims to "protect the important areas of the District's natural environment (species and habitats), landscapes and geology..." if this is so,the Long Walk, a site of ecological value, and the surrounding area, will be detrimentally effected. A housing estate would isolate the habitats of a range of wildlife, including badgers, owls and bats and the noise and light pollution would deter wildlife. The development will certainly create transport problems. Living on Hospital lane I am aware daily of the congestion along what is, effectively a "lane" The development will unquestionably increase the traffic and therefore the potential for accidents on what is often a busy road.There have been several accidents on this road and consideration must also be given to the proximity of the nearby school and the impact this will have upon children's safety. I understand that the core strategy on climate change refers to the importance of good site selection for new developments to minimise flooding.In view of the recent floods affecting many areas of the country, should this not be considered as the north of the Hall Farm estate is very close to a floodplain and other parts of the site are at high risk of flooding. Such a significant development  will unquestionably have an impact on the infrastucture in the area. The area is poorly serviced with public transfort, there being no links with any of the exisiting or planned employment sites throughout the district .Local services such as schools, dentist and doctors surgeries wil also be affected. The development is unsustainable. The health and wellbeing of the community will be detrimentally affected if the development goes ahead. Many groups, ramblers and  walkers, including Blaby Heath Walks use the area and the loss will impact upon them. In an age of obesity, these accessable, valuable spaces must be protected for the local community and not be destroyed. Bouskell Park and the Long Walk are arguably Blaby's finest asset . It should be preserved to protect the quality of life of local residents and provide a haven for wildlife.  Its loss would be a tragedy for Blaby  and the wider area.

Name: Paul Pengelly
CommentOriginal: In the leaflet Gladman released for the Public Consultation of this Potential Residential Development on Hospital Lane they claimed. "Gladman Devolpments are proposing a new residential devolpment of approximately 220 homes on land off Hospital Lane ,Blaby.This will provide for affordable housing,public open space,a play area for children and a footpath network.  "Approximately 25% of these new homes would provide affordable housing for local people" - If they are doing this to provide "much needed affordable housing " why not utilise the 30% maxium percentage of affordable homes in a development ? why stop at "approximately 25%" is that nearer 20% than 25% ? Are they allowed to stipulate these "affordable houses"are for local people only, what constitute local ,are there 55 local families who require affordable homes in Blaby?  "Public Open Space" -How does building houses on 30 acres of Green fields increase our Open Space?, will all these houses be open to the public?  Do they mean the "proposed extension to Bouskkell Park" which is a field that they originally wanted to build 100 more houses on but when they couldn't get access onto Mill Lane they dropped it .And it now becomes a Proposed "Park" except it has been used as that for years and years ,so they are offering us something we already have.  "A play area for children",as there is already a large play area ,with football pitches the other side of Hospital Lane,I think providing two swings and a slide is more for the benefit of the proposed development rather than the rest of Blaby. "A footpath network" This site is already crossed with multiple footpaths ,some of them paved at considerable expense  to stop them becoming huge mudbaths when the site regularly floods.Unless they mean "road network" I think we would end up with less public access.  This proposed devolpment is not needed,there are already plans submitted or approved for over 500 homes in Blaby Parish,and roughly the same again for Countesthorpe which is now only two fields away from joining up with Blaby.  And all built with no  additional amienities ,no more shops or,schools,Drs surgeries ,for a "village" that is already suffering from a lack of the above. The housing developers get what they want and we get lost green space,traffic pollution,congestion,and reduced facilities,then we have to pay again through increased rates as the council then has to build wider roads, new schools,more infrastructure.  Blaby used to be a lovely place to live ,highly rated for its quality of life,with lots of open fields to take the dog for long walks with lots of Birds and Animals to see,sadly it seems this council  and developers are hellbent on turning it into another Suburb of Leicester.  Paul Pengelly

Name: Ian Warner
CommentOriginal: The Proposed housing Development, must not be allowed to go ahead. The land boarders Bouskell Park which is the only country park in the area and is heavily used by residents of Blaby and surrounding areas. As an area with rare nature and natural beauty Bouskell Park is used by all age groups including children for walking and recreational activities. This Development would enclose Bouskell Park in housing all round and it would cease to be a country park. Thus part of Blaby's heritage will be lost forever. This application should have never got this far, both the Parish and District councils are against it, but the land owner just wants to offload this farm land for maximum profit. Unfortunately Leicestershire County Council is the Land owner , Blaby DC hoped Leicestershire CC would act responsibly but they have not and the situation is now very political. This area of Blaby is currently undergoing two major housing developments within half a mile just down the road, again recreational land lost to housing. Additional housing is not needed in Blaby, quotas have already been meet and any more housing will totally destroy the character of Blaby. It is not in the best interest of the Rate Payers of Blaby to allow Leicestershire County Council to force Blaby District Council to fight their proposals using Rate Payers Money, but the Rate Payers will fight to the end by any means possible, and all because Leicestershire County Council wants to sell the land for maximum profit, when Blaby District Council could have bought the land at a fair price. Please get Leicestershire County Council to see sense and work with Blaby District Council for the benefit of the residents of Blaby and surrounding areas.

CommentOriginal: With reference to the above application for up to 220 dwellings on this land which has been widely nominated as LOCAL GREEN SPACE and is therefore of great significance to the residence of Blaby Village as an environmental area where the countryside can be enjoyed by all. This has been widely nominated as Local Green Space in the Development Plan CS15.    According to the Strategic Land Housing Availability Assessment LEICESTERSHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL has classified the heritage potential of this site as HIGH (Grade1}    The building of new houses in Blaby has exceeded the requirement by Blaby policy up to the year 2026 by 26 dwellings.  A further 220 houses in this location would exceed the calculated housing requirement by a considerable amount, approximately 40%.The District  Council has already shown a 5 year land supply to meet requirements for new housing.  I feel it is therefore unnecessary to support a development which is unsustainable, unnecessary and unwanted by the residence of Blaby whose views should be taken into account.  The District and Parish Councils are opposed to this development.    This land is good agricultural land and is at present in use.. I feel that the use of productive agricultural land should not be used as in the long term we will need all the agricultural land to feed ourselves with the growing population.    The extra traffic generated by approximately 220 homes on this already very busy small road should be of great concern.  There is a mini roundabout approximately 400yds from the proposed development which has seen several accidents with the volume of traffic which exists at present.    The proposed development would put great strain on the local facilities.- police, schools, doctors and dentists.  I believe that both schools are near capacity, the dentist has a waiting list for NHS patients and the local police station has been closed.      I am aware that these planning applications are looked at individually but feel that a greater overview should be taken to other developments in the area which, for your information, withiin 1/4 mile from this proposed development there are approximately 210 houses being newly built !   I feel that this volume of houses on this side of the Blaby village will destroy the character of the village.     I therefore object strongly to this application

CommentOriginal: The site is designated as Countryside and this development proposal is not supported by planning policy on Countryside (CS18), which states that  'Within areas designated as Countryside, planning permission will not be granted for built development, or other development which would have a significantly adverse effect on the appearance or character of the landscape.' Name: Richard Baverstock
CommentOriginal: I am opposed to this development in line with the arguements made by the group Land for Life, and re-iterate excerpts of their reasons as follows:  1. Planning Policy on Countryside & the Requirement for New Housing (CS18) (CS5) (LSCA) (NPPF)    The site is designated as Countryside and this development proposal is not supported by planning policy on Countryside (CS18), which states that  'Within areas designated as Countryside, planning permission will not be granted for built development, or other development which would have a significantly adverse effect on the appearance or character of the landscape.' We think it is clear that this proposal will have a significantly adverse effect on the landscape, in particular the appearance and setting of the Blaby Conservation Area, especially Bouskell Park which has an essentially rural parkland character with a strong perceived connection with the wider countryside.  This proposed development would severely degrade Bouskell Park's rural character and its perceived connection to the wider countryside.  The proposal runs counter to the recommendations of the Blaby District Landscape and Settlement Character Assessment (LSCA) which has an important role in assessing the effect a development would have on the countryside's landscape. Blaby District Council already have a 5 year supply of deliverable housing sites (as defined by the NPPF) to meet the District's requirements for new housing, so it is not necessary to support development proposals that do not align with planning policy. A development of this size (over 200 dwellings) in this location is not justified by the outstanding housing requirement numbers for Blaby defined in Policy CS5, Housing Distribution.   2. Policy on Historic Environment and Culture, Conservation and Heritage (CS20) (CS2) (SHLAA)    The proposed site is next to the Blaby Conservation Area which is also designated an 'open area of importance to the form and character of the built environment.'  The proposed development is so close to the Conservation Area it would have a very adverse impact on the area and would be against policy on Historic Environment and Culture (CS20) which seeks to preserve and enhance the cultural heritage of the District and states that proposed development should avoid harm to the significance of historic sites, buildings or areas, including their setting. Policy CS2 ' Design of New Development has as one of its objectives 'to protect the important areas of the District's natural environment (species and habitats), landscape and geology and to improve biodiversity, wildlife habitats and corridors through the design of new developments''.  The proposed development would have a significant negative impact on existing wildlife corridors and the wildlife habitat in and around Bouskell Park which is part of the Conservation Area.  The Strategic Housing Land Availability Assessment (SHLAA) also emphasises the importance of considering the impact any proposed development would have on the Conservation Area. The following three objection points relate directly to these planning policies. Blaby's Bouskell Park which is part of the Conservation Area and just a few metres from the proposed housing site is regarded as the best historical site in the District. Leicestershire County Council has classified the heritage potential of the proposed site as High (Grade 1). It is immediately adjacent to the site of a medieval village ' the original settlement of Blaby.  The Victorian Ice House (Grade II listed) and pond in Bouskell Park will loose all sense of place and context if they are just a few metres from a modern housing estate.  We believe that no amount of interpretative panels and new infrastructure would be able to compensate for this fundamental and irretrievable loss of setting and context.     3. Loss of Valuable Green Space & Infrastructure (CS14) (CS15)   The proposed development on this site is not consistent with policy on Green Infrastructure (CS14). The site is crossed by a popular wooded permissive path (Long Walk), footpaths, a bridleway and a National Cycle Route (Guthlaxton Trail). It is an area loved and enjoyed by many local residents. In addition visitors travel from across the District and in some cases from across the Country to enjoy the area and explore the District's heritage. The government have decided to protect 'green space of special importance to local communities,' now called Local Green Spaces (LGS) in the NPPF (para. 76 ' 77).  This popular and very attractive area falls into this category and meets all the LGS selection criteria defined in the NPPF.  LGS status for the Long Walk area has the overwhelming backing of the community. Policy on Open Spaces, Sport and Recreation (CS15) seeks to ensure that all residents have access to sufficient, high quality, accessible open space, sport and recreation facilities.  It states that existing open space, sport and recreation facilities will be protected, and where possible enhanced. Where development is proposed on existing open space, sport and recreation facilities, land should not be released, either in total or in part unless it can be demonstrated that it is surplus to requirements for its current play and open space function. The Local Plan CS (Issues, problems and challenges facing the District) para. 4.3 states that, 'A recent survey of play and open spaces has indicated that the District is broadly lacking in these facilities.' We believe that this site is clearly a very high quality and valuable open space that is not at all surplus to requirements. Blaby District Green Space Strategy:- refers to the NPPF 'Existing green spaces should not be built on unless they are surplus to requirements and losses are replaced with equivalent or better provision in terms of quantity and quality (NPPF, paragraph 74).' Policy CS14 Green Infrastructure 6.19.  Policy CS2 is also relevant.  4. Prematurity of this Application with regard to Local Green Space Designation   We regard this application as premature as it could prejudice emerging plans.  The adopted Local Plan Core Strategy does not support a housing development on this site.  Moreover, especially relevant to this application is that there is widespread support for designating the area around Long Walk as a Local Green Space (LGS) as defined in the NPPF. The call for LGS designation of this site is supported by local residents, the L&R Wildlife Trust, the RSPB, walking groups, the Leicestershire Footpaths Association, Natural England, local Parish Councils and many District / County Councillors. Site specific planning issues such as LGS designation are covered by the emerging Local Plan Delivery DPD (previously called the Allocations, Designations and Development Management DPD) and also the Neighbourhood Plan being prepared by Blaby Parish Council.  Blaby Parish Council have indicated that they seek to protect this special Green Space in the Neighbourhood Plan. The application proposes a substantial development on this site that will have a significant impact on the future development of Blaby.  If an outline planning application is approved prior to adoption of the Delivery DPD and the Neighbourhood Plan it could prejudice the DPD by predetermining decisions about the scale and location of new development which are being addressed in the DPD.  In view of this, this application is considered to be premature and potentially prejudicial to emerging plans.  5. Flood Risk & Climate Change    Impact on local flooding risk:' the Hall Farm site is close to a floodplain and historically Blaby has had a problem with repeated flooding. We are told that because of climate changes we are to expect more frequent extreme weather events that could lead to localised flooding. Large scale building on the site could compromise flood prevention and mitigation measures and result in increased local flooding risk on the site and more importantly elsewhere. Policy on Climate Change (CS21) and the NPPF refer to the importance of good site selection for new development. It is not unusual for flooding of the River Sence and its tributaries to affect the road connections to Leicester, especially at Crow Mills at South Wigston and the A426 between Blaby and Glen Parva, resulting in severe road congestion in and around Whetstone, Blaby and Wigston as motorists attempt to find alternative routes. An extra 200 plus houses to the east of Blaby off Hospital Lane would make the situation worse, firstly because of the extra traffic that would discharge into Hospital Lane and secondly increased water run-off rate from the site following extreme weather could increase the severity and frequency of flooding.

Name: Mrs J Timson
CommentOriginal: My family have enjoyed the amenities offered by Blaby for many years, one of these being the Long Walk and Bouskell Park.  We utilised Bouskell Park quite often when our children were little and now they are grown we frequently do variations of the Long Walk (and beyond).  It is a way for us to keep fit without having to drive somewhere first.  Always it has felt like we are in open countryside when using these amenities and this will be lost completely if a housing estate of more than 200 houses is plonked on it (including the roads that will cut across some of Long Walk to provide access to it).  I therefore object to this application on the following basis:  Core Strategy Policy CS14 is designed to protect existing networks of multi-functional green spaces.  For the personal reasons stated above, this developments goes against this policy.  Core Strategy Policy CS15 indicates that existing open space, sport and recreation facilities will be protected.  So why is this development being considered, especially as this area has been nominated as local green space?  Core Strategy Policy CS18 - This housing development would impact on the appearance of the surrounding area and would be detrimental to the current "natural" state of the area - Long Walk would virtually be reduced by half as a "nature" walk.  Core Strategy Policy 19 - how does putting this development here protect the important areas of the natural environment?  When undertaking "Long  Walk" we expect to hear and see native wildlife, not smell and hear human cooking, music, TVs, etc  For all these reasons I object as what is lost cannot be brought back.    I also note that the majority of the houses proposed are not even "affordable" as they consist mainly of 4 bed detached houses, so they would not even solve any housing crisis that might exist.

Name: Sally Jarvey
CommentOriginal: My Husband & I bought our home in Enderby Road, Blaby, when we moved out from the city 17 years ago. A large part of the attraction of the village as a place to live was its semi-rural nature and the link between the old part of the village and the countryside accessed via Bouskell Park and Long Walk. This dimension of the village's character has continued to provide us with pleasure ever since. It is fundamentally these characteristics which set Blaby apart from other communities in the area and which will be massively compromised by the proposed development on Hospital Lane. I therefore object to it very strongly.  Aside from my objection on a personal level that building on this beautiful part of our village would compromise the essence of why Blaby has been such a lovely place to live & raise our family, there are also clear and objective planning reasons why this development should not go ahead.   Firstly, we have already built or committed to enough houses in Blaby.  The number of houses that need to be built in Blaby by 2026 has already been exceeded by 26. A development of 220 houses in this location would exceed the calculated housing requirement of 420, by 40%. Blaby District Council has already demonstrated a 5 Year Land Supply to meet the District's requirements for new housing, so it is therefore unnecessary to support a development that is unsustainable and does not align with the Local and National Planning policies.  Secondly, the development compromises 'Green Space, Landscape and Setting'. Core Strategy seeks 'to protect existing ' 'networks of multi-functional green spaces'.' As I know from frequently cycling in the area the site is a well-used, multi-functional green space and an area enjoyed by many local residents and groups of all ages. Core Strategy says that 'existing open space, sport and recreation facilities will be protected..' This open space is unique and not surplus to requirement. The space has been widely nominated as Local Green Space in the Development Plan Document (as referred to in CS15). Thirdly, this development would affect the 'Historic Environment and Culture'. The Core Strategy aims to '..preserve and enhance the cultural heritage of the District..'   The proposed housing development would border on the Blaby Conservation Area and the Victorian Ice House (Grade II listed) and pond in Bouskell Park will lose all sense of context if they are just a few metres from a housing estate. According to the Strategic Land Housing Availability Assessment Leicestershire County Council has classified the heritage potential of this site as High (Grade 1). This development would have a significantly adverse effect on the appearance and setting of Bouskell Park and its perceived connection with the wider countryside. The Blaby District Landscape and Settlement Character Assessment (LSCA) specifically states that '..development on this site should be resisted..' (Core Strategy Policy CS18). Furthermore, Core Strategy aims to 'protect the important areas of the District's natural environment (species and habitats), landscape and geology''  This site is of ecological value providing important habitat for a range of wildlife including, badgers, bats and owls.  (Core Strategy Policy 19). A housing estate on this site would fragment and isolate these habitats and noise and light pollution would deter wildlife. The development would create Flood Risk. The Core Strategy on Climate Change (CS21) and the NPPF refer to the importance of good site selection for new development to minimise flooding.  The north of the Hall Farm estate site is very close to a floodplain and other parts of the site are at high risk of surface water flooding. The development would create transport problems. My daily commute currently involves a detour in order to avoid the Lutterworth Road / Enderby Road roundabout as it is already congested early each morning and I also know that the A426 and Soar Valley Way are currently extremely congested during peak travel times, these are just 2 routes with no capacity for the increased traffic that would result from a development of this size in this area.

CommentOriginal: As a resident in Blaby I would like to voice my concerns regarding the proposed development: I personally do not feel that Blaby can withhold anymore development, my reasons are detailed below: '	Schools ' The schools within the Blaby area are already at capacity.  With the potential planning of an additional 220 houses  along with the additional houses that have started to be built in Countesthorpe & Blaby, where would all the extra children be educated?  My daughter is currently a pupil at Blaby Stokes school and I do not wish for her education to suffer because of overloaded classes or inadequate facilities.  It is not only the Infant & Primary schools that will suffer it is also the Secondary schools. The area on Hospital Lane is a great spot for children to ride the bikes in a safe environment free from traffic.  The area is also used a great deal of people that use this area to walk their dogs and it is also used by people riding horses.  This area would be greatly missed.   My daughter & I use this walking area quite frequently to get through to Glen Parva or to get to Northfield Park.  We enjoy this time together as not only are we exercising, we are cutting down the usage of our car thus attempting to help the environment & improving our leisure time. This was obviously not a true representation of the volume of traffic that normally runs through the village.  At peak times both Winchester Road & Hospital get very busy & congested.  With the extra developments this will make the traffic within our village even worse.  Also the routes out of the village are incredibly busy the majority of times.  To get into town via Lutterworth Road regularly means queuing from the County Arms all the way to Soar Valley Way adding a considerable time to your journey. '	Doctors/Dentist ' As with the schools the Doctors & Dentists in the village are also at capacity.  There are always long waits to see the doctor.  Even when  you have an appointment there can still be long waits before actually seeing the doctor. '	I chose to move to my current home because I like the area & what Blaby had to offer my family.  A great busy village centre, whilst being able to enjoy the countryside on our doorstep at the same time. All the car parks within the village centre seem to be busy most of the time especially Aldi which people tend to use because it is the only free car park in the village.  There is also a problem of poor parking around the village schools.  As mentioned, my daughter attends Blaby Stokes & the parking around the school are is not acceptable.  We generally walk to & from school but on the odd occasions do have to drive, but I always ensure that I park legally & with consideration to the residents in the area.  Others do not do this with people parking half or fully on the pavements & then just pulling off without even looking, again potentially putting the children in danger.  If there are more pupils attending the school, surely the situation is only going to get worse!! I also believe that the site for the development is very close to a floodplain which could give a very high risk of flooding & there are other area's of the site that are at a high risk to surface water flooding.  It would not be good to bring this risk to the area especially with the vast change to the weather that have experienced within recent years.

Name: bharat rana
CommentOriginal: Dear Sirs,   There are many reasons why I think the area behind Bouskell Park with the beautiful woodland walk and very well used network of paths should be protected and not turned into a large housing estate.  This application is totally misplaced.  The following are my objections that are particularly well supported by technical planning considerations.   1. Planning Policy on Countryside & the Requirement for New Housing (CS18) (CS5) (LSCA) (NPPF)  The site is designated as Countryside and this development proposal is not supported by planning policy on Countryside (CS18), which states that  'Within areas designated as Countryside, planning permission will not be granted for built development, or other development which would have a significantly adverse effect on the appearance or character of the landscape.' I think it is clear that this proposal will have a significantly adverse effect on the landscape, in particular the appearance and setting of the Blaby Conservation Area, especially Bouskell Park which has an essentially rural parkland character with a strong perceived connection with the wider countryside.  This proposed development would severely degrade Bouskell Park's rural character and its perceived connection to the wider countryside.  The proposal runs counter to the recommendations of the Blaby District Landscape and Settlement Character Assessment (LSCA) which has an important role in assessing the effect a development would have on the countryside's landscape. Blaby District Council already have a 5 year supply of deliverable housing sites (as defined by the NPPF) to meet the District's requirements for new housing, so it is not necessary to support development proposals that do not align with planning policy. A development of this size (over 200 dwellings) in this location is not justified by the outstanding housing requirement numbers for Blaby defined in Policy CS5, Housing Distribution.  2. Policy on Historic Environment and Culture, Conservation and Heritage (CS20) (CS2) (SHLAA)  The proposed site is next to the Blaby Conservation Area which is also designated an 'open area of importance to the form and character of the built environment.'  The proposed development is so close to the Conservation Area it would have a very adverse impact on the area and would be against policy on Historic Environment and Culture (CS20) which seeks to preserve and enhance the cultural heritage of the District and states that proposed development should avoid harm to the significance of historic sites, buildings or areas, including their setting. Policy CS2 ' Design of New Development has as one of its objectives 'to protect the important areas of the District's natural environment (species and habitats), landscape and geology and to improve biodiversity, wildlife habitats and corridors through the design of new developments''.  The proposed development would have a significant negative impact on existing wildlife corridors and the wildlife habitat in and around Bouskell Park which is part of the Conservation Area.  The Strategic Housing Land Availability Assessment (SHLAA) also emphasises the importance of considering the impact any proposed development would have on the Conservation Area. The following three objection points relate directly to these planning policies. Blaby's Bouskell Park which is part of the Conservation Area and just a few metres from the proposed housing site is regarded as the best historical site in the District. Leicestershire County Council has classified the heritage potential of the proposed site as High (Grade 1). It is immediately adjacent to the site of a medieval village ' the original settlement of Blaby.  The Victorian Ice House (Grade II listed) and pond in Bouskell Park will lose all sense of place and context if they are just a few metres from a modern housing estate.  I believe that no amount of interpretative panels and new infrastructure would be able to compensate for this fundamental and irretrievable loss of setting and context.  3. Loss of Valuable Green Space & Infrastructure (CS14) (CS15)  The proposed development on this site is not consistent with policy on Green Infrastructure (CS14). The site is crossed by a popular wooded permissive path (Long Walk), footpaths, a bridleway and a National Cycle Route (Guthlaxton Trail). It is an area loved and enjoyed by many local residents. In addition visitors travel from across the District and in some cases from across the Country to enjoy the area and explore the District's heritage. The government have decided to protect 'green space of special importance to local communities,' now called Local Green Spaces (LGS) in the NPPF (para. 76 ' 77).  This popular and very attractive area falls into this category and meets all the LGS selection criteria defined in the NPPF.  LGS status for the Long Walk area has the overwhelming backing of the community. Policy on Open Spaces, Sport and Recreation (CS15) seeks to ensure that all residents have access to sufficient, high quality, accessible open space, sport and recreation facilities.  It states that existing open space, sport and recreation facilities will be protected, and where possible enhanced. Where development is proposed on existing open space, sport and recreation facilities, land should not be released, either in total or in part unless it can be demonstrated that it is surplus to requirements for its current play and open space function. The Local Plan CS (Issues, problems and challenges facing the District) para. 4.3 states that, 'A recent survey of play and open spaces has indicated that the District is broadly lacking in these facilities.' I believe that this site is clearly a very high quality and valuable open space that is not at all surplus to requirements. Blaby District Green Space Strategy:- refers to the NPPF 'Existing green spaces should not be built on unless they are surplus to requirements and losses are replaced with equivalent or better provision in terms of quantity and quality (NPPF, paragraph 74).' Policy CS14 Green Infrastructure 6.19.  Policy CS2 is also relevant.  4. Prematurity of this Application with regard to Local Green Space Designation I regard this application as premature as it could prejudice emerging plans.  The adopted Local Plan Core Strategy does not support a housing development on this site.  Moreover, especially relevant to this application is that there is widespread support for designating the area around Long Walk as a Local Green Space (LGS) as defined in the NPPF. The call for LGS designation of this site is supported by local residents, the L&R Wildlife Trust, the RSPB, walking groups, the Leicestershire Footpaths Association, Natural England, local Parish Councils and many District / County Councillors. Site specific planning issues such as LGS designation are covered by the emerging Local Plan Delivery DPD (previously called the Allocations, Designations and Development Management DPD) and also the Neighbourhood Plan being prepared by Blaby Parish Council.  Blaby Parish Council have indicated that they seek to protect this special Green Space in the Neighbourhood Plan. The application proposes a substantial development on this site that will have a significant impact on the future development of Blaby.  If an outline planning application is approved prior to adoption of the Delivery DPD and the Neighbourhood Plan it could prejudice the DPD by predetermining decisions about the scale and location of new development which are being addressed in the DPD.  In view of this, this application is considered to be premature and potentially prejudicial to emerging plans.   5. Flood Risk & Climate Change   Impact on local flooding risk:' the Hall Farm site is close to a floodplain and historically Blaby has had a problem with repeated flooding. I am told that because of climate changes we are to expect more frequent extreme weather events that could lead to localised flooding. Large scale building on the site could compromise flood prevention and mitigation measures and result in increased local flooding risk on the site and more importantly elsewhere. Policy on Climate Change (CS21) and the NPPF refer to the importance of good site selection for new development. It is not unusual for flooding of the River Sence and its tributaries to affect the road connections to Leicester, especially at Crow Mills at South Wigston and the A426 between Blaby and Glen Parva, resulting in severe road congestion in and around Whetstone, Blaby and Wigston as motorists attempt to find alternative routes. An extra 200 plus houses to the east of Blaby off Hospital Lane would make the situation worse, firstly because of the extra traffic that would discharge into Hospital Lane and secondly increased water run-off rate from the site following extreme weather could increase the severity and frequency of flooding.   Kind regards Bharat Rana

CommentOriginal: I object in the strongest possible terms, to the planned building of housing on the former Hall Farm land off Hospital Lane , Blaby Leicestershire.  it is my opinion that the development is unnecessary, as the target  for new housing to be built by year 2026, has already been achieved and exceeded.  the access to the  proposed development is shown to be immediately adjacent to a primary school, which is situated on a small country lane with a school drop off point outside the school, and about 200 yards from an already busy junction of roads ,  building 220 houses where proposed will be dangerous to the local residents, in particular to the children at school start and finish times, and commuter rush hours, with heavy goods vehicles delivering building materials and earth moving plant during the ground works stage of the proposed development , and if the development does proceed , 220 houses will mean at least that many cars, if not more using the already busy narrow country lane .  on the basis that there is nowadays more than one car per household, there is very likely going to be a lot more than only 220 extra vehicles using the access to the proposed site.  further, there is also the impact of the extra population and their transport to Blaby village centre, and its infrastructure e g parking, doctors surgery,  places at local schools for the inevitable influx of children.  there is also the effect of extra traffic to take into account further afield e g , the approaches to and  from the local motorways m1/m69 /m6 and indeed to Leicester city itself.  I am also concerned about the proximity of the proposed development on its northern edge to the local river, which I have seen flood local farmland very quickly in extended periods of heavy rain fall.  there is also the effect that the proposed development would have upon the local wildlife, the open farmland on which the development is proposed is currently home to badgers,foxes muntjac deer, bats and owls .  noise and light pollution will deter local wildlife.   building 220 houses on that land would probably force the animals to find somewhere else to live.   the proposed development  will adversely affect the heritage of the area .  there will no longer be a direct link from Bouskell Park to open countryside as there is presently,   as the owner of 3 dogs, I know from speaking to other dog owners when out walking my  dogs that some dog owners come from several miles away to walk their dogs across the existing right of way, through open countryside where they can let their dogs run off lead in safety , in preference to dog walks more local to where they reside , a development of 220 houses where proposed would have a significantly detrimental and adverse effect on the appearance and setting of Bouskell Park and its perceived connection with  the wider countryside .

Name: Alan Wilson
CommentOriginal: Concerning the above planning application I wish for it to be noted that I strongly object to these plans on a number of grounds as set out later. I am a local resident to this proposed development and have lived in the area for about 30 years. Over that time I have seen my "village" be swallowed up by housing developments, though not happy have had to accept the local need for housing.  Concerning this development I feel that it is one step to far and perhaps the most beautiful part of Blaby is under threat. It will not only be a loss of precious green space but also have a serious impact on the infrastructure of the village.  1. The site is designated countryside and this development proposal is not supported by planning policy on Countryside which in simple terms states that "Within areas designated as countryside, planning permission will not be granted for build development, or other development that would have an adverse effect on the appearance or character of the landscape. Bearing in mind this would encroach on two important and historic areas, namely 'Old Blaby' which is a conservation area and also the rural parkland known as Bouskell Park.  2.  Blaby Council already has a five year supply of deliverable housing to meet the required quota . So it is not necessary to support development proposals that do not align with planning policy. So a development of this size (200 houses) in the suggested location is not justified by the outstanding housing requirement for Blaby.  3.  As previously stated this proposal is in the Blaby Conservation area which is designated as an open area of importance therefore it would obviously impact . The following 3 objections points relate directly: Bouskell Park is part of the Conservation area and only yards from the new development. Leicestershire County Council has classified the heritage potential of the proposed site as High (Grade 1). It is next to the historic medieval village. The Victorian Ice House in the park is Grade 11 listed building and would be almost swallowed by the development.  4.There will be loss of green space and Infrastructure. There is a wooded path which is extremely popular by walkers, cyclists and dog walkers. This is not only local residents but also people from far and wide. The government has decided to protect green space of special importance to local communities. This area certainly falls within that category. There is a strong commitment from the community to back this and keep the status of the Long Walk.  5. This land is on a flood plane and historically Blaby has suffered from flooding. Large scale building on the site would compromise flood prevention.  6.The area is a haven for wild life which obviously would be lost. Badgers, bats and other rare species are known to live in the area and it is without doubt their habitat will be lost if building takes place.  7. Parks and like areas provide visual breaks in the built up areas and contribute to the health and well being of local residents by offering both formal and informal leisure, sport and play for all. A large building development would have a serious impact on this. This area is used by organisations and groups for various sporting activities.  8. There is not the infrastructure in the village to support this development. The schools are already over capacitated and dentists and doctors would be swamped. Hospital Lane is already congested. There is no nearby bus service which would therefore mean more cars on the road in that vicinity.  In conclusion if this development goes ahead an important and historic area of Blaby will be lost for ever. To the locals  this is a haven to escape to in the bustling build up areas. We are loosing so much green areas in the Blaby district we are desperate to hang on to this tranquil, beautiful and enchanting oasis.  Thank you for taking the time to read this correspondence

Name: Luke Wasteney
CommentOriginal: We would like to register our objection to the proposed development at Hospital Lane, Blaby.  There are various reasons why we believe that this planning application should be denied: -	The beautiful and well used countryside from Bouskell Park at one end along Mill Lane to South Wigston past fields, stables and bridleways provides unspoilt access to nature.  This whole area including the Long Walk bordered by fields with the sounds of nature and quiet surroundings is unique in the Blaby parish and provides an alternative to the man made functional green areas of Northfield and Oakfield parks.  We feel very strongly that access to the open spaces of the countryside is vitally important to the community of Blaby and especially to the younger members of the parish.  It is key that everybody is able to experience and enjoy the benefits of having this area completely separate from the main conurbation, yet within walking distance.  Building this development would irreversibly change the quality and character of this area to the detriment of Blaby. -	 We support the designation of the area around the Long Walk as a Local Green Space and we have personally encountered numerous different species in the area since moving which would be adversely affected by changing their habitat. -	Bouskell Park is an important historical site in the County including a Victorian ice house and site of a medieval village.  Locating a housing development of 220 dwellings within metres of this Conservation area will completely change the context and setting and diminish the powerful impact they have on the landscape. -	The fields around the site have been flooded in the last few years that we have lived in Blaby and building a large number of houses close to a floodplain is likely to increase the risk that excess rainwater is forced into residential areas and roads. -	Having lived in Blaby for several years commuting to Leicester and the motorways, there is already significant congestion.  Any number of additional vehicles will put more pressure onto already stretched transport links and result in ever longer commutes and the potential for more accidents.

Name: Miss Helen Crocker
CommentOriginal: At this moment in time Blaby is a village/small town which is in grave danger of becoming an urban sprawl with new housing developments 'popping up' in the surrounding countryside.    Blaby has already met its target for housing requirements and does not therefore need to expand any further.    Building on this designated countryside adjacent to Bouskell Park will significantly detract from the appearance/ character of the park, affecting not only the wildlife which at present inhabit the park (including herons, ducks, bats, badgers and muntjac deer) but also its present human users.  I religiously walk my dogs twice a day on the park and in the wooded permissive path and have done so for the past 12 years.  With an additional housing estate abuting the park, cemetry and 'Long Walk', comes litter and noise polution.  The local infrastructure will not be able to suppport a development of this size.  The infant and junior schools are already over subscribed.  There is not sufficient health care services for additional residents i.e. GP practices, dentists.  Hospital Lane is congested at peak times with commuter traffic and school traffic.  An additional access road entering Hospital Lane will greatly compound this problem.  Crossing the road is already difficult at any time of day, especially as this is quite a 'fast' road, and this difficulty will be increased.

Name: Robert Marsham
CommentOriginal: Application S62A/2014/0001/Hospital Lane Blaby  I object strongly to this Application, due to the reasons detailed below.  1. Planning Policy on Countryside & the Requirement for New Housing (CS18) (CS5) (LSCA) (NPPF)  The site is designated as Countryside and this development proposal is not supported by planning policy on Countryside (CS18), which states that 'Within areas designated as Countryside, planning permission will not be granted for built development, or other development which would have a significantly adverse effect on the appearance or character of the landscape.'  I think it is clear that this proposal will have a significantly adverse effect on the landscape, in particular the appearance and setting of the Blaby Conservation Area, especially Bouskell Park which has an essentially rural parkland character with a strong perceived connection with the wider countryside. This proposed development would severely degrade Bouskell Park's rural character and its perceived connection to the wider countryside.  The proposal runs counter to the recommendations of the Blaby District Landscape and Settlement Character Assessment (LSCA) which has an important role in assessing the effect a development would have on the countryside's landscape. Blaby District Council already have a 5 year supply of deliverable housing sites (as defined by the NPPF) to meet the District's requirements for new housing, so it is not necessary to support development proposals that do not align with planning policy.  A development of this size (over 200 dwellings) in this location is not justified by the outstanding housing requirement numbers for Blaby defined in Policy CS5, Housing Distribution.   2. Policy on Historic Environment and Culture, Conservation and Heritage (CS20) (CS2) (SHLAA)   The proposed site is next to the Blaby Conservation Area which is also designated as an 'open area of importance to the form and character of the built environment.' The proposed development is so close to the Conservation Area it would have a very adverse impact on the area and would be against policy on Historic Environment and Culture (CS20) which seeks to preserve and enhance the cultural heritage of the District and states that proposed development should avoid harm to the significance of historic sites, buildings or areas, including their setting.  Policy CS2 ' Design of New Development has as one of its objectives 'to protect the important areas of the District's natural environment (species and habitats), landscape and geology and to improve biodiversity, wildlife habitats and corridors through the design of new developments''. The proposed development would have a significant negative impact on existing wildlife corridors and the wildlife habitat in and around Bouskell Park which is part of the Conservation Area. The Strategic Housing Land Availability Assessment (SHLAA) also emphasises the importance of considering the impact any proposed development would have on the Conservation Area.  The following three objection points relate directly to these planning policies:-  1.	Blaby's Bouskell Park, which is part of the Conservation Area and just a few metres from the proposed housing site, is regarded as the best historical site in the District.  2.	Leicestershire County Council has classified the heritage potential of the proposed site as High (Grade 1). It is immediately adjacent to the site of a medieval village ' the original settlement of Blaby.  3.	The Victorian Ice House (Grade II listed) and pond, both in Bouskell Park, will lose all sense of place and context if they are just a few metres from a modern housing estate. I believe that no amount of interpretative panels and new infrastructure would be able to compensate for this fundamental and irretrievable loss of setting and context.   3. Loss of Valuable Green Space & Infrastructure (CS14) (CS15)    The proposed development on this site is not consistent with policy on Green Infrastructure (CS14). The site is crossed by a popular wooded permissive path (Long Walk), footpaths, a bridleway and a National Cycle Route (Guthlaxton Trail). It is an area loved and enjoyed by many local residents. In addition visitors travel from across the District and in some cases from across the Country to enjoy the area and explore the District's heritage. The government have decided to protect 'green space of special importance to local communities,' now called Local Green Spaces (LGS) in the NPPF (para. 76 ' 77). This popular and very attractive area falls into this category and meets all the LGS selection criteria defined in the NPPF. LGS status for the Long Walk area has the overwhelming backing of the community.  Policy on Open Spaces, Sport and Recreation (CS15) seeks to ensure that all residents have access to sufficient, high quality, accessible open space, sport and recreation facilities. It states that existing open space, sport and recreation facilities will be protected, and where possible enhanced. Where development is proposed on existing open space, sport and recreation facilities, land should not be released, either in total or in part unless it can be demonstrated that it is surplus to requirements for its current play and open space function. The Local Plan CS (Issues, problems and challenges facing the District) para. 4.3 states that, 'A recent survey of play and open spaces has indicated that the District is broadly lacking in these facilities.' I believe that this site is clearly a very high quality and valuable open space that is not at all surplus to requirements.  Blaby District Green Space Strategy:- refers to the NPPF 'Existing green spaces should not be built on unless they are surplus to requirements and losses are replaced with equivalent or better provision in terms of quantity and quality (NPPF, paragraph 74).' Policy CS14 Green Infrastructure 6.19.  Policy CS2 is also relevant.   4. This Application is Premature with regard to Local Green Space Designation   I regard this application as premature because it could prejudice emerging plans. The adopted Local Plan Core Strategy does not support a housing development on this site. Also, with particular relevance to this application, there is widespread support for designating the area around Long Walk as a Local Green Space (LGS) as defined in the NPPF.  The call for LGS designation of this site is supported by local residents, the L&R Wildlife Trust, the RSPB, walking groups, the Leicestershire Footpaths Association, Natural England, local Parish Councils and many District and County Councillors. Site specific planning issues such as LGS designation are covered by the emerging Local Plan Delivery DPD (previously called the Allocations, Designations and Development Management DPD) and also the Neighbourhood Plan being prepared by Blaby Parish Council. Blaby Parish Council has indicated that they seek to protect this special Green Space in the Neighbourhood Plan.  The application proposes a substantial development on this site that will have a significant impact on the future development of Blaby. If an outline planning application is approved prior to adoption of the Delivery DPD and the Neighbourhood Plan it could prejudice the DPD by predetermining decisions about the scale and location of new development which are being addressed in the DPD. In view of this, the application is considered to be premature and potentially prejudicial to emerging plans.   5. Flood Risk & Climate Change   The Hall Farm site is close to a floodplain and, historically, Blaby has had a problem with repeated flooding. We are told that, because of climate changes, we are to expect more frequent extreme weather events that could lead to localised flooding. Large scale building on the site could compromise flood prevention and mitigation measures, and result in increased local flooding risk on the site and more importantly elsewhere. Policy on Climate Change (CS21) and the NPPF refer to the importance of good site selection for new development.  It is not unusual for flooding of the River Sence and its tributaries to affect the road connections to Leicester, especially at Crow Mills at South Wigston and the A426 between Blaby and Glen Parva, resulting in severe road congestion in and around Whetstone, Blaby and Wigston, as motorists attempt to find alternative routes. An extra 200 plus houses to the east of Blaby, off Hospital Lane, would make the situation worse, because of the extra traffic that would discharge into Hospital Lane and because increased water run-off rate from the site following extreme weather could increase the severity and frequency of flooding.

It has been owned by Leicestershire County Council since 1931 and it forms the eastern boundary of Blaby.  It borders the Blaby Conservation Area and an attractive park (Bouskell) with beautiful protected specimen trees, a restored Grade 2 listed Victorian Icehouse and a pond. The Long Walk woodland with a very popular and attractive permissive path runs from Bouskell Park through the centre of the site and links with other popular walking routes.  There are also footpaths, a bridleway and a National Cycle Route passing through the site.  Fields on Hall Farm land have been sensitively farmed for many years by a local farmer, other parts of the estate have been left relatively undisturbed. Long Walk links directly to the Guthlaxton Cycle Trail, a bridleway and other paths enabling walkers and riders to undertake 'combination walks' linking together popular areas such as the Ford at Glen Parva, Oakfield Park & Blaby Oaks (Woodland Trust), Crow Mill and the canal path. A walk from Bouskell Park features in a book on walks in Leicestershire from the country parks.  Many people do walks of several miles, which is possible because of the different links that are available. Over recent years the County Council, Blaby District Council and the Parish Council have invested in improved infrastructure, better access, signage and footpaths etc to improve the amenity value of the area. A well known local county and district councillor described this network as Blaby's primary area for walking, exercise and leisure in the countryside. Leicestershire County Council designated the Long Walk woodland a (albeit rather small) Country Park in 2009. It was called the 'Long Wood' on some signs. Local residents and people from across the district now use the area as a base for outdoor recreation and exercise, often starting from Bouskell Park itself and continuing on through Long Walk to link up with other popular areas. We have survey evidence that reveals that people from across the county (especially south of Leicester) and even from across the country visit the area to take advantage of the excellent walking and exercise opportunities available here. Bouskell Park is characterised by a very strong perceived connection to the wider countryside, if the area around Long Walk were to be developed that connection would be lost and its amenity value would be severely degraded.  A very valuable wildlife corridor would also be lost or severely degraded. Survey evidence indicates that many regular visitors would not use Bouskell Park as the starting point for their walks if the Long Walk surroundings were developed for housing because the perceived connection to the countryside would be lost. It is an area of varied landscape and diverse habitat: with parkland, mixed woodland, hedgerows, bushes, small trees and scrub, farm land, small brooks and ponds.  It leads to further diverse areas, this makes it a particularly interesting environment and the diversity of habitat and the wildlife corridors favour wildlife. We think it is one of the best areas for outdoor recreation and the appreciation of nature and heritage to the immediate south of Leicester and we think this justifies calling it a truly multi-functional green space. The 'Vision' of the Local Plan Core Strategy says that 'there will be a comprehensive and connected network of Green Infrastructure where habitats will be protected and a variety of species will be encouraged to thrive' (CS 2.3). Those without that option would loose a valuable opportunity for outdoor exercise and would be severely disadvantaged.  4. Leicestershire County Council designated the Long Walk woodland a (albeit rather small) Country Park in 2009. It was called the 'Long Wood' on some signs.  Local residents and people from across the district now use the area as a base for outdoor recreation and exercise, often starting from Bouskell Park itself and continuing on through Long Walk to link up with other popular areas. We have survey evidence that reveals that people from across the county (especially south of Leicester) and even from across the country visit the area to take advantage of the excellent walking and exercise opportunities available here. Bouskell Park is characterised by a very strong perceived connection to the wider countryside, if the area around Long Walk were to be developed that connection would be lost and its amenity value would be severely degraded.  A very valuable wildlife corridor would also be lost or severely degraded.  Survey evidence indicates that many regular visitors would not use Bouskell Park as the starting point for their walks if the Long Walk surroundings were developed for housing because the perceived connection to the countryside would be lost. It is an area of varied landscape and diverse habitat: with parkland, mixed woodland, hedgerows, bushes, small trees and scrub, farm land, small brooks and ponds.  It leads to further diverse areas, this makes it a particularly interesting environment and the diversity of habitat and the wildlife corridors favour wildlife.  We think it is one of the best areas for outdoor recreation and the appreciation of nature and heritage to the immediate south of Leicester and we think this justifies calling it a truly multi-functional green space. The 'Vision' of the Local Plan Core Strategy says that 'there will be a comprehensive and connected network of Green Infrastructure where habitats will be protected and a variety of species will be encouraged to thrive' (CS 2.3).  Building here would compromise a connected network that already exists.  Blaby District Green Space Strategy 2012: The National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF para. 74) provides against building on green spaces and the sites of sports and recreational buildings for non-recreational uses. The NPPF (para. 76) indicates that local communities can identify for special protection green areas of particular importance by designating land as Local Green Space. Policy CS14 Green Infrastructure (GI) (page 76) Blaby District Council and its partners will seek to protect existing, and provide new, networks of multi-functional green spaces. This network will comprise public and privately owned land. Green Infrastructure can include formal open spaces for sport and recreation, green areas that can be used for informal recreation, areas that are valuable for their biodiversity (flora and fauna and network links), areas that are of cultural importance (heritage assets and their settings), areas that maintain natural and ecological processes (such as floodplains) and other areas that contribute to the health and quality of life of communities.  Policy CS14 (page 76) In accordance with the Blaby Town Centre Masterplan opportunities will be explored with partners to improve Bouskell Park as a recreational resource. We think that building on the land immediately adjacent to Bouskell Park and around Long Walk will destroy the sense of openness and space in the park and destroy the apparent connection to the wider countryside.  We maintain this will very seriously degrade the recreational and wildlife resource that we already have in Bouskell Park    4.	Prematurity of this Application with regard to Local Green Space Designation  We regard this application as premature as it could prejudice emerging plans.  The adopted Local Plan Core Strategy does not support a housing development on this site.  Moreover, especially relevant to this application is that there is widespread support for designating the area around Long Walk as a Local Green Space (LGS) as defined in the NPPF.  The call for LGS designation of this site is supported by local residents, the L&R Wildlife Trust, the RSPB, walking groups, the Leicestershire Footpaths Association, Natural England, local Parish Councils and many District / County Councillors.  Site specific planning issues such as LGS designation are covered by the emerging Local Plan Delivery DPD (previously called the Allocations, Designations and Development Management DPD) and also the Neighbourhood Plan being prepared by Blaby Parish Council.  Blaby Parish Council have indicated that they seek to protect this special Green Space in the Neighbourhood Plan.  The application proposes a substantial development on this site that will have a significant impact on the future development of Blaby.  If an outline planning application is approved prior to adoption of the Delivery DPD and the Neighbourhood Plan it could prejudice the DPD by predetermining decisions about the scale and location of new development which are being addressed in the DPD.  In view of this, this application is considered to be premature and potentially prejudicial to emerging plans.  Supporting Notes Policy CS 14 (GI) (page 77) In line with emerging national policy, this Council will explore the use of the emerging Local Green Space designation in identifying, for special protection, green areas of particular importance to local communities, and apply this where appropriate through the Allocations, Designations and Development Management DPD. (Now renamed the Delivery DPD.)  5.	Flood Risk & Climate Change  Impact on local flooding risk: the Hall Farm site is close to a floodplain and historically Blaby has had a problem with repeated flooding. We are told that because of climate changes we are to expect more frequent extreme weather events that could lead to localised flooding. Large scale building on the site could compromise flood prevention and mitigation measures and result in increased local flooding risk on the site and more importantly elsewhere. Policy on Climate Change (CS21) and the NPPF refer to the importance of good site selection for new development.   It is not unusual for flooding of the River Sence and its tributaries to affect the road connections to Leicester, especially at Crow Mills at South Wigston and the A426 between Blaby and Glen Parva, resulting in severe road congestion in and around Whetstone, Blaby and Wigston as motorists attempt to find alternative routes. An extra 200 plus houses to the east of Blaby off Hospital Lane would make the situation worse, firstly because of the extra traffic that would discharge into Hospital Lane and secondly increased water run-off rate from the site following extreme weather could increase the severity and frequency of flooding.  Supporting Notes The River Sence floodplain (Flood Zone 2/3) is to the immediate north of the site. A Flood Risk Assessment (FRA) will be required as part of any planning application to demonstrate how surface water run off will be managed on the low permeability soil. Flood risk on the site, and upstream and downstream must not be increased and where possible should be reduced. NPPF Para 103. When determining planning applications, local planning authorities should ensure flood risk is not increased elsewhere and only consider development appropriate in areas at risk of flooding where, informed by a site-specific flood risk assessment.   Policy CS21 Climate Change (page 92) 7.21.4 The Council recognises that preparing for the effects of climate change (adaptation) by minimising vulnerability and providing resilience is also important. Some degree of climate change is already inevitable, and is likely to have a range of impacts, including increased temperatures in the summer and increased risk of flooding or droughts. The Council will encourage development to plan for these impacts recognising the role of Green Infrastructure in bringing together important considerations of biodiversity, heat, water, healthy living and transport needs to create environments in which people want to live and work in the future. Good site selection is also important, particularly in relation to flooding and water resources.   Other Objections    1.	General Objections and Quotes   We are certainly not opposed to all new development in principle.  The government have decided to devolve more power over planning decisions to local communities (Localism Bill & NPPF). The community think this proposal is a singularly inappropriate and unwelcome development which has wide ranging negative implications for the environment and residents of the District (survey and petition evidence is available).  The proposed site is not just another area of green space / countryside on the 'edge of town'  it is a particularly valuable area with high amenity value to the local community and to a wider community in the region.  It is also described as important to the form and character of the landscape and it has high heritage potential.  Bouskell Park, the historic Long Walk and the green spaces that surround it form Blaby's breathing space, its green 'Jewel in the Crown,' arguably Blaby's finest asset  it should be preserved to protect the quality of life of local residents and provide a haven for wildlife.  Its loss would be a tragedy for Blaby on several levels.  Bouskell Park is one of the Council's strategic green spaces and we strive to keep improving it. Blaby District Green Space Strategy 2012.  We think it is undeniable that this proposed development will harm Bouskell Park.  This outline planning application is opposed by the overwhelming majority of the community, many local Councillors and the Parish Council.  This is not a NIMBY protest - the community want to have a say in shaping their local environment and want to protect this vital green infrastructure as a key part of the settlement of Blaby.  Bouskell Park is a beautiful public park on the site of a 10th century medieval village (the original settlement of Blaby) with a pond and a Victorian Ice House (a Grade II Listed building).  Interpretative panels give visitors the history of the area and the wildlife to be seen.  If the park was to be 'hemmed-in' by housing it would loose much of its amenity value to residents and it would be too small and isolated to be the valuable habitat for wildlife it is at present.  If the wooded Long Walk with its very popular permissive path were to be surrounded with an estate of over 200 houses it would result in a considerable reduction in the amenity value of the Long Walk area to local residents and is very strongly opposed by the community.  If the proposed development went ahead it would isolate Long Walk from the surrounding countryside and it is then likely that it would become unpopular with many users who use it extensively at present.  It could easily become an unattractive wooded 'back ally' in the centre of a housing estate, which could attract fly tipping and anti-social behaviour.  2.	Protected Species   Badgers are known to live in the area and the site provides them with good quality foraging habitat and cover (see WYG Blaby District Council: Phase 1 Habitat Survey 2008  LDF evidence base). Badgers and their setts are protected under the Protection of Badgers Act 1992.  Bats are known to roost close by (possibly the old Hall Farm buildings) and Long Walk is a very important wildlife corridor that provides both feeding habitat and links between other important feeding sites.  The Bouskell Park area is used for local 'bat walks' organised by Blaby District Council. Bats are poorly catered for in planning development.  Bat boxes are a very poor substitute for the habitat loss which bats often suffer and there is a low occupancy rate. The real issue is usually the loss of bats' feeding areas. They need a large area over which to forage. The loss of the included farmland would be a real loss to the many bats that live and feed on the Hall Farm estate land.  All British bat species and their roosts are legally protected under the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981.a member of the local bat group.  There is potential for white-clawed crayfish and possibly water voles in the small brook running parallel to Hospital Lane and further survey work should be performed to assess the potential loss of habitat.  Sometimes the water flow is low, but in recent years it has rarely run dry and 'deeper pools may sustain wildlife during drought.' See the WYG 2008 Phase 1 Habitat Survey reference above.       3.	Health and Wellbeing BDC state on their website that Our parks and open spaces provide visual breaks in the built environment and contribute to the health of the local residents by creating clean and attractive environments that provide opportunities for a wide range of formal and informal leisure, sport, recreational and play for all ages, as well as offering other social benefits such as community cohesion, learning and development.  We agree completely with this statement and believe that a large scale building development on this site would substantially degrade Bouskell Park and the surrounding open spaces that make it a very special and valuable place.  This a very important area for recreation, sport, leisure and social cohesion within the community. It is regularly used by people from many different parts of the District and further afield (we have survey evidence). Please don't allow it to be spoilt, to do so would be a disgrace to the District and the County of Leicestershire. Instead please give it protection from inappropriate development by making it a special 'Local Green Space' in line with the NPPF (NPPF para 76  77 refers).  The area is used as part of the Blaby Health Walks programme organised by Blaby District Sports Alliance and Blaby District Council aimed at encouraging local people of all ages to take more exercise. 'Blaby Buggy Walks', organised by Blaby District Council use Bouskell Park.  Parents with young children frequently use Long Walk as a safe and healthy way of accessing the countryside.  The network of paths which has Bouskell Park and Long Walk at its heart is used by orienteering, walking and running groups and clubs, including Leicestershire & Rutland Walking Group. The proposed development would seriously compromise this centre of health and wellbeing.  Blaby scores highly in Quality of Life surveys  see for example BDC Contact spring 2010 issue  good access to high quality countryside is an important factor.  Many residents have based their decision to move to and live in the district largely because of the easily accessible green spaces. Long Walk behind Bouskell Park is at the heart of this special local green infrastructure.  If a housing development of the type and scale proposed was to go ahead, a very likely consequence of the degradation of this green space would be that residents who have the option would get in their cars and drive to more distant areas to enjoy the countryside. Those without that option would loose a valuable opportunity for outdoor exercise and would be severely disadvantaged.  4.	Inadequate Local Infrastructure  Local infrastructure is not capable of supporting a development of this size and in this location. We do not think the proposed development is properly sustainable.  The size of the proposed residential development significantly exceeds the residual housing requirement for Blaby as defined by the Local Plan, CS5, Housing distribution.  Hospital Lane is already severely congested during peak periods especially at the junction with Leicester Road / Countesthorpe Road to the east of Blaby. Welford Road in Blaby is also now congested at busy times and can be difficult for pedestrians to cross. The proposed development would make the situation a great deal worse in Blaby, Whetstone, Glen Parva

CaseNodeId: Ecology  The unusually wide range of habitats in a relatively small area encourages a rich variety of wildlife. Over 50 species of birds have been reported using Bouskell Park and the surrounding area. We have a list of recent wildlife sightings in and around the park and Long Walk.  The different closely connected elements in the area create an interesting and diverse habitat that encourages a variety of wildlife. On Hall Farm estate itself habitats include, mixed woodland, hedgerows, small areas of young trees and bushes, small areas of scrub, small brooks and a well vegetated pond plus the included farmed estate land which is often used for grass. There is excellent hunting habitat for birds of prey such as owls and kestrels. The immediately adjacent park land of Bouskell contains a pond (next to the Icehouse and less than 30m from the proposed housing development), the Black Spinney and several magnificent protected specimen trees. There is a larger pond close by on private land. Take one part of the habitat mix away and the whole environmental infrastructure would be degraded and could collapse and disappear.
