CommentOriginal: The following proposal is in conflict with both the adopted Blaby District Core Strategy & 'saved' local plan policies (for the purposes of this statement will be referred to as the adopted development plan) and well as the National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) & its associated guidance (for the purposes of this statement government policy) for the following reasons and should be refused.  The main reasons we will cover are as follows:-  Blaby does have a 5 year land supply both at a district level and at Parish level. With the Parish having a proven track record of meeting its local plan housing targets. The development is contrary to national guidance on sustainable development specifically paragraphs 6 to 16 of the National Planning Policy framework (Achieving sustainable development and the presumption in favour of sustainable development) and that the applicant has failed to assess other potentially more sustainable sites.   5 year land supply  The applicant does not contest that the site is, neither an allocated site for development by any part of the adopted development, or that it would be allocated in the near future, if at all. The applicant also acknowledges that this site would not normally be suitable for development especially residential development. The main basis for the applicants argument for approving a site which the applicant itself admits would not be suitable, is that Blaby district has not got a five year land supply.  This is an erroneous and flawed argument for the following reasons: - District wide  Due to the adoption of the Blaby Core Strategy and the fact the Lubbesthorpe SUE (which is Blaby's single largest housing allocation) has been granted outline permission Blaby district does indeed have a five year land supply which should not be open to debate. This is further backed up by the Planning Inspectorate in recent appeal decision received in January 2014 regard Land at Seine Lane/Forest Road, Enderby, Leicestershire (APP/T2405/A/13/2200867) where the inspector states that 'I am satisfied that the Council has been able to demonstrate that it has a five year supply of deliverable housing sites in accordance with the National Planning Policy Framework (Framework)'. This decision was less than 6 months ago and considering that  house building has increased significantly recently with government reporting that 'housing starts have reached a 6 year high' (http://www.bbc.co.uk/news/business-26271803) therefore in all probability development is likely to come forward sooner than suggested, so Blaby will have more deliverable sites within the next 5 years rather than fewer so it is likely they can demonstrate an even more healthy five year supply.  The applicants basis for suggesting that the council has hasn't actually got a 5 year land supply seems based primarily on the validity of the build rates of the Lubbesthorpe SUE  because of: - a)	The on-going legal challenge from Leicestershire Police  SUE  b)	The build rates have been over estimated Lubbesthorpe SUE  Due to a legal challenge by Leicestershire Police the Lubbesthorpe SUE will be delayed or not developed at all This legal challenge is not against the precedent or the legality of the actual development per se but against whether there is a legal basis to infrastructure provision specifically whether police infrastructure funding should come at the start or be phased during the development process. Therefore Leicestershire Police which has submitted the legal challenge has acknowledged that this development will happen, so to argue it will or it won't is not a valid argument it is just a challenge regarding infrastructure. Also just because someone has raised a legal challenge on a planning approval doesn't invalidate the decision only if the legal challenge is successful, so for any 5 year land supply this should be counted as a valid approval and should be counted as a deliverable site. This is further enhanced by the fact that all infrastructure providers (except Leicestershire Police), local authorities (County and District), and the one single land owner are supporting and expecting this development to go ahead. If the Planning Inspector agrees with the applicant's argument that the ongoing legal challenge does undermine any 5 year land supply then this could potentially set a precedent which will lead to developers submitting spurious legal challenges on nearby developments to undermine local authority's 5 year land supply.  The build rates have been over estimated Lubbesthorpe SUE Whilst it is accepted that development has not yet started at Lubbesthorpe, as mentioned previously development starts are at a 6 year high, which means that once the reserve matters planning application has been granted (under  government guidance this should take no longer than 13 weeks) development can start extremely quickly as there is obviously demand for the housing. This argument is further enhanced by the fact that the land is mainly owned by one single land owner so there will be no issue over delays caused by multiple land owners and is allocated in a local plan which means that the precedent for the development has been established. It also located in a sustainable location on the western boundary of the city of Leicester with significant infrastructure being provided to make the development as sustainable as possible especially in regards to the provision extensive bus routing (which it is worth reminding the inspector and the applicant that no sustainable transport measures are proposed for this particular development)  We would respectfully remind the Planning Inspector again of recent appeal decision Land at Seine Lane/Forest Road, Enderby, Leicestershire (APP/T2405/A/13/2200867) where the Inspector in this case ruled that Blaby does have a 5 year land supply, with the inspector being happy with the proposed build rates at the SUE which for record is located less than 1km away from that the Seine Lane/Forest Road appeal site.  5 Year land supply at a Parish Level.  The Parish of Blaby has a housing target identified within the adopted Blaby Core Strategy of a minimum of 420 houses to be built by 2029 and following the recent approval for 46 dwellings at the Leicester Lions Rugby Football Club (13/0941/1/OX) the Parish of Blaby is now has (approved and under construction) a total 446 dwellings with about 15 years of the plan remaining, which is about 6% over its target. This shows that Blaby as Parish has pragmatically met its housing requirements and also that no additional dwellings in the short term are needed.  It's also worth highlighting the fact that this housing figure is based on an 'objectively assessed housing need' which means this is the number of dwellings that Blaby as a town can support has now been exceeded.  This is particularly important as the only basis for approval on lack of 5 year land supply is that this proposal will meet a short term need in the next 5 years which cannot be provided elsewhere. However it is obvious that Blaby Parish has no need for an additional 220 houses which means that this particular development would not meet a short term need. Also approving these additional 220 dwellings would mean that Blaby will provide 666 dwellings which would be an additional 37% beyond its original target still with about 15 years of the plan to run, putting immense pressure on the existing services including schools, medical facilities, and the local transport network. Also Blaby Parish Council has recently started the process to prepare a Neighbourhood Plan, and has been granted neighbourhood forum status. It could therefore be argued that the applicant is attempting to bypass the plan making process by not engaging in the neighbourhood plan making process. Recent planning appeals have backed the right of neighbourhood forums to guide development even if the neighbourhood plan has yet to be consulted on.   The development is contrary national guidance on sustainable development specifically paragraphs 6 to 16 of the National Planning Policy framework (Achieving sustainable development & the presumption in favour of sustainable development) and that the applicant has failed to assess other potentially more sustainable sites.  Whilst the applicant is arguing that the Blaby District does not have a 5 year land supply, (and whilst it is the opinion of Blaby Parish council that Blaby has), even if they didn't have a 5 year land supply government guidance is very clear that this does not mean that every site within the local authority area would be available for development. Development has to be proved to be sustainable which this particular site clearly is not.   This particular site is an unallocated greenfield site as defined by the Blaby Development plan. There appears to have been no attempt made at any stage to properly allocate this site for development through the local planning process and the applicant as part of their supporting information have acknowledged that this is a site that would not be normally suitable for development. The applicant has made no attempt to prove that there are no more suitable sites for development within Blaby District, the Government has again recently repeated that development should be focused on Brownfield previously developed sites, before high quality greenfield sites are looked at for development. Various former factory sites exist in both Blaby and Whetstone which are vacant awaiting developers to acquire them for residential development.  In this case it is quite obvious this is a high quality green field site because it has extensive heritage, natural and social value. It is adjacent to the Blaby conservation area and listed Blaby Icehouse, it is also located close to existing heritage assets such as Parish church and Blaby hall. It is a site of obvious biodiversity benefit, both for both plants and animal and well as an important recreational facility including a public bridleway & a local footpath known as a the Long Walk. The applicant stresses the fact that they will provide access green space as part of the development however this will be significantly less than the already accessible green space which currently exists. This particular development will also significantly impact the local road network due to the increased car use, at the last census (2011) 87% of the households of Blaby have at least 1 car, and assuming that car ownership at the proposed development is the Blaby minimum, it would mean at least an additional 191 vehicles. The main access to the site is via the already congested hospital Lane, which we would strongly suggest the planning inspector visits this road during the AM peak to show how busy it already is again contrary to the transport assessments which have been prepared by the County Council. Also contrary to the views of the Leicestershire County Council which it needs to be stressed are both the local transport authority and also the applicant for the planning application, it is located nowhere near any existing bus stops so would not be served by a good bus service. Even at the closest point of the site next to the Thistly Meadow Primary school it is over 600metres away from the nearest bus with the centre of the site over 1km away. It is important to point out that this is contrary to the Department of Transport's recommendation, that all no development should be more than maximum of 400 metres away for a bus stop and the County Council's own guidance that at least 75% of development should be 250metres from a bus stop. This would mean that residents will not use the local bus service as suggested but will be encouraged to use the car, this will add further pressure to the existing constrained road network and will increase emissions, further highlighting that this is not a sustainable development. It is accepted however the site is currently served by a very good cycle route, however looking at the proposed Masterplan little attempt has been made at this stage to integrate this with this proposed development, which would mean that proposed residents will not use this important assets and this would almost certainly deter current uses, which further damages this developments sustainable credentials. The applicant states that this will provide affordable housing which is needed in the area and so ensure that the development is sustainable, however as the applicant is the County Council who will not be building these particular houses but will be selling the land to a house builder. Recent changes in legalisation regarding section 106 mean that an applicant can renegotiate affordable housing part of a signed 106 which means that whilst the County may agree to this there is no guarantee that these affordable houses will be delivered meaning that this particular argument is not valid.

The Parish of Blaby has a housing target identified within the adopted Blaby Core Strategy of a minimum of 420 houses to be built by 2029 and following the recent approval for 46 dwellings at the Leicester Lions Rugby Football Club (13/0941/1/OX) the Parish of Blaby is now has (approved and under construction) a total 446 dwellings with about 15 years of the plan remaining, which is about 6% over its target. This shows that Blaby as Parish has pragmatically met its housing requirements and also that no additional dwellings in the short term are needed.  It's also worth highlighting the fact that this housing figure is based on an 'objectively assessed housing need' which means this is the number of dwellings that Blaby as a town can support has now been exceeded.   This is particularly important as the only basis for approval on lack of 5 year land supply is that this proposal will meet a short term need in the next 5 years which cannot be provided elsewhere. However it is obvious that Blaby Parish has no need for an additional 220 houses which means that this particular development would not meet a short term need. Also approving these additional 220 dwellings would mean that Blaby will provide 666 dwellings which would be an additional 37% beyond its original target still with about 15 years of the plan to run, putting immense pressure on the existing services including schools, medical facilities, and the local transport network.  Also Blaby Parish Council has recently started the process to prepare a Neighbourhood Plan, and has been granted neighbourhood forum status. It could therefore be argued that the applicant is attempting to bypass the plan making process by not engaging in the neighbourhood plan making process. Recent planning appeals have backed the right of neighbourhood forums to guide development even if the neighbourhood plan has yet to be consulted on.    The development is contrary national guidance on sustainable development specifically paragraphs 6 to 16 of the National Planning Policy framework (Achieving sustainable development & the presumption in favour of sustainable development) and that the applicant has failed to assess other potentially more sustainable sites.  Whilst the applicant is arguing that the Blaby District does not have a 5 year land supply, (and whilst it is the opinion of Blaby Parish council that Blaby has), even if they didn't have a 5 year land supply government guidance is very clear that this does not mean that every site within the local authority area would be available for development. Development has to be proved to be sustainable which this particular site clearly is not.   This particular site is an unallocated greenfield site as defined by the Blaby Development plan. There appears to have been no attempt made at any stage to properly allocate this site for development through the local planning process and the applicant as part of their supporting information have acknowledged that this is a site that would not be normally suitable for development. The applicant has made no attempt to prove that there are no more suitable sites for development within Blaby District, the Government has again recently repeated that development should be focused on Brownfield previously developed sites, before high quality greenfield sites are looked at for development. Various former factory sites exist in both Blaby and Whetstone which are vacant awaiting developers to acquire them for residential development.  In this case it is quite obvious this is a high quality green field site because it has extensive heritage, natural and social value. It is adjacent to the Blaby conservation area and listed Blaby Icehouse, it is also located close to existing heritage assets such as Parish church and Blaby hall. It is a site of obvious biodiversity benefit, both for both plants and animal and well as an important recreational facility including a public bridleway & a local footpath known as a the Long Walk. The applicant stresses the fact that they will provide access green space as part of the development however this will be significantly less than the already accessible green space which currently exists. This particular development will also significantly impact the local road network due to the increased car use, at the last census (2011) 87% of the households of Blaby have at least 1 car, and assuming that car ownership at the proposed development is the Blaby minimum, it would mean at least an additional 191 vehicles. The main access to the site is via the already congested hospital Lane, which we would strongly suggest the planning inspector visits this road during the AM peak to show how busy it already is again contrary to the transport assessments which have been prepared by the County Council. Also contrary to the views of the Leicestershire County Council which it needs to be stressed are both the local transport authority and also the applicant for the planning application, it is located nowhere near any existing bus stops so would not be served by a good bus service. Even at the closest point of the site next to the Thistly Meadow Primary school it is over 600metres away from the nearest bus with the centre of the site over 1km away. It is important to point out that this is contrary to the Department of Transport's recommendation, that all no development should be more than maximum of 400 metres away for a bus stop and the County Council's own guidance that at least 75% of development should be 250metres from a bus stop. This would mean that residents will not use the local bus service as suggested but will be encouraged to use the car, this will add further pressure to the existing constrained road network and will increase emissions, further highlighting that this is not a sustainable development. It is accepted however the site is currently served by a very good cycle route, however looking at the proposed Masterplan little attempt has been made at this stage to integrate this with this proposed development, which would mean that proposed residents will not use this important assets and this would almost certainly deter current uses, which further damages this developments sustainable credentials. The applicant states that this will provide affordable housing which is needed in the area and so ensure that the development is sustainable, however as the applicant is the County Council who will not be building these particular houses but will be selling the land to a house builder. Recent changes in legalisation regarding section 106 mean that an applicant can renegotiate affordable housing part of a signed 106 which means that whilst the County may agree to this there is no guarantee that these affordable houses will be delivered meaning that this particular argument is not valid.

Name: Cllr Christine Merrill
Address:
16 Walnut Grove
Glen Parva
Leicester
LE2 9HT
CommentOriginal: I am a Blaby District Councillor for Saxondale ward, which borders the proposed development.  I believe that there are clear planning reasons why this application should be refused.  Using up-to-date figures, Blaby District can demonstrate a five year housing land supply; indeed in the non-PUA area, the figures go well beyond five years.  Blaby has a Core Strategy which was approved last year and in that a minimum of 420 dwellings should be built in the settlement of Blaby within the period covered by the Strategy, which runs until 2029.  Counting sites built, being built or approved, that minimum figure has already been exceeded.  To add another 220 houses on top would exceed that minimum figure by nearly 60%.  To approve this application would therefore go against policy CS5 - Housing Distribution and be counter to the District's strategic aims on where new housing should be located.  The application site is located in countryside.  Policy CS 18 ' Countryside states that the need to retain Countryside will be balanced against the need to provide new development (including housing) in the most sustainable locations.  As there is no pressing need to approve such a large development for the settlement of Blaby, approval would go against policy CS18.  Blaby Parish has recently been designated as a Neighbourhood Planning area.  The DCLG publication on Neighbourhood Planning says that this is 'a new way for communities to decide the future of the places where they live and work. They will be able to choose where they want new homes, shops and offices to be built.'  To approve this application would therefore undermine the ability of the Parish to drive development at a local level and be counter to government policy.    Paragraph 4.5.4 of LVA part 1 of the application states that the site 'does not contain any specific landscape features of acknowledged importance (although they are of moderate quality and have local value). The landscape character is not rare and the site has no particular scenic quality or conservation value. It does however, have a recreational value associated with Long Walk woodland and the public rights of way.'  This grudging acknowledgement of the site's local importance seriously underestimates what the site really means to locals.  This is not the Cotswolds or the Lake District.  It is a piece of land of varied character on the edge of a semi-urban settlement; indeed I estimate that by the nearest walking route it is only ½ mile from the Leicester City boundary.  It offers a peaceful, extended oasis and is well-used, not just by residents of Blaby village, but by those from other local settlements.  The application preserves the footpaths and the Long Walk, but not their surroundings.  The current 'openness' contributes to the value of the open space even for those parts which are not publically accessible.  Approval would therefore have a significant detrimental impact on visual amenity.   The area provides important links to historical settlements ' to Bouskell Park, the conservation area of Blaby and the moat area of Glen Parva.  The varied nature of the wider surroundings ' semi-managed parkland, the coniferous woodland of the Long Walk, field paths across cultivated fields, newly planted traditional woodland in Blaby Oaks ' adds to the enjoyment for walkers, cyclists and horse riders. This variety must also be good for wildlife ' others are better qualified than I to comment on this, although I have seen muntjac here.  Two of the key parts of Blaby's vision for the District are 'Health and well being for all' and 'Sustaining and improving the environment'.  Yes, that includes providing appropriate, well-designed housing, but not at the expense of damaging an area which already serves a significant role in pursuing this vision.

Name: J Michelle Watkiss
CommentOriginal: I object to the proposed development of 220 new dwellings off Hospital Lane in Blaby.  As a local resident I am extremely concerned that this development could me approved despite the virtually unanimous opposition of local residents.  The following are my objections: Bouskell Park and the adjoining Long Walk as well as the parkland belonging to Blaby Hall are areas of essentially rural habitat which are of significant benefit to local people, both in terms of their physical health and mental health.  The introduction to the National Planning Policy Framework states that 'Our natural environment is essential to our wellbeing, and it can be better looked after than it has been.'  The obvious antithesis to this is that the degradation of our natural environment will have detrimental effects on the wellbeing of the local community.  Many residents have chosen a home in Blaby precisely because they enjoy this specific countryside which is now under threat. The introduction to the National Planning Policy Framework also states that 'Sustainable means ensuring that better lives for ourselves don't mean worse lives for future generations.'  If the planned development of 220 houses were to go ahead, removing the link between Bouskell park and the countryside around it and leaving the Long Walk as an island of woodland inside a housing development, my own children, their peers and the future generations would literally be losing out due to this government's insistence on building houses in order to 'create churn in the market' (the last is a quote from a Gladman representative, acknowledging that there was in fact no housing shortage in the area, on Monday 7th October 2013 when I spoke to him at Thistly Meadow primary school.)  The housing would break the link between Hospital lane, Bouskell Park and rural areas such as Mill Lane bridal way, the river Sence, Glen Parva Moat land and Alison's acre as well as the canal which together form regular leisure routes for walkers and cyclists.  The walks, bird watching, bike rides and running routes we now enjoy would be spoiled for future generations. This objection is supported by planning policy on countryside (CS18) which states that 'Within areas designated as Countryside, planning permission will not be granted for built development, or other development which would have a significantly adverse effect on the appearance or character of the landscape.'  This land is designated as Countryside, and breaking the link between these local rural areas will have a significantly adverse effect not only on the character of the landscape but also on the existing wildlife corridors and the wildlife habitat in and around Bouskell Park which is part of the Conservation Area.  Furthermore, Policy CS2, Design of New Development, states that it has as one of its objectives to 'protect the important areas of the District's natural environment (species and habitats), landscape and geology and to improve biodiversity, wildlife habitats and corridors through the design of new developments'' A development of this size in this location runs completely counter to this objective.  Animals and birds which currently live and nest in the Long Walk and the area near the pond in Bouskell park will not continue to live in an isolated strip of land so close to dwellings and which will doubtless be degraded by its juxtaposition to human population. It is surely impossible to disregard the above, particularly in the light of the fact that these new houses are not required in this area.  In August 2013 the Planning Inspectorate accepted that Blaby District Council had demonstrated a five year supply of deliverable housing sites in accordance with the NPPF.  The 220 houses would result in a local housing supply more than 50% over the CS target, with 15 years still to run.  The statement in Appendix A page 17 of Gladman's 'Statement of Community Involvement' which says 'It is clear that there is a substantial shortage of housing to meet the present and future needs of the community within the district of Blaby.' is evidently not factually correct.    On the same page in Appendix A Gladman poses the question 'Why is the site suitable for development?' In answering the question Gladman states that the area 'offers access to the surrounding countryside.' In fact, on the contrary, this development actually destroys a significant section of the surrounding countryside by blocking the path to that countryside for humans and wildlife.  It must not be allowed to go ahead.

52 Little Glen Road
Glen Parva
Leicestershire
LE2 9TS
CommentOriginal: I object on the grounds that I believe the development to be totally inappropriate for this location.    The site is designated as Countryside and this development proposal is not supported by planning policy on Countryside (CS18).  The site is part of the first major countyside space outside of the urban buildings spreading out from Leicester city centre.    This development will have a major adverse effect on the Blaby Conservation area!  It takes away access to land that links the site of the original medieval village, Blaby Hall and its Ice House, Bouskell Park, Glen Parva Manor and its Moat Land and Alison's Acre.  This area is a major recreational facility with recognised cycle routes, footpaths and bridle routes.  It is an area that links Bouskell Park with and the Long Walk and provides access to Mill Lane, a traffic safe route for walkers, cyclists and horse riders going to Glen Parva Manor area or Crow Mills.   I believe this development would have a major impact on the traffic movement in this part of Leicestershire, especially during times of flooding.  The proposed site borders the river Sence flood plain.  That river floods regularly at Kilby Bridge (A5199) to the east, Crow Mills/Countesthorpe Road to the east and Leicester Road (A426) to the north.  When such flooding occurs the only exit from Blaby is west along the B582 to Enderby.  This route is congested at peak times even in good conditions, at times of flooding the B4114 could give one of the few routes into the city from a huge portion of the south of the county.  The proposed development could have an adverse effect on the already struggling land drainage system and could add to traffic flow problems. Name: Jonathan Smith
CommentOriginal: 1. Planning Policy on Countryside & the Requirement for New Housing (CS18) (CS5) (LSCA) (NPPF) ' The site is designated as Countryside and this development proposal is not supported by planning policy on Countryside (CS18), which states that  'Within areas designated as Countryside, planning permission will not be granted for built development, or other development which would have a significantly adverse effect on the appearance or character of the landscape.' 'We think it is clear that this proposal will have a significantly adverse effect on the landscape, in particular the appearance and setting of the Blaby Conservation Area, especially Bouskell Park which has an essentially rural parkland character with a strong perceived connection with the wider countryside.  This proposed development would severely degrade Bouskell Park's rural character and its perceived connection to the wider countryside. ' The proposal runs counter to the recommendations of the Blaby District Landscape and Settlement Character Assessment (LSCA) which has an important role in assessing the effect a development would have on the countryside's landscape. 'Blaby District Council already have a 5 year supply of deliverable housing sites (as defined by the NPPF) to meet the District's requirements for new housing, so it is not necessary to support development proposals that do not align with planning policy. 'A development of this size (over 200 dwellings) in this location is not justified by the outstanding housing requirement numbers for Blaby defined in Policy CS5, Housing Distribution.  2. Policy on Historic Environment and Culture, Conservation and Heritage (CS20) (CS2) (SHLAA) ' The proposed site is next to the Blaby Conservation Area which is also designated an 'open area of importance to the form and character of the built environment.'  The proposed development is so close to the Conservation Area it would have a very adverse impact on the area and would be against policy on Historic Environment and Culture (CS20) which seeks to preserve and enhance the cultural heritage of the District and states that proposed development should avoid harm to the significance of historic sites, buildings or areas, including their setting. 'Policy CS2 ' Design of New Development has as one of its objectives 'to protect the important areas of the District's natural environment (species and habitats), landscape and geology and to improve biodiversity, wildlife habitats and corridors through the design of new developments''.  The proposed development would have a significant negative impact on existing wildlife corridors and the wildlife habitat in and around Bouskell Park which is part of the Conservation Area.  The Strategic Housing Land Availability Assessment (SHLAA) also emphasises the importance of considering the impact any proposed development would have on the Conservation Area. 'The following three objection points relate directly to these planning policies. 1.Blaby's Bouskell Park which is part of the Conservation Area and just a few metres from the proposed housing site is regarded as the best historical site in the District. 2.Leicestershire County Council has classified the heritage potential of the proposed site as High (Grade 1). It is immediately adjacent to the site of a medieval village ' the original settlement of Blaby. 3. The Victorian Ice House (Grade II listed) and pond in Bouskell Park will loose all sense of place and context if they are just a few metres from a modern housing estate.  We believe that no amount of interpretative panels and new infrastructure would be able to compensate for this fundamental and irretrievable loss of setting and context.  3. Loss of Valuable Green Space & Infrastructure (CS14) (CS15) The proposed development on this site is not consistent with policy on Green Infrastructure (CS14). The site is crossed by a popular wooded permissive path (Long Walk), footpaths, a bridleway and a National Cycle Route (Guthlaxton Trail). It is an area loved and enjoyed by many local residents. In addition visitors travel from across the District and in some cases from across the Country to enjoy the area and explore the District's heritage. The government have decided to protect 'green space of special importance to local communities,' now called Local Green Spaces (LGS) in the NPPF (para. 76 ' 77).  This popular and very attractive area falls into this category and meets all the LGS selection criteria defined in the NPPF.  LGS status for the Long Walk area has the overwhelming backing of the community.  ' Policy on Open Spaces, Sport and Recreation (CS15) seeks to ensure that all residents have access to sufficient, high quality, accessible open space, sport and recreation facilities.  It states that existing open space, sport and recreation facilities will be protected, and where possible enhanced. Where development is proposed on existing open space, sport and recreation facilities, land should not be released, either in total or in part unless it can be demonstrated that it is surplus to requirements for its current play and open space function. The Local Plan CS (Issues, problems and challenges facing the District) para. 4.3 states that, 'A recent survey of play and open spaces has indicated that the District is broadly lacking in these facilities.' Ibelieve that this site is clearly a very high quality and valuable open space that is not at all surplus to requirements.  ' Blaby District Green Space Strategy:- refers to the NPPF 'Existing green spaces should not be built on unless they are surplus to requirements and losses are replaced with equivalent or better provision in terms of quantity and quality (NPPF, paragraph 74).' Policy CS14 Green Infrastructure 6.19.  Policy CS2 is also relevant.  4. Prematurity of this Application with regard to Local Green Space Designation 'I regard this application as premature as it could prejudice emerging plans.  The adopted Local Plan Core Strategy does not support a housing development on this site.  Moreover, especially relevant to this application is that there is widespread support for designating the area around Long Walk as a Local Green Space (LGS) as defined in the NPPF. 'The call for LGS designation of this site is supported by local residents, the L&R Wildlife Trust, the RSPB, walking groups, the Leicestershire Footpaths Association, Natural England, local Parish Councils and many District / County Councillors. 'Site specific planning issues such as LGS designation are covered by the emerging Local Plan Delivery DPD (previously called the Allocations, Designations and Development Management DPD) and also the Neighbourhood Plan being prepared by Blaby Parish Council.  Blaby Parish Council have indicated that they seek to protect this special Green Space in the Neighbourhood Plan. 'The application proposes a substantial development on this site that will have a significant impact on the future development of Blaby.  If an outline planning application is approved prior to adoption of the Delivery DPD and the Neighbourhood Plan it could prejudice the DPD by predetermining decisions about the scale and location of new development which are being addressed in the DPD.  In view of this, this application is considered to be premature and potentially prejudicial to emerging plans.  5. Flood Risk & Climate Change ' Impact on local flooding risk:' the Hall Farm site is close to a floodplain and historically Blaby has had a problem with repeated flooding. We are told that because of climate changes we are to expect more frequent extreme weather events that could lead to localised flooding. Large scale building on the site could compromise flood prevention and mitigation measures and result in increased local flooding risk on the site and more importantly elsewhere. Policy on Climate Change (CS21) and the NPPF refer to the importance of good site selection for new development. 'It is not unusual for flooding of the River Sence and its tributaries to affect the road connections to Leicester, especially at Crow Mills at South Wigston and the A426 between Blaby and Glen Parva, resulting in severe road congestion in and around Whetstone, Blaby and Wigston as motorists attempt to find alternative routes. An extra 200 plus houses to the east of Blaby off Hospital Lane would make the situation worse, firstly because of the extra traffic that would discharge into Hospital Lane and secondly increased water run-off rate from the site following extreme weather could increase the severity and frequency of flooding

Name: Robert Kind
CommentOriginal: Application no S62A/2014/001  I would like to object to the planning Application no S62A/2014/001 in regard to the proposed 220 new dwellings at Hospital Lane Blaby,Leicestershire. This is a very important open green space enjoyed by a great many people, This plan would destroy a nominated green space as in the core strategy policy CS15. The effect on Bouskell park would be devastating both on the ecological value and habitat of a range of wild life (see core strategy policy CS 18/19) especially the land east of the long walk. I would like to point out that the new house build in Blaby has already exceeded the amount required to be built by 2026 so this would exceed the amount required by 40% This development would have a negative effect on the conservation area and the grade 11 listed Victorian property. Transport At peak times Hospital lane is heavily congested with traffic from Countesthorpe and South Wigston together with the congestion problems on the A426 and the Soar Vally Way which backs up due to pinch points at the railway bridge, County Arms junction and the new bus lanes which have made the congestion worse, 220 new houses would add approximately a further 300/400 cars the  mix as some homes would have more that one car if both partners worked. No bus links have been planned for this area. Blaby has a 5 year land supply to meet the future requirements so this development is not essential.

Name: Richard Thurlow
CommentOriginal: I feel Blaby will be irreversibly damaged by this proposal for the following reasons We will lose an area of outstanding natural beauty that has been used regularly by the residents of Blaby and beyond for recreational purposes for many years.    The proposed development sits on the edge of a conservation area. Building 220 houses overshadowing this area will cause the conservation area to lose its individual charm forever. This application is in violation of the planning policy on Countryside (CS18) due to the affect it will have on the landscape of that area. As a resident of Blaby I know that historically it has had problems with flooding.  Building 220 houses in this area of natural drainage will surely affect the rest of the village and significantly increase the risk of flooding. Often during the winter nearby Crow Mills floods resulting in increased traffic congestion in the Blaby, South Wigston and Countesthorpe areas. Much of this is on Hospital lane where the proposed development sits. Adding another 220 houses to this area will add more cars on the road coupled with the risk of increased flooding due to the development itself.  Blaby has already exceeded the minimum government requirements for delivering housing for the 5 years. As defined in Policy CS5, Housing Distribution.

Name: Jason Watkiss
CommentOriginal: As a local resident since 1997 I wish to make the following objections on items a) insufficient education spaces b) Insufficient road travel capacity.    On item a)  On consulting document '023 Education Impact Assessment' it gives the impression that there is adequate primary school spare places in Table 2, in fact apparently there are 555 spare primary school places in a 2 mile radius. However, upon closer inspection, ~20% (109/555) comes from Parklands in South Wigston and a further ~17% (94/555) from Blaby Stokes school. Unfortunately, after being a local resident and having to make difficult choices of where to send my children we elected Thistly Meadow School instead, and transpired to be overall a great school, whereas as from Table 2 you will see that this school only has 1 spare place (2012), due to the view held still today of its high achievement and which would be within walking distance to the proposed new development.  A further 238 places ~40% (238/550) are available if residents travel between 1.2 and 1.9 miles. Therefore, making this development gives poor provision for education because ~37% (20%+17%) residents would get substandard primary education or 40% of residents have to drive their children to school. Clearly the statistics presented are missing key quality education evidence and reinforces the car travel concern for this potential development.  In fact the conclusions made in section 4.2 are misleading as the report states mitigation no S106 form is required but will be needed for the correct quality of education places i.e. expansion of Thistly meadow. In addition not having sufficient local primary school places will not meet, Policy CS10 states: 'In order to limit the impacts of new development on levels of vehicle movements, congestion and on the environment the preferred approach of Blaby District Council is to seek to reduce the need to travel by private car by locating new development so that people can access services and facilities without reliance on 'Private motor vehicles'.'    On item b) A further 220 houses with each owning 1 car each would indeed lead to at least 220 cars being added to the already overcrowded hospital lane proposed access at a rate dependant on time of day. From the traffic assessment report (Ref: 1342/2/E) section 8.11.3, does suggest a maximum of a vehicle increase of +192 (AM) +193 (PM), at SJ2 Site Access 2/Hospital Lane at peak times (i.e. nearly 220 cars), which would seem unacceptable given that people are also trying to deliver their children to Thistly Meadow school. The traffic assessment report also measures point SJ10 Enderby Road/Blaby By-pass which people also  join top of the  Blaby By-pass by using the road I live on 'Heybrook Avenue' and the Grove Road as a short cut, so the modelling should be improved to address all 'actual traffic routes'. Finally the traffic assessment does not cover the local flooding effect of the river sense when crow mills become flooded once per year and so will not allow access to South Wigston by Countesthorpe Road for this period.  In conclusion, Thistly Meadow School prevents the increase of traffic flow in a safe manner and although the report suggests in section 9.14 with no severe impact the development will have a major impact.

Name: Mrs H Parker
CommentOriginal: Application Reference: S62A/2014/0001/Hospital Lane Blaby  I wish to object to the above planning application as follows:-   Blaby have already built or committed to enough houses that is required to be built in Blaby by 2026 In fact will exceed the requirement by 26.  Therefore the development of 220 houses in this location would exceed the calculated housing requirement of 420 by 40%. Blaby District Council has already demonstrated a 5 year land supply to meet the District's requirements for new housing, it is unnecessary to support a development that is unsustainable and does not align with the Local and National Planning policies. The development compromises green space, landscape and setting.  This site is a well-used, multi-functional green space and an area enjoyed by many local residents and groups of all ages.  It is unique and not surplus to requirement.  The space has been widely nominated as local green space in the Development Plan Document.  This development would have a significantly adverse effect on the appearance and setting of Bouskell Park and its perceived connection with the wider countryside. The Blaby District Landscape and Settlement Character Assessment specifically states that '.development on this site should be resisted'. This site is of ecological value providing important habitat for a range of wildlife including, badgers, bats and owls.  A housing estate on this site would fragment and isolate these habitats and noise and light pollution would deter wildlife. The development would affect the 'Historic Environment and Culture' as it would border on the Blaby Conservation Area and the Victorian Ice House (Grade II listed) and pond in Bouskell Park these will lose all sense of context if they are just a few metres from a housing estate.  According to the Strategic Land Housing Availability Assessment, Leicestershire County Council has classified the heritage potential of this site as High (Grade 1). The development would also create transport problems as the A426 and Soar Valley Way are already extremely congested during peak travel times with no capacity for the increased traffic that would result from a development of this size in this location.  There are no public transport links with any of the existing or planned employment sites throughout the District. In fact there are no bus stops at all along Hospital Lane and Welford Road. The development would create a flood risk.  The north of the Hall Farm estate site is very close to a floodplain and other parts of the site are at high risk of surface water flooding.  The Core Strategy on Climate Change (CS21)  refer to the importance of good site selection for new development to minimise flooding  I trust you will take my views into consideration and will reject this planning application and look forward to hearing from you in due course.   Yours faithfully  H Parker

Name: Amy Cooke
CommentOriginal: I wish to make an objection to the proposed housing development.   The site is designated as Countryside and this development proposal is not supported by planning policy on Countryside (CS18), which states that  'Within areas designated as Countryside, planning permission will not be granted for built development, or other development which would have a significantly adverse effect on the appearance or character of the landscape.'  It is clear that this proposal will have a significantly adverse effect on the landscape, in particular the appearance and setting of the Blaby Conservation Area, especially Bouskell Park which has an essentially rural parkland character with a strong perceived connection with the wider countryside.  This proposed development would severely degrade Bouskell Park's rural character and its perceived connection to the wider countryside. The building development will have cause a loss of natural habitat for wildlife, including protected species such as bats and badgers.   The Hall Farm site is close to a floodplain and Blaby has had problems with repeated flooding. We are told that because of climate changes we are to expect more frequent extreme weather events that could lead to localised flooding. Large scale building on the site could compromise flood prevention and mitigation measures and result in increased local flooding risk on the site and more importantly elsewhere. Policy on Climate Change (CS21) and the NPPF refer to the importance of good site selection for new development. It is not unusual for flooding of the River Sence and its tributaries to affect the road connections to Leicester, especially at Crow Mills at South Wigston and the A426 between Blaby and Glen Parva, resulting in severe road congestion in and around Whetstone, Blaby and Wigston as motorists attempt to find alternative routes. An extra 200 plus houses to the east of Blaby off Hospital Lane would make the situation much worse, firstly because of the extra traffic that would discharge into Hospital Lane and secondly increased water run-off rate from the site following extreme weather could increase the severity and frequency of flooding.  A development of this size (over 200 dwellings) in this location is not justified by the outstanding housing requirement numbers for Blaby defined in Policy CS5, Housing Distribution.   Overall the development will have an adverse effect on Blaby, and one of its best-loved green spaces. Please consider the effects the development will have on the residents of Blaby and its wildlife.

Name: Kathleen Francis
CommentOriginal: I find this planning application very hard to accept for many reasons.   We already have many newly constructed and planned developments in the village, already exceeding the calculated housing requirement. This development would certainly have a detrimental effect on traffic in the area.  Hospital Lane is already very heavily used and is certainly not a major road so that sole access to this many houses would add greatly to volume of traffic and result in safety issues.  Further the A426 Leicester Road to the city is already extremely congested at peak times. This area of Blaby is a very valuable green space for residents and groups of all ages.  Simply surrounding a limited green area with buildings would not be sufficient to benefit people or wildlife. I would urge you to look carefully at these plans and consider the strong feelings of concerned residents

Name: Robert Turnbull
CommentOriginal: My first objection towards this development is around the additional traffic this will cause on an already congested road system.  The proposed 220 houses and potential additional road users will add more pressure to the roads around Blaby and Countesthorpe.  Many of these roads are considered to be country lanes and are already increasing in use with many people ignoring the speed limits.  There have been several accidents recently on Welford Road and Winchester Road which is where the majority of the Hospital Lane traffic will join.  The roads to the motorways are already congested with frequent accidents and constant queuing during the day, and the main route into Leicester is already seriously congested with an almost permanent 'crawl' speed from Blaby to the City centre.  More houses and cars will simply add more pressure to an already over used road system.  Blaby district has already met it's quota for new houses with several large developments already underway in Blaby and Countesthorpe.   My second objection is based on the area.  The land on which this development is planned is in an area of outstanding beauty and historical interest.   The proposed 220 houses will be built on land surrounding the historic Bouskell Park, Ice House, Lake and where it is believed the original medieval settlement of Blaby is.  The houses that will back on to the long walk will cause this area to become an alleyway/cut through and probably a dumping ground.   Currently Bouskell Park, The Long Walk, Mill Lane and surrounding areas are used a great deal by walkers, dog walkers, cyclists and horse riders and is enjoyed by a hundreds of people every day.   This development is not required or wanted by the vast majority of local residents not just because of the additional traffic this will cause to an already busy area - but also because of the historic interest of the area that the houses are to be build on/around.

Name: Kathryn Hall
CommentOriginal: Main Objection - do not destroy our Countryside in Blaby. The proposed site is designated Countryside and should remain so for the existing residents of Blaby and surrounding villages: 1. Planning Policy on Countryside & the Requirement for New Housing (CS18) (CS5) (LSCA) (NPPF)    states that  'Within areas designated as Countryside, planning permission will not be granted for built development, or other development which would have a significantly adverse effect on the appearance or character of the landscape.' It will have an adverse effect on the landscape, in particular the appearance and setting of the Blaby Conservation Area, especially Bouskell Park which has an essentially rural parkland character with a strong perceived connection with the wider countryside.   2. Policy on Historic Environment and Culture, Conservation and Heritage (CS20) (CS2) (SHLAA)    The proposed site is next to the Blaby Conservation Area which is also designated an 'open area of importance to the form and character of the built environment.'  The proposed development is so close to the Conservation Area it would have a very adverse impact on the area and would be against policy on Historic Environment and Culture (CS20) which seeks to preserve and enhance the cultural heritage of the District and states that proposed development should avoid harm to the significance of historic sites, buildings or areas, including their setting. Policy CS2 ' Design of New Development has as one of its objectives 'to protect the important areas of the District's natural environment (species and habitats), landscape and geology and to improve biodiversity, wildlife habitats and corridors through the design of new developments''.  The proposed development would have a significant negative impact on existing wildlife corridors and the wildlife habitat in and around Bouskell Park which is part of the Conservation Area.  The Strategic Housing Land Availability Assessment (SHLAA) also emphasises the importance of considering the impact any proposed development would have on the Conservation Area. The following three objection points relate directly to these planning policies. Blaby's Bouskell Park which is part of the Conservation Area and just a few metres from the proposed housing site is regarded as the best historical site in the District. Leicestershire County Council has classified the heritage potential of the proposed site as High (Grade 1). It is immediately adjacent to the site of a medieval village ' the original settlement of Blaby.  The Victorian Ice House (Grade II listed) and pond in Bouskell Park will loose all sense of place and context if they are just a few metres from a modern housing estate.  We believe that no amount of interpretative panels and new infrastructure would be able to compensate for this fundamental and irretrievable loss of setting and context. 3. Loss of Valuable Green Space & Infrastructure (CS14) (CS15)  The proposed development on this site is not consistent with policy on Green Infrastructure (CS14). The site is crossed by a popular wooded permissive path (Long Walk), footpaths, a bridleway and a National Cycle Route (Guthlaxton Trail). It is an area loved and enjoyed by many local residents. In addition visitors travel from across the District and in some cases from across the Country to enjoy the area and explore the District's heritage. The government have decided to protect 'green space of special importance to local communities,' now called Local Green Spaces (LGS) in the NPPF (para. 76 ' 77).  This popular and very attractive area falls into this category and meets all the LGS selection criteria defined in the NPPF.  LGS status for the Long Walk area has the overwhelming backing of the community. Policy on Open Spaces, Sport and Recreation (CS15) seeks to ensure that all residents have access to sufficient, high quality, accessible open space, sport and recreation facilities.  It states that existing open space, sport and recreation facilities will be protected, and where possible enhanced. Where development is proposed on existing open space, sport and recreation facilities, land should not be released, either in total or in part unless it can be demonstrated that it is surplus to requirements for its current play and open space function. The Local Plan CS (Issues, problems and challenges facing the District) para. 4.3 states that, 'A recent survey of play and open spaces has indicated that the District is broadly lacking in these facilities.' We believe that this site is clearly a very high quality and valuable open space that is not at all surplus to requirements. Blaby District Green Space Strategy:- refers to the NPPF 'Existing green spaces should not be built on unless they are surplus to requirements and losses are replaced with equivalent or better provision in terms of quantity and quality (NPPF, paragraph 74).' Policy CS14 Green Infrastructure 6.19.  Policy CS2 is also relevant. 4. Prematurity of this Application with regard to Local Green Space Designation The adopted Local Plan Core Strategy does not support a housing development on this site.  Moreover, especially relevant to this application is that there is widespread support for designating the area around Long Walk as a Local Green Space (LGS) as defined in the NPPF. The call for LGS designation of this site is supported by local residents, the L&R Wildlife Trust, the RSPB, walking groups, the Leicestershire Footpaths Association, Natural England, local Parish Councils and many District / County Councillors. Site specific planning issues such as LGS designation are covered by the emerging Local Plan Delivery DPD (previously called the Allocations, Designations and Development Management DPD) and also the Neighbourhood Plan being prepared by Blaby Parish Council.  Blaby Parish Council have indicated that they seek to protect this special Green Space in the Neighbourhood Plan. The application proposes a substantial development on this site that will have a significant impact on the future development of Blaby.  If an outline planning application is approved prior to adoption of the Delivery DPD and the Neighbourhood Plan it could prejudice the DPD by predetermining decisions about the scale and location of new development which are being addressed in the DPD.  In view of this, this application is considered to be premature and potentially prejudicial to emerging plans.  5. Flood Risk & Climate Change  Impact on local flooding risk:' the Hall Farm site is close to a floodplain and historically Blaby has had a problem with repeated flooding. We are told that because of climate changes we are to expect more frequent extreme weather events that could lead to localised flooding. Large scale building on the site could compromise flood prevention and mitigation measures and result in increased local flooding risk on the site and more importantly elsewhere. Policy on Climate Change (CS21) and the NPPF refer to the importance of good site selection for new development. It is not unusual for flooding of the River Sence and its tributaries to affect the road connections to Leicester, especially at Crow Mills at South Wigston and the A426 between Blaby and Glen Parva, resulting in severe road congestion in and around Whetstone, Blaby and Wigston as motorists attempt to find alternative routes. An extra 200 plus houses to the east of Blaby off Hospital Lane would make the situation worse, firstly because of the extra traffic that would discharge into Hospital Lane and secondly increased water run-off rate from the site following extreme weather could increase the severity and frequency of flooding.   The community of Blaby and its residents think this proposal is a singularly inappropriate and unwelcome development which has wide ranging negative implications for the environment and residents of the District (survey and petition evidence is available). The proposed site is not just another area of green space / countryside on the 'edge of town' ' it is a particularly valuable area with high amenity value to the local community and to a wider community in the region.  It is also described as important to the form and character of the landscape and it has high heritage potential. 'Bouskell Park, the historic Long Walk and the green spaces that surround it form Blaby's breathing space, its green 'Jewel in the Crown,' arguably Blaby's finest asset ' it should be preserved to protect the quality of life of local residents and provide a haven for wildlife.  Its loss would be a tragedy for Blaby on several levels.' 'Bouskell Park is one of the Council's strategic green spaces and we strive to keep improving it.' ' Blaby District Green Space Strategy 2012.  We think it is undeniable that this proposed development will harm Bouskell Park. This outline planning application is opposed by the overwhelming majority of the community, many local Councillors and the Parish Council. 'This is not a NIMBY protest ' the community want to have a say in shaping their local environment and want to protect this vital green infrastructure as a key part of the settlement of Blaby.' Bouskell Park is a beautiful public park on the site of a 10th century medieval village (the original settlement of Blaby) with a pond and a Victorian Ice House (a Grade II Listed building).  Interpretative panels give visitors the history of the area and the wildlife to be seen.  If the park was to be 'hemmed-in' by housing it would loose much of its amenity value to residents and it would be too small and isolated to be the valuable habitat for wildlife it is at present. If the wooded Long Walk with its very popular permissive path were to be surrounded with an estate of over 200 houses it would result in a considerable reduction in the amenity value of the Long Walk area to local residents and is very strongly opposed by the community. If the proposed development went ahead it would isolate Long Walk from the surrounding countryside and it is then likely that it would become unpopular with many users who use it extensively at present.  It could easily become an unattractive wooded 'back ally' in the centre of a housing estate which could attract fly tipping and anti-social behaviour.   2. Protected Species     Badgers are known to live in the area and the site provides them with good quality foraging habitat and cover (see WYG Blaby District Council: Phase 1 Habitat Survey 2008 ' LDF evidence base). Badgers and their setts are protected under the Protection of Badgers Act 1992. Bats are known to roost close by (possibly the old Hall Farm buildings) and Long Walk is a very important wildlife corridor that provides both feeding habitat and links between other important feeding sites. The Bouskell Park area is used for local 'bat walks' organised by Blaby District Council. 'Bats are poorly catered for in planning development.  Bat boxes are a very poor substitute for the habitat loss which bats often suffer and there is a low occupancy rate. The real issue is usually the loss of bats' feeding areas. They need a large area over which to forage. The loss of the included farmland would be a real loss to the many bats that live and feed on the Hall Farm estate land.  All British bat species and their roosts are legally protected under the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981.' ' a member of the local bat group. There is potential for white-clawed crayfish and possibly water voles in the small brook running parallel to Hospital Lane and further survey work should be performed to assess the potential loss of habitat.  Sometimes the water flow is low, but in recent years it has rarely run dry and 'deeper pools may sustain wildlife during drought.'      3. Health and Wellbeing  BDC state on their website that 'Our parks and open spaces provide visual breaks in the built environment and contribute to the health of the local residents by creating clean and attractive environments that provide opportunities for a wide range of formal and informal leisure, sport, recreational and play for all ages, as well as offering other social benefits such as community cohesion, learning and development.'  We agree completely with this statement and believe that a large scale building development on this site would substantially degrade Bouskell Park and the surrounding open spaces that make it a very special and valuable place. 'This a very important area for recreation, sport, leisure and social cohesion within the community. It is regularly used by people from many different parts of the District and further afield (we have survey evidence). Please don't allow it to be spoilt, to do so would be a disgrace to the District and the County of Leicestershire. Instead please give it protection from inappropriate development by making it a special 'Local Green Space' in line with the NPPF' (NPPF para 76 ' 77 refers). The area is used as part of the Blaby Health Walks programme organised by Blaby District Sports Alliance and Blaby District Council aimed at encouraging local people of all ages to take more exercise. 'Blaby Buggy Walks', organised by Blaby District Council use Bouskell Park.  Parents with young children frequently use Long Walk as a safe and healthy way of accessing the countryside. The network of paths which has Bouskell Park and Long Walk at its heart is used by orienteering, walking and running groups and clubs, including Leicestershire & Rutland Walking Group. The proposed development would seriously compromise this centre of health and wellbeing. Blaby scores highly in Quality of Life surveys ' see for example BDC Contact spring 2010 issue ' good access to high quality countryside is an important factor. Many residents have based their decision to move to and live in the district largely because of the easily accessible green spaces. Long Walk behind Bouskell Park is at the heart of this special local green infrastructure. If a housing development of the type and scale proposed was to go ahead, a very likely consequence of the degradation of this green space would be that residents who have the option would get in their cars and drive to more distant areas to enjoy the countryside. Those without that option would loose a valuable opportunity for outdoor exercise and would be severely disadvantaged.     4. Inadequate Local Infrastructure     Local infrastructure is not capable of supporting a development of this size and in this location. We do not think the proposed development is properly sustainable.  The size of the proposed residential development significantly exceeds the residual housing requirement for Blaby as defined by the Local Plan, CS5, Housing distribution. Hospital Lane is already severely congested during peak periods especially at the junction with Leicester Road / Countesthorpe Road to the east of Blaby. Welford Road in Blaby is also now congested at busy times and can be difficult for pedestrians to cross. The proposed development would make the situation a great deal worse in Blaby, Whetstone, Glen Parva, Countesthorpe and South Wigston.     5. Ecology     The unusually wide range of habitats in a relatively small area encourages a rich variety of wildlife. Over 50 species of birds have been reported using Bouskell Park and the surrounding area. We have a list of recent wildlife sightings in and around the park and Long Walk add hyperlink. The different closely connected elements in the area creates an interesting and diverse habitat that encourages a variety of wildlife. On Hall Farm estate itself habitats include, mixed woodland, hedgerows, small areas of young trees and bushes, small areas of scrub, small brooks and a well vegetated pond plus the included farmed estate land which is often used for grass. There is excellent hunting habitat for birds of prey such as owls and kestrels. The immediately adjacent park land of Bouskell contains a pond (next to the Icehouse and less than 30m from the proposed housing development), the Black Spinney and several magnificent protected specimen trees. There is a larger pond close by on private land. Take one part of the habitat mix away and the whole environmental infrastructure would be degraded and could collapse and disappear. The Leicestershire & Rutland Wildlife Trust and the RSPB have recognised the importance of wildlife corridors on the site and the role these play in sustaining a variety of wildlife in the area and increasing the value of the area to visitors. NPPF Para 118. When determining planning applications, local planning authorities should aim to conserve and enhance biodiversity by applying the following principles:  If significant harm resulting from a development cannot be avoided (through locating on an alternative site with less harmful impacts), adequately mitigated, or, as a last resort, compensated for, then planning permission should be refused. The estate provides corridors for wildlife that we think play an important role in the wider wildlife context of the area. (see 2008 Phase 1 Habitat Survey for details) We think that the area is quite special and possibly unique in this region to the south of Leicester which is relatively poor in good habitat compared with many other parts of the county. Policy CS19 Bio-diversity and geo-diversity (page 86) In terms of species protection, the Council will protect those species which do not receive statutory protection under a range of legislative provisions, but have been identified as requiring conservation action as a species of principal importance for the conservation of biodiversity nationally. Any development proposals should ensure that these species and their habitats are protected from the adverse effects of development through the use of appropriate mitigation measures.
