Bouskell Park, the historic Long Walk and the green spaces that surround it form Blaby's breathing space, its green 'Jewel in the Crown,' arguably Blaby's finest asset  it should be preserved to protect the quality of life of local residents and provide a haven for wildlife.  Its loss would be a tragedy for Blaby on several levels.  Bouskell Park is one of the Council's strategic green spaces and we strive to keep improving it. Blaby District Green Space Strategy 2012.  We think it is undeniable that this proposed development will harm Bouskell Park. This outline planning application is opposed by the overwhelming majority of the community, many local Councillors and the Parish Council.  This is not a NIMBY protest - the community want to have a say in shaping their local environment and want to protect this vital green infrastructure as a key part of the settlement of Blaby.  Bouskell Park is a beautiful public park on the site of a 10th century medieval village (the original settlement of Blaby) with a pond and a Victorian Ice House (a Grade II Listed building).  Interpretative panels give visitors the history of the area and the wildlife to be seen.  If the park was to be 'hemmed-in' by housing it would loose much of its amenity value to residents and it would be too small and isolated to be the valuable habitat for wildlife it is at present. If the wooded Long Walk with its very popular permissive path were to be surrounded with an estate of over 200 houses it would result in a considerable reduction in the amenity value of the Long Walk area to local residents and is very strongly opposed by the community. If the proposed development went ahead it would isolate Long Walk from the surrounding countryside and it is then likely that it would become unpopular with many users who use it extensively at present.  It could easily become an unattractive wooded 'back ally' in the centre of a housing estate which could attract fly tipping and anti-social behaviour.   2. Protected Species     Badgers are known to live in the area and the site provides them with good quality foraging habitat and cover (see WYG Blaby District Council: Phase 1 Habitat Survey 2008 - LDF evidence base). Badgers and their setts are protected under the Protection of Badgers Act 1992. Bats are known to roost close by (possibly the old Hall Farm buildings) and Long Walk is a very important wildlife corridor that provides both feeding habitat and links between other important feeding sites. The Bouskell Park area is used for local 'bat walks' organised by Blaby District Council.  Bats are poorly catered for in planning development.  Bat boxes are a very poor substitute for the habitat loss which bats often suffer and there is a low occupancy rate. The real issue is usually the loss of bats' feeding areas. They need a large area over which to forage. The loss of the included farmland would be a real loss to the many bats that live and feed on the Hall Farm estate land.  All British bat species and their roosts are legally protected under the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981.a member of the local bat group. There is potential for white-clawed crayfish and possibly water voles in the small brook running parallel to Hospital Lane and further survey work should be performed to assess the potential loss of habitat.  Sometimes the water flow is low, but in recent years it has rarely run dry and 'deeper pools may sustain wildlife during drought.'      3. Health and Wellbeing  BDC state on their website that 'Our parks and open spaces provide visual breaks in the built environment and contribute to the health of the local residents by creating clean and attractive environments that provide opportunities for a wide range of formal and informal leisure, sport, recreational and play for all ages, as well as offering other social benefits such as community cohesion, learning and development.'  We agree completely with this statement and believe that a large scale building development on this site would substantially degrade Bouskell Park and the surrounding open spaces that make it a very special and valuable place.  This a very important area for recreation, sport, leisure and social cohesion within the community. It is regularly used by people from many different parts of the District and further afield (we have survey evidence). Please don't allow it to be spoilt, to do so would be a disgrace to the District and the County of Leicestershire. Instead please give it protection from inappropriate development by making it a special 'Local Green Space' in line with the NPPF (NPPF para 76 - 77 refers). The area is used as part of the Blaby Health Walks programme organised by Blaby District Sports Alliance and Blaby District Council aimed at encouraging local people of all ages to take more exercise. 'Blaby Buggy Walks', organised by Blaby District Council use Bouskell Park.  Parents with young children frequently use Long Walk as a safe and healthy way of accessing the countryside. The network of paths which has Bouskell Park and Long Walk at its heart is used by orienteering, walking and running groups and clubs, including Leicestershire & Rutland Walking Group. The proposed development would seriously compromise this centre of health and wellbeing. Blaby scores highly in Quality of Life surveys - see for example BDC Contact spring 2010 issue - good access to high quality countryside is an important factor. Many residents have based their decision to move to and live in the district largely because of the easily accessible green spaces. Long Walk behind Bouskell Park is at the heart of this special local green infrastructure. If a housing development of the type and scale proposed was to go ahead, a very likely consequence of the degradation of this green space would be that residents who have the option would get in their cars and drive to more distant areas to enjoy the countryside. Those without that option would loose a valuable opportunity for outdoor exercise and would be severely disadvantaged.     4. Inadequate Local Infrastructure     Local infrastructure is not capable of supporting a development of this size and in this location. We do not think the proposed development is properly sustainable.  The size of the proposed residential development significantly exceeds the residual housing requirement for Blaby as defined by the Local Plan, CS5, Housing distribution. Hospital Lane is already severely congested during peak periods especially at the junction with Leicester Road / Countesthorpe Road to the east of Blaby. Welford Road in Blaby is also now congested at busy times and can be difficult for pedestrians to cross. The proposed development would make the situation a great deal worse in Blaby, Whetstone, Glen Parva, Countesthorpe and South Wigston.     5. Ecology     The unusually wide range of habitats in a relatively small area encourages a rich variety of wildlife. Over 50 species of birds have been reported using Bouskell Park and the surrounding area. We have a list of recent wildlife sightings in and around the park and Long Walk add hyperlink. The different closely connected elements in the area creates an interesting and diverse habitat that encourages a variety of wildlife. On Hall Farm estate itself habitats include, mixed woodland, hedgerows, small areas of young trees and bushes, small areas of scrub, small brooks and a well vegetated pond plus the included farmed estate land which is often used for grass. There is excellent hunting habitat for birds of prey such as owls and kestrels. The immediately adjacent park land of Bouskell contains a pond (next to the Icehouse and less than 30m from the proposed housing development), the Black Spinney and several magnificent protected specimen trees. There is a larger pond close by on private land. Take one part of the habitat mix away and the whole environmental infrastructure would be degraded and could collapse and disappear. The Leicestershire & Rutland Wildlife Trust and the RSPB have recognised the importance of wildlife corridors on the site and the role these play in sustaining a variety of wildlife in the area and increasing the value of the area to visitors. NPPF Para 118. When determining planning applications, local planning authorities should aim to conserve and enhance biodiversity by applying the following principles:  If significant harm resulting from a development cannot be avoided (through locating on an alternative site with less harmful impacts), adequately mitigated, or, as a last resort, compensated for, then planning permission should be refused. The estate provides corridors for wildlife that we think play an important role in the wider wildlife context of the area. (see 2008 Phase 1 Habitat Survey for details) We think that the area is quite special and possibly unique in this region to the south of Leicester which is relatively poor in good habitat compared with many other parts of the county. Policy CS19 Bio-diversity and geo-diversity (page 86) In terms of species protection, the Council will protect those species which do not receive statutory protection under a range of legislative provisions, but have been identified as requiring conservation action as a species of principal importance for the conservation of biodiversity nationally. Any development proposals should ensure that these species and their habitats are protected from the adverse effects of development through the use of appropriate mitigation measures.

CommentOriginal: I object to the proposal to build an estate of houses that will visually threaten the enjoyment of Bouskall Park. The development will absolutely destroy the character of the park and the long walk, the amenity value of the park and pathways will be lost entirely. It is laughable to suggest that any amount of landscaping or planting could possibly disguise the impact of buildings so close to the beautiful conservation area and listed buildings.  The proposal is inherently unsustainable with the immediate roads clearly unable to cope with any more traffic. The local infrastructure will likewise be unable to cope, schools are full, doctors and dentist surgeries oversubscribed. The impact of the recent new homes at the opposite end of hospital lane has yet to be felt as those developments are not yet fully complete.   Furthermore, I feel that it is morally reprehensible of Leicestershire County Council to offer this land for such a purpose. It is like selling the family silver - never to be replaced - in a one off deal to raise a few pounds that will disappear into the coffers of the County Council.  Although Bouskall Park itself is not threatened -yet - it is an encroachment of the visual amenity in a jewel of Blaby's crown.  I am sure there are plenty of other sites in our area that would create much less impact, than these outlandish proposals have the potential to do, although in the short term they may generate a smaller financial gain.  This is not a nimby objection, almost anywhere in my backyard would be preferable.  Once a precious environment such as this is gone it is lost forever.  I am seventy years old and the impact of these proposals will be small, but someone has to take account of future generations who will ask- how did you let this happen? How could a body acting on behalf of the people of Leicestershire do such a dastardly deed?

CommentOriginal: As a local resident and business owner on Mill Lane, this would impact my business and other local business.  My horse related business is one of the few sustainable on a flood plain such as this whilst also enhancing the countryside enjoyment which is busily used by the many and diversified users of this area for recreation, health and relaxation, who walk, cycle, jog, use mobility scooters etc.  It is a local facility for health and enjoyment of the surrounding population that should not be taken away when there are other areas within Blaby available for building.  The local council is well aware of the problems with flooding in this area, including the problems to graves flooding in the adjacent cemetery.  To build here on this flood plain at this time of increased flooding and climate change would be inviting trouble.  I attended the recent Land for Life meeting and all of the objections they have clearly outlined a totally agree with. Particularly those below:-  3. Loss of Valuable Green Space & Infrastructure (CS14) (CS15) '  The proposed development on this site is not consistent with policy on Green Infrastructure (CS14). The site is crossed by a popular wooded permissive path (Long Walk), footpaths, a bridleway and a National Cycle Route (Guthlaxton Trail). It is an area loved and enjoyed by many local residents. In addition visitors travel from across the District and in some cases from across the Country to enjoy the area and explore the District's heritage. The government have decided to protect 'green space of special importance to local communities,' now called Local Green Spaces (LGS) in the NPPF (para. 76 ' 77).  This popular and very attractive area falls into this category and meets all the LGS selection criteria defined in the NPPF.  LGS status for the Long Walk area has the overwhelming backing of the community.   Policy on Open Spaces, Sport and Recreation (CS15) seeks to ensure that all residents have access to sufficient, high quality, accessible open space, sport and recreation facilities.  It states that existing open space, sport and recreation facilities will be protected, and where possible enhanced. Where development is proposed on existing open space, sport and recreation facilities, land should not be released, either in total or in part unless it can be demonstrated that it is surplus to requirements for its current play and open space function. The Local Plan CS (Issues, problems and challenges facing the District) para. 4.3 states that, 'A recent survey of play and open spaces has indicated that the District is broadly lacking in these facilities.' We believe that this site is clearly a very high quality and valuable open space that is not at all surplus to requirements.  '  Blaby District Green Space Strategy:- refers to the NPPF 'Existing green spaces should not be built on unless they are surplus to requirements and losses are replaced with equivalent or better provision in terms of quantity and quality (NPPF, paragraph 74).' Policy CS14 Green Infrastructure 6.19.  Policy CS2 is also relevant.  5. Flood Risk & Climate Change    ' Impact on local flooding risk:' the Hall Farm site is close to a floodplain and historically Blaby has had a problem with repeated flooding. We are told that because of climate changes we are to expect more frequent extreme weather events that could lead to localised flooding. Large scale building on the site could compromise flood prevention and mitigation measures and result in increased local flooding risk on the site and more importantly elsewhere. Policy on Climate Change (CS21) and the NPPF refer to the importance of good site selection for new development. 'It is not unusual for flooding of the River Sence and its tributaries to affect the road connections to Leicester, especially at Crow Mills at South Wigston and the A426 between Blaby and Glen Parva, resulting in severe road congestion in and around Whetstone, Blaby and Wigston as motorists attempt to find alternative routes. An extra 200 plus houses to the east of Blaby off Hospital Lane would make the situation worse, firstly because of the extra traffic that would discharge into Hospital Lane and secondly increased water run-off rate from the site following extreme weather could increase the severity and frequency of flooding.  I can see no reason whatsoever to ruin this area used by residents far and wide, home to local wildlife and in danger of increasing the flooding already experienced, whilst there are an abundance of building areas already identified above and beyond what is required for the Blaby area.

Name: Jan Johnson
CommentOriginal: My family has lived in Blaby since 1923 I have therefore witnessed many changes to the village over many years. Although it is my understanding that each individual application for planning is entitled to fair and unbiased scrutiny I feel I must object to this latest planning proposal for the reasons listed below. 1.It is my understanding that Blaby has already met government policy for  new housing numbers and indeed has exceeded this target by 26 to date.It is also my understanding that due to this fact the village SHOULD NOT be required to consider further applications for additional housing until 2026.Furthermore, I understand that if this latest application is approved the proposed 220 dwellings will in fact take our village to 40% OVER  government requirements. 2.It is my understanding that it is totally unnecessary to support this application as Blaby District Council has already met the Districts requirements for new housing as demonstrated in a 5 Year Land Supply. 3.I strongly believe that it is unsustainable to consider that Blaby can accommodate any more traffic.Those of us that live in the village are aware how how congested the local roads and the main A426 artery into Leicester are.We are already in the process of having to accommodate the additional traffic capacity with the Winchester Road development which is underway at present. Traffic from this and the proposed Hospital Lane development will meet at the two mini roundabouts where these two roads meet Western Drive and then continue towards the city via  the roundabout where the Blaby Bypass and the main road through the village meet.All of this additional traffic will then meet the already congested Soar Valley Way junction which serves Fosse Park and the M1. All of this without any possibility of improving traffic flow makes this proposed planning application UNSUSTAINABLE. 4. Although the A426 has recently been modified to include 24 hour bus lanes there are NO public transport supporting any of the existing or planned housing sites. 5.It is my understanding that if this application were to go ahead the area will be at HIGH RISK of flooding rendering the proposed site contra to government policy regarding climate change. 6.The area at present is a varied and well used green space enjoyed by the existing residents, it includes a rich variety  of wildlife  and the open area support sport and recreation.It is mt understanding that government policy PROTECTS such LOCAL GREEN SPACE and any development would render the area greatly diminished and detrimental top all existing wildlife species.It is also my understanding that The Blaby District Landscape and Settlement Character Assessment specifically states that this site development should be resisted.  Finally,the local residents have a greatly enhanced quality of life with this beautiful area and this would be greatly diminished if this application is approved.

CommentOriginal: Dear Ms O'Brien,    Planning Application: S62A/2014/0001: Outline planning application with access only. Proposed construction of up to 220 new dwellings (use class C3) and school drop off/pick up zone, with access and associated infrastructure: Land to the North of Hospital Lane, to the South of Mill Lane and to the East of Bouskell Park, Blaby, Leicestershire    Archaeological considerations    Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the above scheme.  Our comments below should be read in conjunction with our earlier correspondences of the 9th and 28th January 2014, and are informed by consideration of the recent Planning Inspectorate Pre-Application Issues Report.      Following further consideration of the development proposals, including on-site inspection, we would reiterate our previous recommendation that the advice of English Heritage and the Conservation Officer is sought regarding the proposed setting impacts to the Conservation Area, Blaby Hall and the associated Bouskell Park and listed Ice House.  We have particular concerns about the intervisibility between Bouskell Park and the development site, which do not appear to be separated by a strong vegetational boundary as the submitted Archaeological Desk-Based Assessment (CgMs October 2013, revised April 2014) suggests.    The retention of Long Walk as a landscape feature within the proposed development is welcomed.  It is disappointing that opportunities to retain Ridge and Furrow earthworks within the development area have not been pursued.  A Topographical Survey of the Ridge and Furrow earthworks should be undertaken prior to the commencement of development, however a conditioned approach to this would be acceptable.      The Leicestershire and Rutland Historic Environment Record (HER) shows that the application site lies within a landscape where archaeological remains are frequent and could reasonably be expected to be encountered within a development of this scale.  Cropmarks thought to represent a series of prehistoric enclosures and a possible drove-way (HER ref: MLE24) are recorded c. 240m to the east of the proposed development site.  Neolithic or Bronze Age worked flint, including a scraper, was recovered to the immediate north of the application site during archaeological monitoring of groundworks in 1998 (HER ref: MLE16145).  A Bronze Age site including a circular structure, cobbled area, hearth, oven and gully (HER ref: MLE140) is also present on the island of the Scheduled moated site at Glen Parva (SM ref: 1008259), c.300m to the north of the application site.  This medieval moated site includes the above-ground remains of a mortared granite wall and below-ground remains of mud walls.  To the west of the application site lies the Historic Settlement Core of Blaby (HER ref: MLE9336) and extensive earthwork and below-ground remains of medieval settlement have been recorded in Bouskell Park (HER ref: MLE19), including finds of medieval pottery and ironworking slag.      Taking into account the known archaeological resource outline above, we disagree with the conclusions of the submitted Archaeological Desk-Based Assessment and feel that the site has potential to contain previously unidentified archaeological remains, however the submitted information is insufficient to ascertain the significance of such remains and therefore to determine the impact of the development.    Although the geophysical survey (ASC report 1313/BHL/01) undertaken in 2010 did not identify any areas of definite archaeological interest, there is a possibility that significant remains are present that have not shown up in the data.  It should be noted that whilst aerial photographic evidence for the application area shows that much of the development area was formerly covered by ridge and furrow earthworks, normally visible to geophysical survey, very little trace of these features is apparent in the submitted report.  This either suggests that the site has been extensively damaged by recent cultivation, or alternatively questions the effectiveness of the survey results.    With regard to the capabilities of geophysical survey (specifically magnetometry), prehistoric features are often poorly defined by such techniques, perhaps due to their shallow nature, small size in plan, similarity of backfill to the natural soils, or paucity of cultural material.  There have been numerous examples of sites in Leicestershire, particularly on clayey soils such as this, where archaeological remains have only been identified as a result of subsequent trial trenching.  Given the presence of prehistoric settlement and activity in the vicinity, there is a potential for archaeological remains of this period to be present within the application site.  Section 4 of the Geophysical Survey report (page 16) states:     'The results of geophysical surveys and interpretation of collected data should not be treated as an absolute representation of the underlying archaeological and non-archaeological remains. Confirmation of the origin of geophysical anomalies and the presence or absence of archaeological remains can only be achieved by direct investigation of sub-surface deposits.'      This is in line with professional archaeological practices and guidance from English Heritage (Geophysical Survey in Archaeological Field Evaluation, English Heritage 2008), which states:     'Lack of geophysical anomalies cannot be taken to imply a lack of archaeological features, and in such cases an alternative evaluation procedure ' eg trial trenching, or the use of a different geophysical technique ' should be considered.'      In our opinion, trial trenching is required to ascertain whether significant archaeological remains are present, to allow an appropriate mitigation strategy to be defined and to demonstrate the sustainability of the proposals as currently tabled.  The submitted scheme demonstrates an incapacity to accommodate change should significant archaeological remains worthy of preservation in situ be identified, hence there is a need to undertake evaluation prior to determination of this application to enable identification of archaeological remains that would warrant re-design or engineering solutions.      The preservation of archaeological remains is, of course, a 'material consideration' in the determination of planning applications. The proposals include operations that may destroy any buried archaeological remains that are present, but the archaeological implications cannot be adequately assessed on the basis of the currently available information.  Since it is possible that archaeological remains may be adversely affected by this proposal, we recommend that the applicant complete an Archaeological Trial Trench Evaluation of the proposed development site prior to determination of any forthcoming planning application.    This will require provision by the applicant for:    '	A field evaluation, by appropriate techniques including trial trenching, to identify and locate any archaeological remains of significance, and propose suitable treatment to avoid or minimise damage by the development.  Further design, civil engineering or archaeological work may then be necessary to achieve this.    This information should be submitted to the Planning Inspectorate before any decision on a future planning application is taken, so that an informed decision can be made.  These recommendations conform to the advice provided in DCLG National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) Section 12, paras. 128, 129 & 135).    The Historic & Natural Environment Team (HNET), Leicestershire County Council, as advisors to the planning authority, will provide a formal Brief for the work and approve a Specification for the Evaluation at the request of the applicant.      Should you have any further queries please do not hesitate to contact us.    Yours sincerely,    Teresa Hawtin  Senior Planning Archaeologist  Leicestershire County Council

Name: Peter Anthony Harvey
CommentOriginal: Planning Applicatin - Hospital Lane S62A/2014/001  I am well aware of the need tom provide additional housing , according to the district planning. Even so, I must object to the above application and would like to support this with the following comments. 1. Within Blaby District , and particularly the village of Blaby, there are already numerous developments underway or recently completed. These are having a great  negative impact on the village and this will only be increased with yet further house building-, especially such a large development of up to 220 houses. Blaby has already exceeded the houses needed to be built. We have enough new housing estates  in Blaby. 2. Hospital Lane provides a vital link road between the  neighbouring villages. It is already congested and the volume of traffic can only increase with this development. The fact that Thistly Meadow School is sited at the Blaby end of the lane has meant that this congestion has increased at the beginning and end of the school day. Already, 2 crossing patrols are needed to keep the children safe. The additional traffic from this development will only add to this hazard and to the local congestion..   3. The area of land intended for development on hospital Lane ,Blaby, is a well-loved, well used area, providing leisure, educational and health promoting activities for local residents,  The numerous well used footpaths offer local residents as well as those from surrounding villages who make use of Bouskell Park and the fields around  access to the wider countryside. It is well used by families, individuals and local groups  for such things as bird-watching, social gatherings , dog walking  and by organised walking groups from the wider Leicestershire areas. 4. This land has been nominated as a Local Green space. It provides a range of habitats which attract and cater for a variety of birds, pond life and animals.. It is used by the local council to promote its Health Walks and for 'bat walks' , because of the high density of bats living there. The Long Walk is realised as a unique resource throughout the region. It is protected by these fields,  5. The designated fields border the old village of Blaby, Blaby Hall and are the site of Blaby's 10th Century medieval village. Their use and conversion to a housing estate would impact on the whole area and destroy much of the historical aspect of the village.  No provision seems tomhave been made mandatory in the plans for development to ensure that the local amenities - medical, schooling, transport - will be improved, extended and developed to cater for the increased village population.  More importantly, this space ids unique and not surplus to requirement. (core strategy Policy CS15)and is widely nominated as Local Green Space.  As such it should be protected for our future residents.

Name: Mrs Gill Hammond-Evans
CommentOriginal: I strongly object ot this planning application. this area is a much-loved and well-used amenity for the people of Blaby and the surrounding area. It is a place of rural tranquility on the edge of Blaby village and is used by walkers, cyclist and horse riders to access a little bit of countryside for exercise and recreation. (Core strategy Policy CS14 and CS15) It is also valuable farm land which produced an excellent crop of maize last year, as well as grazing for cattle. if we continue to build on good farming land then there will be less for this country to grow food to feed the population, leading to an increasing reliance on imports of food. there is no need for such a large number of houses to be built in Blaby, as the number of houses that need to be built in Blaby by 2026 has already been exceeded by 26, so a development of 220 houses in this location would exceed the calculated housing requirement by 40%! There are already two large housing developments being built at this moment in Blaby on previously green field sites, and the infrastructure of roads, schools, doctors and dentists will not be able to cope with any more housing. The local schools are full and it is very difficult tnow o get a doctor's appoinment at either of the two surgeries.  Hospital Lane is a very busy and narrow road which at peak times can take several minutes waiting to cross on foot at the moment, let aone when a further 220 houses are entering and exiting onto Hospital Lane. The A426 and Soar Valley Way leading to the M1 and M69 motorways are already extremely congested at peak travel times with no capacity for the increased traffic that would result from a development of this size in this location. There are no public transport links with any of the existing or planned employment sites throughout the district. this development would also have an adverse effect on the appearance and setting of Bouskell Park and its perceived connection to the wider countryside.(Policy CS18) this is a beautiful and historic park with a Victorian ice house and much wildlife such as bats, badgers and owls which of course uses the land in question as well as the Park itself -wildlife ranges over the area proposed for housing too. there is also a significant risk of Flood Risk, as the site in question is very close to a floodplain and other parts of the site are at high risk of surface water flooding. (CS21) After the very wet winter we have had, this is a significant factor in this area and must be taken seriuosly. it is foolish to build housing so close to the river and its floodplain. Please listen to these clear points of objection. Thank you.

CommentOriginal: We have already built or committed to enough houses in blaby. According to blaby policy the number of houses that need to be built in blaby by 2006 has already been exceeded by 26. A development of 220 houses in this location would exceed the calculated housing requirement by 40% Blaby District council has already demonstrated a 5 year land supply to meet the district requirement for new housing. it is unnecessary to support a development that is unsustainable and does not align with the local and national planning policies. This site is a well used, multi funstional green space and an area enjoyed by many local residents and groups of all ages. (Core strategy policy cs14) Core strategy says that existing open space . sport and recreation facilities will be protected. The open space is unique and not surplus to requirement ( core strategy Policy cs15) The space has been widely nominated as local green space in the development plan document (as referred to in cs15) This development would have a significantly adverse effect on the appearance and the setting of Bouskell Park and its perceived connection with the wider and countryside. The Blaby district Landscape and Settlement Character assessment (LSCA) specifically states that development on this site should be resisted (policy cs18) Core strategy aims to protect the important areas of the districts natural environment (species and habitats) landscape and geology. Name: April Beeby
CommentOriginal: I have lived here in Blaby all my life. I walk and run in Bouskell Park, through the woods behind the park and on the path parallel to the woods a few times every week. Blaby does not need more houses, and our beautiful green space, home to many wildlife, does not deserve to suffer. A modern housing estate will not aesthetically fit in to the old, traditional character of Blaby. Not only will this change our living environment, but it will ruin the landscape. Building new houses will also increase the risk of flooding, which is unfair to the current Blaby community. There is already risk of global warming and extreme weather conditions so we do not need to contribute and stimulate these issues. As well as this, I drive down Hospital Lane everyday during peak times and already the traffic is horrendous therefore we do not need more people with more cars in Blaby. The local schools and doctors are already over subscribed, for example it's extremely difficult to get a doctors appointment and not all local children may be able to attend local schools. Both education and health are vital in life so why make these aspects suffer in such rural idyll? I went to Thistly Meadow Primary School and it's school field backs onto Bouskell Park. With more students attending, more mobile classrooms will have to be built and the only place for these is on the school field. This means there will be less green space for the children to play during lunch times, PE lessons and sports days. What happened to encouraging a healthy lifestyle? I am deeply saddened by this prospect. Once happened, never reversed. As a young member of the community I feel extremely passionate about this. Please do not ruin our village.

Name: Dr Sue Hardy
CommentOriginal: I wish to object to the proposed development on Hospital Lane for the following reasons:  'The Countryside and the requirement for new housing' The proposed site has been designated 'Countryside' and therefore is not supported by planning policy (CS18).  Blaby District Council have in fact demonstrated that they have an adequate 5-year plan without the need to develop this site. The Planning Inspectorate have previously accepted (2013) that the BDC have shown a deliverable 5-year plan persuant to the NPPF.   'The 6Cs guidance adopted by the Leicestershire County Council' The problems associated with the Applicant's travel plan are of great concern. The 6Cs states that 'generally walking distance to bus stops in urban areas should be a maximum of 400 m and preferably no more than 250 m'. The applicant states that the development layout is suitable for bus access and provides opportunity for bus operators to serve the site. In reality there will be no bus stops inside a distance of 800 m of the site. It is extremely unlikely that Arriva (the county's bus service) will detour via Welford Road, Hospital Lane and the site in order to serve 220 houses. Therefore the application does not meet the requirements of the 6Cs guidance.   I am concerned that the Applicant believes that the majority of the traffic from the site will exit Hospital Lane via the mini roundabout on Welford Road. Many inhabitants of Blaby, who work in Leicester do not travel to work via Aylestone Road, rather preferring to go via South Wigston. They therefore exit Hospital Lane at the Countesthrorpe Road junction. Casual observations of morning rush hour traffic suggest that any additional traffic would be a major problem.  At peak times, the traffic queues from that junction tail back beyond the turn for the old Blaby Hospital site. Realistically there would be at least one car per household with a large number of inhabitants commuting to work each morning along a road that is unable to cope with the present volume of traffic.   Current use of the site Many people walk through Bouskell Park, the Long Walk and out onto Hospital Lane. The area has great value to the local inhabitants and beyond. The Pre Application Report states (6.15) 'the proposed development would undoubtedly have an impact on the setting of the routes and the experience of the users' (6.16) 'the largely undeveloped character of the area will be eroded' 'the undeveloped character of the site is an intrinsic element of the recreation resource'   Impact on local services Assuming 2.5 persons per house would mean that there would be an additional 550 people to register at the GP surgery. Whilst there would seem to be a sufficient number of GPs to cope with the demand it is without doubt there would be adverse impact on current waiting times.   There would be an increase in demand for school places. This would probably not affect the secondary schools but there are inadequate places available at Thistly Meadow to serve the site. There is another primary school available (Blaby Stokes) but this is beyond a reasonable walking distance for young families. The area around Blaby Stokes suffers congestion from school traffic at drop off and pick up times. Any additional traffic would greatly increase the hazard risk in that area - a problem seemingly ignored by the Applicant.   Any development would have an adverse effect on the local wildlife. Retaining hedgerows and building bat boxes will not lead to the animals remaining at the site. The additional human activity, particularly at night will drive the wildlife from the site.

Name: kathryn groves
CommentOriginal: i believe the planned build in Blaby, Leicestershire between Hospital Lane and Crow Mills for 220 dwellings should not go ahead.  Not only does our local Blaby Council not approve it but also the local people surrounding the area, which include myself, certainly does not approve it.  The area of Countryside and this development proposal is not supported by planning policy on Countryside (CS18), which states that  'Within areas designated as Countryside, planning permission will not be granted for built development, or other development which would have a significantly adverse effect on the appearance or character of the landscape.'  I believe the character and the ambiance of the beautiful Blaby area will be ruined. We currently already have other dwellings being built in the surrounding area which I did not have objections too but I believe covers our new build quota. Blaby District Council already have a 5 year supply of deliverable housing sites (as defined by the NPPF) to meet the District's requirements for new housing, so it is not necessary to support development proposals that do not align with planning policy.  Another issue added for the build being entirely in the wrong place is flood plains. I know from experience that the area is prone to flooding with even sometimes a nightfall's worth of rain. I could not imagine how bad the floods in that area will be once the planned housing area is built. It is not unusual for flooding of the River Sence and its tributaries to affect the road connections to Leicester, especially at Crow Mills at South Wigston and the A426 between Blaby and Glen Parva, resulting in severe road congestion in and around Whetstone, Blaby and Wigston as motorists attempt to find alternative routes. An extra 200 plus houses to the east of Blaby off Hospital Lane would make the situation worse, firstly because of the extra traffic that would discharge into Hospital Lane and secondly increased water run-off rate from the site following extreme weather could increase the severity and frequency of flooding.       I believe the actual character of Blaby would be at risk. The area itself is currently a nature walk/ bicycle path and is part of the Blaby Health Walks programme organised by Blaby District Sports Alliance and Blaby District Council aimed at encouraging local people of all ages to take more exercise. A lot of residents and people from all over Leicestershire use the area as a rural walk, which encourages people to improve their health and I don't believe you can treat health as a simple walking workout or a cycle workout but it must be treated as a whole and holistically using the area and the actual green space helps improve peoples health. I could not imagine people wishing to walk or cycle around the area once 220 dwelling surround them.  The network of paths which has Bouskell Park and Long Walk at its heart is used by orienteering, walking and running groups and clubs, including Leicestershire & Rutland Walking Group. The proposed development would seriously compromise this center of health and wellbeing. I believe overall the build will be departmental to the area and will influence people's health in a negative way.   Hospital Lane is already severely congested during peak periods especially at the junction with Leicester Road / Countesthorpe Road to the east of Blaby. Welford Road in Blaby is also now congested at busy times and can be difficult for pedestrians to cross. The proposed development would make the situation a great deal worse in Blaby, Whetstone, Glen Parva, Countesthorpe and South Wigston.  These are just some of the reasons I believe the build should not go ahead, I sincerely hope you take the time to think about the issues I have raised also take the time to actually investigate the area, as I can not emphasis enough how this is entirely the wrong build for this area.  It is truly a beautiful corner of Leicestershire I believe we should preserve for our future generations.

Name: Mark Lovell
CommentOriginal: Dear Sir, Reference: PLANNING APPLICATION NO S62A/2014/0001 Outline planning application with access only. Proposed construction of up to 220 new dwellings (use class C3) and school drop off/pick up zone, with access and associated infrastructure, by Gladman Developments Ltd. on Land to the North of Hospital Lane, to the South of Mill Lane and to the East of Bouskell Park, Blaby, Leicestershire. I write in connection with the above planning application. I have examined the plans and I know the site well. I wish to object strongly to this development in this location, for reasons outlined below:  1. Planning Policy on Countryside & the Requirement for New Housing (CS18) (CS5) (LSCA) (NPPF) '	The site is designated as Countryside and this development proposal is not supported by planning policy on Countryside (CS18), which states that 'Within areas designated as Countryside, planning permission will not be granted for built development, or other development which would have a significantly adverse effect on the appearance or character of the landscape." '	I think it is clear that this proposal will have a significantly adverse effect on the landscape, in particular the appearance and setting of the Blaby Conservation Area, especially Bouskell Park which has an essentially rural parkland character with a strong perceived connection with the wider countryside.  This proposed development would severely degrade Bouskell Park's rural character and its perceived connection to the wider countryside. '	The proposal runs counter to the recommendations of the Blaby District Landscape and Settlement Character Assessment (LSCA) which has an important role in assessing the effect a development would have on the countryside's landscape. '	Blaby District Council already have a 5 year supply of deliverable housing sites (as defined by the NPPF) to meet the District's requirements for new housing, so it is not necessary to support development proposals that do not align with planning policy. '	A development of this size (over 200 dwellings) in this location is not justified by the outstanding housing requirement numbers for Blaby defined in Policy CS5, Housing Distribution.    2. Policy on Historic Environment and Culture, Conservation and Heritage (CS20) (CS2) (SHLAA) '	The proposed site is next to the Blaby Conservation Area which is also designated an 'open area of importance to the form and character of the built environment.'  The proposed development is so close to the Conservation Area it would have a very adverse impact on the area and would be against policy on Historic Environment and Culture (CS20) which seeks to preserve and enhance the cultural heritage of the District and states that proposed development should avoid harm to the significance of historic sites, buildings or areas, including their setting. '	Policy CS2 - Design of New Development has as one of its objectives "to protect the important areas of the District's natural environment (species and habitats), landscape and geology and to improve biodiversity, wildlife habitats and corridors through the design of new developments...'The proposed development would have a significant negative impact on existing wildlife corridors and the wildlife habitat in and around Bouskell Park which is part of the Conservation Area.  The Strategic Housing Land Availability Assessment (SHLAA) also emphasises the importance of considering the impact any proposed development would have on the Conservation Area.  The following three objection points relate directly to these planning policies. 1.	Blaby's Bouskell Park which is part of the Conservation Area and just a few metres from the proposed housing site is regarded as the best historical site in the District. 2.	Leicestershire County Council has classified the heritage potential of the site as High (Grade 1). It is immediately adjacent to the site of a medieval village - probably the original settlement of Blaby. 3.	The Victorian Ice House (Grade II listed) and pond in Bouskell Park will loose all sense of place and context if they are just a few metres from a modern housing estate.  We believe that no amount of interpretative panels and new infrastructure would be able to compensate for this fundamental and irretrievable loss of setting and context.   3. Loss of Valuable Green Space & Green Infrastructure (CS14) (CS15) '	Building on this site is not consistent with policy on Green Infrastructure (CS14), which seeks to protect existing, and provide new 'networks of multi-functional green spaces.' The proposed development site represents a well developed and high quality multi-functional green space.  It is crossed by a popular wooded permissive path (Long Walk), footpaths, a bridleway and a National Cycle Route (Guthlaxton Trail).  It is an area loved and enjoyed by many local residents. In addition visitors travel from across the District and in some cases from across the country to enjoy the area and explore the District's heritage. '	The government have decided to protect 'green space of special importance to local communities,' now called Local Green Spaces (LGS) - this area falls into this category and meets all the LGS selection criteria. '	Building on this site is also not consistent with planning policy on Open Spaces, Sport and Recreation (CS15), which states that existing open space, sport and recreation facilities will be protected, and where possible enhanced. Development is allowed only if the area is surplus to requirements. In this case the area clearly has a very high amenity value as open space and is not surplus to requirements.  4. Prematurity of this Application with regard to Local Green Space Designation (NPPF) '	I regard this application as inappropriate and premature as it could prejudice both current and emerging plans. Government introduced a new land designation in 2011 called Local Green Space. As soon as the new designation was announced there was widespread support for designating the area around Long Walk as a Local Green Space (LGS).  Local residents, Parish Councils, wildlife conservation groups and District / County Councillors now support LGS designation for this special site. '	Site specific planning issues such as LGS designation are covered by Neighbourhood Plans and Local Plans.  Blaby Parish Council has indicated that they propose to protect this special Green Space in the Neighbourhood Plan (Blaby Plan) currently under development. '	The application proposes a substantial development on this site that will have a significant impact on the future development of Blaby.  If the application is approved prior to adoption of the Delivery DPD and the Neighbourhood Plan it could prejudice and undermine local plans by predetermining decisions about the scale and location of new development.  In view of this, this application is considered to be premature and prejudicial to current and emerging plans.   5. Flood Risk & Climate Change (CS21) '	This development could have an impact on local flooding risk.  Blaby has had a problem with repeated flooding.  The north of the Hall Farm Estate site is close to a floodplain and parts of the site are at high risk of surface water flooding.  Large scale building on the site could result in increased local flooding risk on the site and more importantly elsewhere. Policy on Climate Change (CS21) and the NPPF refer to the importance of good site selection for new development. '	Flooding of the River Sence and its tributaries often affect the road connections to Leicester, resulting in severe road congestion in and around Blaby as motorists attempt to find alternative routes.  An extra 200 plus houses to the east of Blaby off Hospital Lane would make the situation worse, firstly because of the extra traffic that would discharge into Hospital Lane and secondly because increased water run-off rate from the site following extreme weather events is likely to increase the severity and frequency of flooding. '	It is generally accepted that we should expect and plan for an increased frequency of extreme weather events because of climate change. I would be grateful if the Planning Inspectorate would take my objections into consideration when deciding this application.   Yours faithfully,    M Lovell (Mr)

The government have decided to protect 'green space of special importance to local communities,' now called Local Green Spaces (LGS) - this area falls into this category and meets all the LGS selection criteria.  Building on this site is also not consistent with planning policy on Open Spaces, Sport and Recreation (CS15), which states that existing open space, sport and recreation facilities will be protected, and where possible enhanced. Development is allowed only if the area is surplus to requirements. In this case the area clearly has a very high amenity value as open space and is not surplus to requirements.  4. Prematurity of this Application with regard to Local Green Space Designation (NPPF)  I regard this application as inappropriate and premature as it could prejudice both current and emerging plans. Government introduced a new land designation in 2011 called Local Green Space. As soon as the new designation was announced there was widespread support for designating the area around Long Walk as a Local Green Space (LGS).  Local residents, Parish Councils, wildlife conservation groups and District / County Councillors now support LGS designation for this special site.  Site specific planning issues such as LGS designation are covered by Neighbourhood Plans and Local Plans.  Blaby Parish Council has indicated that they propose to protect this special Green Space in the Neighbourhood Plan (Blaby Plan) currently under development.  The application proposes a substantial development on this site that will have a significant impact on the future development of Blaby.  If the application is approved prior to adoption of the Delivery DPD and the Neighbourhood Plan it could prejudice and undermine local plans by predetermining decisions about the scale and location of new development.  In view of this, this application is considered to be premature and prejudicial to current and emerging plans.   5. Flood Risk & Climate Change (CS21)  This development could have an impact on local flooding risk.  Blaby has had a problem with repeated flooding.  The north of the Hall Farm Estate site is close to a floodplain and parts of the site are at high risk of surface water flooding.  Large scale building on the site could result in increased local flooding risk on the site and more importantly elsewhere. Policy on Climate Change (CS21) and the NPPF refer to the importance of good site selection for new development.  Flooding of the River Sence and its tributaries often affect the road connections to Leicester, resulting in severe road congestion in and around Blaby as motorists attempt to find alternative routes.  An extra 200 plus houses to the east of Blaby off Hospital Lane would make the situation worse, firstly because of the extra traffic that would discharge into Hospital Lane and secondly because increased water run-off rate from the site following extreme weather events is likely to increase the severity and frequency of flooding.  It is generally accepted that we should expect and plan for an increased frequency of extreme weather events because of climate change.  I would be grateful if the Planning Inspectorate would take my objections into consideration when deciding this application.

Name: Laura Thurlow
CommentOriginal: I strongly believe this type of housing development will have a detrimental effect on the local area for a variety of reasons.   Blaby is already a large village to increase the number of homes by 220 will in turn be making a village a town without the require amenities. An area of outstanding natural beauty that is used regularly by the residents of Blaby and beyond for recreational purposes for many years will disappear overnight. There is health problem in this country and to remove an outdoors area such as this  where children can play, run around and spend time safely away from the TV with their parents or guardians would be a huge blow for this area. Blaby District Green Space Strategy contains references to the NPPF `Existing green spaces should not be built on unless they are surplus to requirements and losses are replaced with equivalent or better provision in terms of quantity and quality (NPPF, paragraph 74).` Policy CS14 Green Infrastructure 6.19.  I do not see this replacement in any of the plans and as such this development is breaking this important Green regulations set in place to protect our countryside.    The proposed development sits on the edge of a conservation area of which part is Blaby's Bouskell Park this park is regarded as the best historical site in the District. Building 220 houses overshadowing this area will cause the conservation area to lose its individual charm forever. This application is in violation of the planning policy on Countryside (CS18) due to the affect it will have on the landscape of that area.   In fact Leicestershire County Council (LCC) has classified the heritage potential of the proposed site as high (Grade 1). It is immediately adjacent to the site of a medieval village ' the original settlement of Blaby and the fanatically interesting Victorian Ice House (Grade II listed) and pond in Bouskell Park will lose all sense of place and context if they are just a few metres from a modern housing estate.  We believe that no amount of interpretative panels and new infrastructure would be able to compensate for this fundamental and irretrievable loss of setting and context. Why should we throw away such history and context all for the sake of 220 new boxy houses.    As a resident and a multiple home owner of Blaby I know that historically it has had problems with flooding.  Building 220 houses in this area of natural drainage will surely affect the rest of the village and significantly increase the risk of flooding. Often during the winter nearby Crow Mills floods resulting in increased traffic congestion in the Blaby, South Wigston and Countesthorpe areas. Much of this is on Hospital lane where the proposed development sits. Adding another 220 houses to this area will add more cars on the road coupled with the risk of increased flooding due to the development itself. The developer may argue that a bus lane was added to the main route into Leicester in the last 12 months however this addition has created far more travel problems than it has resolved ' it costs more for two people to travel into Leicester town centre by bus than it does to drive and park for two hours.   Blaby has already exceeded the minimum government requirements for delivering housing for the 5 years. As defined in Policy CS5, Housing Distribution therefore an additional 220 is purely a money making exercise for the already wealthy fat cats.

Name: Kate Kemp
CommentOriginal: I object to the development on the grounds that this area represents an accessible area of natural beauty cherished by the local community for decades. Ask any individual enjoying this stunning area and they will confirm that the open countryside on their doorstep gives them a sense of piece and tranquility; a refuge from modern life and all of its strains.  One only has to take a walk in the area to see how many residents are enjoying all it has to give - come rain or shine you will always encounter families, walkers, cyclists, horseriders, schools and community groups taking advantage of this precious jewel in the heart of Blaby.   Given that the government, doctors and the media tell us so often about the rise in obesity, lack of physical health and fitness, particularly amongst the younger generation, and the obsession of the young with 'screen based' activity - it would be madness to sacrifice this area when the benefits are so clear.   Children need freedom that our streets cannot provide and without areas like this they will be denied the sheer joy of spending time in the great outdoors. The creep of urban sprawl means that spaces on the edge of towns are now being lost forever. These are the places where children make their memories: fishing in ponds, building dens, family picnics, feeding ducks, climbing trees - loosing these spaces is "bad for their happiness" (Dame Fiona Reynolds, head of National Trust.  In addition, we must also seek to preserve the habitat which sustains a wide variety of trees, plants, birds and animals. Again, spaces like these are the only spaces where many city and town dwellers are able to get up close to nature and appreciate its beauty.  Of course, the need for new housing for our ever growing population is undeniable. The issue at hand is where should these new houses go? GIven the points made above we must consider that the negative impact on the local environment, local residents and the excessive strain put on the local infrastructure, which is already bursting at the seams, means that it clearly does not make sense to deny us of this area. It is loved and cherished and we must fight to ensure that future generations experience just what makes this place so special.

Name: Lynn Walker
CommentOriginal: There are numerous reasons why I object to this application to build a housing estate adjacent to Bouskell Park, which is a valuable resource that I have enjoyed using for a great many years as a resident of Blaby district.  1.  Blaby has already committed to and exceeded its housing quota, without this developement.  Blaby District Council already have a 5 year supply of deliverable housing sites (as defined by the NPPF) to meet the District's requirements for new housing, so it is not necessary to support development proposals that do not align with planning policy. A development of this size (over 200 dwellings) in this location is not justified by the outstanding housing requirement numbers for Blaby defined in Policy CS5, Housing Distribution.  2. The location is completely inappropriate due to the proximity of the conservation area and heritage sites.  The proposed site is next to the Blaby Conservation Area which is also designated an 'open area of importance to the form and character of the built environment.'  The proposed development is so close to the Conservation Area it would have an adverse impact on the area and would be against policy on Historic Environment and Culture (CS20) which seeks to preserve and enhance the cultural heritage of the District and states that proposed development should avoid harm to the significance of historic sites, buildings or areas, including their setting.  The 'Ice House' and adjacent pond would be completely overwhelmed by this housing estate.   3. A housing estate would cause a significant loss of this well used and valuable green space and would break the network of byways used by many people for a variety of leisure activities. The proposed development on this site is not consistent with policy on Green Infrastructure (CS14). The site is crossed by a popular wooded permissive path (Long Walk), footpaths, a bridleway and a National Cycle Route (Guthlaxton Trail). It is an area loved and enjoyed by many local residents. In addition visitors travel from across the District and in some cases from across the Country to enjoy the area and explore the District's heritage. The government have decided to protect 'green space of special importance to local communities,' now called Local Green Spaces (LGS) in the NPPF (para. 76 ' 77).  This popular and very attractive area falls into this category and meets all the LGS selection criteria defined in the NPPF.  LGS status for the Long Walk area has the overwhelming backing of the community.  4.  The proposed site is close to a floodplain; Blaby has had a problem with repeated flooding. Due to climate change we should expect more frequent extreme weather events that could lead to localised flooding. Large scale building on the site could compromise flood prevention and mitigation measures and result in increased local flooding risk on the site and more importantly elsewhere. Policy on Climate Change (CS21) and the NPPF refer to the importance of good site selection for new development. It is not unusual for flooding of the River Sence and its tributaries to affect the road connections to Leicester, especially at Crow Mills at South Wigston and the A426 between Blaby and Glen Parva, resulting in severe road congestion in and around Whetstone, Blaby and Wigston as motorists attempt to find alternative routes. An extra 200 plus houses to the east of Blaby off Hospital Lane would make the situation worse, firstly because of the extra traffic that would discharge into Hospital Lane and secondly increased water run-off rate from the site following extreme weather could increase the severity and frequency of flooding.  5.  The area is home to wildlife.  Badgers are known to live in the area and the site provides them with good quality foraging habitat and cover (see WYG Blaby District Council: Phase 1 Habitat Survey 2008 ' LDF evidence base). Badgers and their setts are protected under the Protection of Badgers Act 1992.   Bats are known to roost close by (possibly the old Hall Farm buildings) and Long Walk is a very important wildlife corridor that provides both feeding habitat and links between other important feeding sites. CommentRedacted: There are numerous reasons why I object to this application to build a housing estate adjacent to Bouskell Park, which is a valuable resource that I have enjoyed using for a great many years as a resident of Blaby district.  1.  Blaby has already committed to and exceeded its housing quota, without this developement.  Blaby District Council already have a 5 year supply of deliverable housing sites (as defined by the NPPF) to meet the District's requirements for new housing, so it is not necessary to support development proposals that do not align with planning policy. A development of this size (over 200 dwellings) in this location is not justified by the outstanding housing requirement numbers for Blaby defined in Policy CS5, Housing Distribution.  2. The location is completely inappropriate due to the proximity of the conservation area and heritage sites.  The proposed site is next to the Blaby Conservation Area which is also designated an 'open area of importance to the form and character of the built environment.'  The proposed development is so close to the Conservation Area it would have an adverse impact on the area and would be against policy on Historic Environment and Culture (CS20) which seeks to preserve and enhance the cultural heritage of the District and states that proposed development should avoid harm to the significance of historic sites, buildings or areas, including their setting.  The 'Ice House' and adjacent pond would be completely overwhelmed by this housing estate.   3. A housing estate would cause a significant loss of this well used and valuable green space and would break the network of byways used by many people for a variety of leisure activities. The proposed development on this site is not consistent with policy on Green Infrastructure (CS14). The site is crossed by a popular wooded permissive path (Long Walk), footpaths, a bridleway and a National Cycle Route (Guthlaxton Trail). It is an area loved and enjoyed by many local residents. In addition visitors travel from across the District and in some cases from across the Country to enjoy the area and explore the District's heritage. The government have decided to protect 'green space of special importance to local communities,' now called Local Green Spaces (LGS) in the NPPF (para. 76 - 77).  This popular and very attractive area falls into this category and meets all the LGS selection criteria defined in the NPPF.  LGS status for the Long Walk area has the overwhelming backing of the community.  4.  The proposed site is close to a floodplain; Blaby has had a problem with repeated flooding. Due to climate change we should expect more frequent extreme weather events that could lead to localised flooding. Large scale building on the site could compromise flood prevention and mitigation measures and result in increased local flooding risk on the site and more importantly elsewhere. Policy on Climate Change (CS21) and the NPPF refer to the importance of good site selection for new development. It is not unusual for flooding of the River Sence and its tributaries to affect the road connections to Leicester, especially at Crow Mills at South Wigston and the A426 between Blaby and Glen Parva, resulting in severe road congestion in and around Whetstone, Blaby and Wigston as motorists attempt to find alternative routes. An extra 200 plus houses to the east of Blaby off Hospital Lane would make the situation worse, firstly because of the extra traffic that would discharge into Hospital Lane and secondly increased water run-off rate from the site following extreme weather could increase the severity and frequency of flooding.  5.  The area is home to wildlife.  Badgers are known to live in the area and the site provides them with good quality foraging habitat and cover (see WYG Blaby District Council: Phase 1 Habitat Survey 2008 - LDF evidence base). Badgers and their setts are protected under the Protection of Badgers Act 1992.   Bats are known to roost close by (possibly the old Hall Farm buildings) and Long Walk is a very important wildlife corridor that provides both feeding habitat and links between other important feeding sites.  All British bat species and their roosts are legally protected under the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981.

CommentOriginal: I wish to object against the planning application S62A/2014/0001 Hospital Lane Blaby . Blaby District Council already have a 5 year supply of deliverable housing sites to meet the District's requirements for new housing, so it is not necessary to support development proposals that do not align with planning policy. A development of this size (over 200 dwellings) in this location is not justified by the outstanding housing requirement numbers for Blaby. Leicestershire County Council has classified the heritage potential of the proposed site as High (Grade 1). It is immediately adjacent to the site of a medieval village ' the original settlement of Blaby. it is clear that this proposal will have a significantly adverse effect on the landscape. It will also result in the loss of valuable green space and Infrastructure. Many people, including those from the wider area, use this valued amenity and the loss of it will have a severe effect upon their health and well being. There are also protected species in the area and the loss of their habitat will inevitably impact upon them. If the proposed development went ahead it would isolate the Long Walk from the surrounding countryside and it is then likely that it would become unpopular with many users who use it extensively at present.   Blaby District Green Space Strategy states that 'Existing green spaces should not be built on unless they are surplus to requirements and losses are replaced with equivalent or better provision in terms of quantity and quality" This area is not surplus to requirements but essential the the people of Blaby and the wider community. It should be protected not destroyed.

In this time it has gone form a simple route between the villages of Blaby, Countesthorpe and Wigston to a major arterial roadway. The amount of vehicles using this road daily is now in the thousands and it is unable to cope with this number without major improvement works. There is only a paved path for part of its length and rough grass verges for the rest. Traffic jams, both morning and evening form from its eastern end to well past the old hospital entrance, well over half the roads length. Just off the eastern end of Hospital Lane around 200 houses are nearing completion while 300 yards from its western end almost 300 houses are under construction. The road, in its present condition is unable to cope with such a massive increase in traffic. To add a further 200+ houses to be built on Hospital Lane, without major improvements would create a very dangerous, over crowded road. The field hedges in places are almost to the edge of the road which block the vision of what's ahead for the driver. Pedestrians are forced to walk in this narrow road - day and night - or stumble through rough grass verges. Although a 7.5 ton weight restriction is in force the road still carries major HGV construction traffic and is an illegal short-cut from J21, M1 to J2, A14 for 44 ton articulated vehicles - mainly foreign running on domestic sat-nav's.     I would ask the planners to PLEASE consider the impact on this road before passing these new housing plans.    I am a 30 year resident of Hospital Lane

CommentOriginal: I consider that a large development such as is proposed would do considerable harm to the area, especially Bouskell Park and the woodland and other walks.  The proposed development is opposed by Blaby District Council and large numbers of Blaby residents for many different reasons on  planning and local house building requirements: The development would be well in excess of the number of houses required in Blaby, reference CS5 of the local plan.  The site in question is designated as COUNTRYSIDE in the "Planning Policy on Countryside and the Requirement for New Housing", Refs. CS5; CS18; LSCA and NPDF. CS18 states that "Within  areas designated as countryside, planning permission will not be granted for built development or other development which could have a significantly adverse effect on the appearance or character of the landscape."  I consider that the proposed development would be well within the scope of planning refusal and would be a complete blight on the landscape.  Loss of Valuable Green Space & Infrastructure (CS14) (CS15)     The proposed development on this site is not consistent with policy on Green Infrastructure (CS14). The site is crossed by a popular wooded permissive path (Long Walk), footpaths, a bridleway and a National Cycle Route (Guthlaxton Trail). It is an area loved and enjoyed by many local residents. In addition visitors travel from across the District and in some cases from across the Country to enjoy the area and explore the District's heritage. The government have decided to protect 'green space of special importance to local communities,' now called Local Green Spaces (LGS) in the NPPF (para. 76 ' 77).  This popular and very attractive area falls into this category and meets all the LGS selection criteria defined in the NPPF.  LGS status for the Long Walk area has the overwhelming backing of the community. Policy on Open Spaces, Sport and Recreation (CS15) seeks to ensure that all residents have access to sufficient, high quality, accessible open space, sport and recreation facilities.  It states that existing open space, sport and recreation facilities will be protected, and where possible enhanced. Where development is proposed on existing open space, sport and recreation facilities, land should not be released, either in total or in part unless it can be demonstrated that it is surplus to requirements for its current play and open space function. The Local Plan CS (Issues, problems and challenges facing the District) para. 4.3 states that, 'A recent survey of play and open spaces has indicated that the District is broadly lacking in these facilities.' We believe that this site is clearly a very high quality and valuable open space that is not at all surplus to requirements. Blaby District Green Space Strategy:- refers to the NPPF 'Existing green spaces should not be built on unless they are surplus to requirements and losses are replaced with equivalent or better provision in terms of quantity and quality (NPPF, paragraph 74).' Policy CS14 Green Infrastructure 6.19.  Policy CS2 is also relevant.  Traffic Congestion: Hospital Lane and surrounding areas are already heavily congested, especially at peak times; Hospital Lane being a "Rat Run" for the motorways and surrounding areas. The possibility of hundreds more vehicles from the  proposed development pouring from the only exit roads from the development onto Hospital Lane would only make the situation considerably worse in Hospital Lane, Welford road, Aylestone road and roads to Countesthorpe and Wigston.  I consider that based on planning rules of Blaby District Council, civil amenities contravention, Sufficient proposed building sites already earmarked for future housing development and the probable diminishing of the Blaby environment, this planning application should be refused.
