CommentOriginal: I am writing to object to the outline planning application by Gladman Developments Ltd. for 220 houses on land off Hospital Lane, Blaby. Ref. S62A/2014/0001/Hospital Lane Blaby   There are many reasons for my objection to this application.   Community Space: First and foremost, the land in question is SO well loved by the community of Blaby, as it lies just behind Bouskell Park and provides a wonderful backdrop and feeling of 'the countryside' like no other space in, or in the vicinity of Blaby.  The area is well used by many people, locally and from further afield, as somewhere that they can enjoy walking and wild life.  It's a real 'community' space that should not be given over to development, as it is unique and could never be replaced.   Walking along the paths and bridleway, you can hear the amazing birdsong of such a variety of birds and feel 'remote' from the 'hustle and bustle' of daily life.  Building houses on this site would bring the 'hustle and bustle' right into the heart of these lovely county footpaths, so that they no longer offered the tranquility that they do now.   I have attached a photograph of one of the footpaths we regularly use (Photograph 1) It is proposed to build houses on either side of this footpath. I hope you can appreciate from the photograph that It simply would not be the same experience with houses either side and wouldn't be somewhere I, or many others would choose to walk and enjoy if houses were built there.   Landscape Views: I object to houses being built on either side of the Long Walk.  Long Walk is essentially an extension of Bouskell Park and the views across Bouskell Park would be totally ruined.  This is actually a very historic Park and marks the site of the original village of Blaby.  It surely cannot be appropriate to place a housing estate on adjacent land that would spoil the views so drastically and insensitively. The housing estate would dominate the view as you walked around the Park and there is no amount of screening that could hide these houses from view.  Wildlife / Bats: The Long Walk forms part of a network of wildlife corridors connecting the surrounding fields, and a housing estate on either side would cut it off completely.  It is well known and a matter of record that bats populate this area.  Bats are a protected species and are susceptible to light pollution.   It will not be possible to maintain adequate darkness throughout the wooded area or in Bouskell Park with housing so close ' any development on this site will damage the existing bat population.  Safety: The Long Walk would no longer be part of the Countryside, but instead would be 'Inside' a housing estate.  I don't understand how this could ever have been considered as a sensible or rational idea.   There will be safety issues associated with having an enclosed dark strip of woodland running through the middle of a residential area potentially exposing people, children especially, to personal risk.  It will completely change the nature of that pathway from a natural and peaceful walking route to one that attracts rubbish, fly tipping, and anti social behaviour.  How are these safety issues going to be addressed?   Flooding: I am also surprised that this site has been considered for building on, as it sits between two areas that frequently flood. Every year Mill Lane floods and causes dreadful problems not only for the residents of Mill Lane but it also has a knock-on effect on the surrounding road networks, which are also prone to flooding. (See picture 2.) Hospital Lane can also suffer from flooding and building houses on this site will reduce drainage and exacerbate the problem, potentially putting the houses and residents located on the site at risk. Given the terrible flooding that has occurred nationally this year, this should be as issue which is considered very carefully indeed.   People who object to housing development are often referred to as NIMBYs.  However, this is not my Back Yard.  I live in the neighboring Parish of Glen Parva, but feel compelled to object strongly to this application as it would destroy a much loved and valued area that is important to the District.  I attended a consultation event in Geln Parva for another large housing development in the Parish of Glen Parva.  This was a totally different experience to the so-called consultation event held by Gladman Developments.  The developers hosting the event in Glen Parva (Framptons I believe?) were proactively engaging with the public and answering questions; any questions they couldn't answer on the night, they pledged to follow up with a response. However Gladman's consultation was lacking in information and hosted by 'agents' that either could not or would not answer questions.  I also attended a Blaby Parish meeting where Gladman were due to make a presentation, but they failed to turn up.  This shows very poor regard to the local community.  I feel strongly that this is a totally inappropriate location for development, which if allowed, would have a serious and detrimental effect on our green space and our heritage, which has been enjoyed for generations and is irreplaceable.  Please reject this application.

CommentOriginal: The proposed development on this site is not consistent with policy on Green Infrastructure (CS14). The site is crossed by a popular wooded permissive path (Long Walk), footpaths, a bridleway and a National Cycle Route (Guthlaxton Trail). It is an area loved and enjoyed by many local residents. In addition visitors travel from across the District and in some cases from across the Country to enjoy the area and explore the District's heritage. The government have decided to protect 'green space of special importance to local communities,' now called Local Green Spaces (LGS) in the NPPF (para. 76 ' 77).  This popular and very attractive area falls into this category and meets all the LGS selection criteria defined in the NPPF.  LGS status for the Long Walk area has the overwhelming backing of the community. Policy on Open Spaces, Sport and Recreation (CS15) seeks to ensure that all residents have access to sufficient, high quality, accessible open space, sport and recreation facilities.  It states that existing open space, sport and recreation facilities will be protected, and where possible enhanced. Where development is proposed on existing open space, sport and recreation facilities, land should not be released, either in total or in part unless it can be demonstrated that it is surplus to requirements for its current play and open space function. The Local Plan CS (Issues, problems and challenges facing the District) para. 4.3 states that, 'A recent survey of play and open spaces has indicated that the District is broadly lacking in these facilities.' We believe that this site is clearly a very high quality and valuable open space that is not at all surplus to requirements. Blaby District Green Space Strategy:- refers to the NPPF 'Existing green spaces should not be built on unless they are surplus to requirements and losses are replaced with equivalent or better provision in terms of quantity and quality (NPPF, paragraph 74).' Policy CS14 Green Infrastructure 6.19.  Policy CS2 is also relevant.  The proposed site is next to the Blaby Conservation Area which is also designated an 'open area of importance to the form and character of the built environment.'  The proposed development is so close to the Conservation Area it would have a very adverse impact on the area and would be against policy on Historic Environment and Culture (CS20) which seeks to preserve and enhance the cultural heritage of the District and states that proposed development should avoid harm to the significance of historic sites, buildings or areas, including their setting.  Badgers are known to live in the area and the site provides them with good quality foraging habitat and cover (see WYG Blaby District Council: Phase 1 Habitat Survey 2008 ' LDF evidence base). Badgers and their setts are protected under the Protection of Badgers Act 1992. Bats are known to roost close by (possibly the old Hall Farm buildings) and Long Walk is a very important wildlife corridor that provides both feeding habitat and links between other important feeding sites. The Bouskell Park area is used for local 'bat walks' organised by Blaby District Council. 'Bats are poorly catered for in planning development.  Bat boxes are a very poor substitute for the habitat loss which bats often suffer and there is a low occupancy rate. The real issue is usually the loss of bats' feeding areas. They need a large area over which to forage. The loss of the included farmland would be a real loss to the many bats that live and feed on the Hall Farm estate land.  All British bat species and their roosts are legally protected under the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981.' ' a member of the local bat group. There is potential for white-clawed crayfish and possibly water voles in the small brook running parallel to Hospital Lane and further survey work should be performed to assess the potential loss of habitat.  Sometimes the water flow is low, but in recent years it has rarely run dry and 'deeper pools may sustain wildlife during drought.'  Local infrastructure is not capable of supporting a development of this size and in this location. We do not think the proposed development is properly sustainable.  The size of the proposed residential development significantly exceeds the residual housing requirement for Blaby as defined by the Local Plan, CS5, Housing distribution. Hospital Lane is already severely congested during peak periods especially at the junction with Leicester Road / Countesthorpe Road to the east of Blaby. Welford Road in Blaby is also now congested at busy times and can be difficult for pedestrians to cross. The proposed development would make the situation a great deal worse in Blaby, Whetstone, Glen Parva, Countesthorpe and South Wigston.

CommentOriginal: I hereby present my objection to the above S62A/2014/0001:  - Green area: the proposed development is being considered in a green area adjacent to Buskell Park in Blaby. The area is used by all residents, children and dog walkers. It is considered an extension of Buskell Park itself, and the construction of so many houses around the park will disrupt the park itself. Buskell Park is a quiet area within a large and vibrant town, and the government should encourage the keeping of such vital green areas utilised by families. The proposed houses will have direct access the to park path, and the increase in the number of people will damage the park. May I please clarify that the objection is to the construction of houses in the proposed area; housing shortage is an issue in the country and I understand the shortage of houses need to be dealt with somehow; build houses onto brown land is a much better option to house shortages in my opinion.  I understand that the current government is committed on preserving green areas utilised by the wider population;  -Transport and roads: Blaby is a busy town, and the traffic in and out of the town is difficult as it is; AM and PM rush hours are impossible to handle; Enderby Road from the Foxhunter roundabout is constantly gridlocked during my way in and out of work; Leicester Road in Glen Parva is impossible to drive through, I have spent hours sitting on traffic and have driven back home sometimes. Name: Oliver Joseph Ford
CommentOriginal: Dear Sir Thank you for your time in consideration of my objection. As I am sure you have thoroughly looked through all the arguments both for and against I shall only briefly try to convey why I am in objection to this proposed development. 	Having lived in Blaby for all 26 years of my life I have many reservations. Firstly I am concerned for the general feel of Blaby. This is very difficult to describe and so I am sure difficult to understand.  As an area becoming increasingly less rural due to many other areas currently being developed, and although the area is being increased in developed size I feel the area is becoming smaller and the whole landscape of Blaby being significantly altered. Developments are supposed to provide as an economic, social and environmental stimulus and I'm struggling to identify favourable points for any of these both in regards to myself, family and many others who live and visit Blaby. 	The quantity of the proposed housing development of 220 is also very alarming, however, my concern is not just with the quantity but also the location through Blaby's charming green space. Blaby's green space is valued by those who use it and see it, used by many for many different recreational reasons and would impact negatively the positives of Blaby's landscape. Policy CS5, on Housing Distribution try's to advise on the necessary developments in maintaining a natural progression which is palatable. As a village we are barely into our 23 year plan period in fact we are quickly reaching the threshold set for ourselves. The development proposed seems to be excessive in surpassing the figures originally generated and required. There is likely to be further developments over the future decade plus, resulting in further increasing a surplus within the area. 	Sporting facilities within Blaby are minimal, we currently have one football facility and one rugby facility. The rugby facility is currently due to be halved due to a development. These are bye the bye though when considering a multitude of the whole society of Blaby from pushchairs to octogenarians and beyond use the local green space available. It is not merely using the footpaths as a connection from point A to point B but a sense of relaxation and contemplation within the setting that helps to maintain a sort of happiness and wellbeing a priceless commodity. As well due to the nature of the activities offered it helps with spending time with friends, and relatives of cross-generations can spend time together no matter the financial implications. Wildlife can be enjoyed for both young and old removing the local green space would have a severely detrimental impact on the wildlife that live within it. Fragmentation would occur and the natural awesomeness of the area would be completely lost. Once valuable green space is removed it is a long time to get back. The proposed development would slice through the local green space and greatly impact the landscape and cohesion the village currently feels. As a cycling enthusiast who commutes to work daily and the local roads I have great reservations with regards to the extra amount of people using the local roads. At peak times the roads can be particular dangerous for pedestrians, dog walkers, cyclists, children migrating to Thistly Meadow, Leysland and Countesthorpe College and more. The road infrastructure would be terrible and increase the likelihood of injury in my opinion unnecessarily. All the local amenities of which there are few are oversubscribed and not capable of accommodating such an influx of people. Although I have further reservations my biggest grievance from this application and probably my most important is my inability to see how there is any benefit for anyone who already lives in Blaby. As I started my objection to this housing development proposal developments are supposed to provide as an economic, social and environmental stimulus I am either blind to these, there aren't any or the few that do exist do not out way the negatives that there are. Thank you for your time. Best Regards

Name: eva o'connor
CommentOriginal: Dear Planning Inspectorate,  My hart sank when I saw the notice for yet another attempt by Leicestershire County Council (albeit through Gladman Development) to apply for planning permission to build new housing on the Hospital Lane site in Blaby.  I was only a few years ago that Leicestershire County Council tried to get planning for higher density housing at this same site, threatening the future of this beautiful part of Blaby.  My husband and I moved to Blaby 10 years ago, predominantly because of it offered a unique mix of town and country on the doorstep.  Whilst Blaby struggles in some areas, it could be argued it is a true sustainable conurbation both offering a wide range of conveniences and amenities, whilst also having the very accessible countryside on its doorstep.  We have three young children and regularly use the Bouskell Park, Long Walk and the surrounding areas for walks, bike rides and nature spotting.  It upsets me to think that should the proposed housing development be permitted, this local gem would be lost forever.  I appreciate that it would be very difficult to assess, but this local area of footpaths, wooded and country walks must offers an immeasurable health benefit to the local residents of Blaby.  Whenever we go there, there are always lots of people using this space.   I was astonished that in this day and age, it is still possible to promote new housing developments on 'green field' areas when we are surrounded by redundant brown field sites that have all the necessary services readily available.  Recently I have watched mass building of new houses around Blaby and the surrounding areas.  Surely we should be encouraging imaginative sustainable redevelopments of 'brown field' sites rather than allowing them to become dilapidated and attract antisocial behaviour?  Also, with all the new surrounding housing developments, I cannot believe that we need yet more new dwellings in the Blaby area?!  I am not convinced the traffic impact is properly being assessed from all these new housing developments around Blaby, Whetstone, Countesthorpe, Glen Parva etc.  Already, I struggle to cross Leicester Road near our home, something that unnerves me when I have three young children with me.  The proposed housing development will only make things worse.  A few years ago, we learnt that our home was within a flood risk area of the River Sence and we received a number of calls from the Environment Agency about potential risks of flooding.  This was a change from some 10 years ago when we bought our home and were classed as being outside the flood risk zone.  This demonstrates how the effects of climate change and further developments on green field sites impact on built up areas close to natural water courses.  Whilst I have no doubt that the proposed Gladman Development application will pay lip service to sustainable urban drainage matching green field rates of runoff, the simple fact is that this scale of new build will have a negative impact onto the floor risk area of River Sense. The local geology consists predominantly of clayey soils with the land off Hospital Lane regularly becoming very boggy throughout any wet weather.  The wet weather we have had over recent years has highlighted just how vulnerable we are.    I took a run through the proposed site last night ' it was truly beautiful to watch the sun n as it set behind the woods around Bouskell Park and the surrounding fields.  I felt very privileged to have this natural beauty spot just minutes away from our home.  I would like to think that our daughters can still enjoy this space for years to come.  It would be such a shame should it be lost.   I am trying to remain positive and think that there is no hidden agenda with this major applications process, but locals are very suspicious of it , especially as this proposed housing development is its first and only application.  I really do hope that the Planning Inspectorate team really do get to know the area well before making this important decision ' whatever the outcome will have a huge impact on all our future.   Yours sincerely, Eva O'Connor

Name: Mr Edy O'Connor
CommentOriginal: Dear Planning Inspectorate,  As a resident of Blaby, I, together with my wife and three young daughters would be so sorry if the proposed new housing off Hospital Lane was given the go ahead.  This proposed site is what makes Blaby so special.  Bouskell Park itself would be ruined with housing on the back of it rather than beautiful fields and woods.  Also, the surrounding fields, with their lovely footpaths and wooded walks, would no longer have the draw that brings us and other locals there on a regular basis.  We simply love using these walks and have for many years.  It also gives me great pleasure to see our young children running through the fields and woods and fields and getting in touch with nature.  As I drive past dilapidated sites around the Blaby area, I cannot understand why these areas are not redeveloped and brought back to life ahead of choosing new green field sites?  I appreciate that this planning application is considered on its own merit, however, should it be granted, it would set the precedent for allowing building on neighbouring fields.  I am not anti new build.  In fact, I have not opposed any of the many new housing developments in Blaby.  It is building on this particular site that I object to.  As an aside, I understand that with all the new housing developments already going ahead in Blaby and surrounding areas, we do not actually need any further houses in this area.  Should this housing be granted planning, I have grave concerns about our future in Blaby.  We live relatively close to the River Sence and any further development of green field sites within its catchment (the proposed site being one of them) will increase the risk of flooding.     Please ensure that the hearing, assuming it takes place, is held at a suitable time (i.e. after 5pm) so that the majority of locals are able to attend.   Regards  Edy O'Connor

Name: Sophie Edwards
CommentOriginal: I object to the proposed development adjacent to Hospital Lane and Bouskell Park, Blaby, Leicestershire for the following reasons:  Enough houses have been granted permission within Blaby to meet needs over the next five years as identified by the Core Strategy. Further development is both unnecessary and, in my view, unethical.  The proposed development would entirely destroy the unique character and therefore the amenity value of Bouskell and the surrounding walks. No amount of landscaping or planting could mitigate that impact.   Both the park and walks are currently enjoyed intensively, not only by local residents, but also by many people throughout the county. Access to natural green space is a fundamental human right and must be protected. Bouskell and it's environs are a 'green space of special importance to the local community' and it is the County Council's responsibility to curate and conserve such areas on the behalf of the community.   The development would entirely destroy the context of the grade two listed victorian ice house, with the development in such close proximity to the historic building.  The archaeological potential of the building plot has not been adequately investigated. It is clear that there is abundant archaeology throughout the park. The outskirts of settlements, most likely in the proposed development area, often contain the rubbish tips and cemeteries- generally the most valuable and informative evidence of past communities. Geophysical studies and field walking can reveal only a fraction of archaeology present at a site. The only way to truly evaluate the potential is to put in a series of test trenches. Development of this site without thorough archaeological evaluation would destroy forever the evidence of past communities.   The development would present a considerable threat to the rich and diverse wildlife present in the area and also the wider environment, with increased risk of flooding. Unavoidable light pollution would have a significant and detrimental effect on bat populations.   Additionally, the Development is not sustainable for the following reasons: Insufficient public transport  Excessive distance to that transport Inadequate provision of basic services such as schools, doctors and dentists for the proposed increased population  Yours sincerely, Sophie Edwards

CommentOriginal: Dear Ms O'Brien,    Planning Application: S62A/2014/0001: Outline planning application with access only. Proposed construction of up to 220 new dwellings (use class C3) and school drop off/pick up zone, with access and associated infrastructure: Land to the North of Hospital Lane, to the South of Mill Lane and to the East of Bouskell Park, Blaby, Leicestershire  Archaeological considerations  Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the above scheme.  Our comments below should be read in conjunction with our earlier correspondences of the 9th and 28th January 2014, and are informed by consideration of the recent Planning Inspectorate Pre-Application Issues Report.    Following further consideration of the development proposals, including on-site inspection, we would reiterate our previous recommendation that the advice of English Heritage and the Conservation Officer is sought regarding the proposed setting impacts to the Conservation Area, Blaby Hall and the associated Bouskell Park and listed Ice House.  We have particular concerns about the intervisibility between Bouskell Park and the development site, which do not appear to be separated by a strong vegetational boundary as the submitted Archaeological Desk-Based Assessment (CgMs October 2013, revised April 2014) suggests.  The retention of Long Walk as a landscape feature within the proposed development is welcomed.  It is disappointing that opportunities to retain Ridge and Furrow earthworks within the development area have not been pursued.  A Topographical Survey of the Ridge and Furrow earthworks should be undertaken prior to the commencement of development, however a conditioned approach to this would be acceptable.    The Leicestershire and Rutland Historic Environment Record (HER) shows that the application site lies within a landscape where archaeological remains are frequent and could reasonably be expected to be encountered within a development of this scale.  Cropmarks thought to represent a series of prehistoric enclosures and a possible drove-way (HER ref: MLE24) are recorded c. 240m to the east of the proposed development site.  Neolithic or Bronze Age worked flint, including a scraper, was recovered to the immediate north of the application site during archaeological monitoring of groundworks in 1998 (HER ref: MLE16145).  A Bronze Age site including a circular structure, cobbled area, hearth, oven and gully (HER ref: MLE140) is also present on the island of the Scheduled moated site at Glen Parva (SM ref: 1008259), c.300m to the north of the application site.  This medieval moated site includes the above-ground remains of a mortared granite wall and below-ground remains of mud walls.  To the west of the application site lies the Historic Settlement Core of Blaby (HER ref: MLE9336) and extensive earthwork and below-ground remains of medieval settlement have been recorded in Bouskell Park (HER ref: MLE19), including finds of medieval pottery and ironworking slag.    Taking into account the known archaeological resource outline above, we disagree with the conclusions of the submitted Archaeological Desk-Based Assessment and feel that the site has potential to contain previously unidentified archaeological remains, however the submitted information is insufficient to ascertain the significance of such remains and therefore to determine the impact of the development.  Although the geophysical survey (ASC report 1313/BHL/01) undertaken in 2010 did not identify any areas of definite archaeological interest, there is a possibility that significant remains are present that have not shown up in the data.  It should be noted that whilst aerial photographic evidence for the application area shows that much of the development area was formerly covered by ridge and furrow earthworks, normally visible to geophysical survey, very little trace of these features is apparent in the submitted report.  This either suggests that the site has been extensively damaged by recent cultivation, or alternatively questions the effectiveness of the survey results.  With regard to the capabilities of geophysical survey (specifically magnetometry), prehistoric features are often poorly defined by such techniques, perhaps due to their shallow nature, small size in plan, similarity of backfill to the natural soils, or paucity of cultural material.  There have been numerous examples of sites in Leicestershire, particularly on clayey soils such as this, where archaeological remains have only been identified as a result of subsequent trial trenching.  Given the presence of prehistoric settlement and activity in the vicinity, there is a potential for archaeological remains of this period to be present within the application site.  Section 4 of the Geophysical Survey report (page 16) states:   The results of geophysical surveys and interpretation of collected data should not be treated as an absolute representation of the underlying archaeological and non-archaeological remains. Confirmation of the origin of geophysical anomalies and the presence or absence of archaeological remains can only be achieved by direct investigation of sub-surface deposits.   This is in line with professional archaeological practices and guidance from English Heritage (Geophysical Survey in Archaeological Field Evaluation, English Heritage 2008), which states:   Lack of geophysical anomalies cannot be taken to imply a lack of archaeological features, and in such cases an alternative evaluation procedure eg trial trenching, or the use of a different geophysical technique should be considered.    In our opinion, trial trenching is required to ascertain whether significant archaeological remains are present, to allow an appropriate mitigation strategy to be defined and to demonstrate the sustainability of the proposals as currently tabled.  The submitted scheme demonstrates an incapacity to accommodate change should significant archaeological remains worthy of preservation in situ be identified, hence there is a need to undertake evaluation prior to determination of this application to enable identification of archaeological remains that would warrant re-design or engineering solutions.    The preservation of archaeological remains is, of course, a material consideration in the determination of planning applications. The proposals include operations that may destroy any buried archaeological remains that are present, but the archaeological implications cannot be adequately assessed on the basis of the currently available information.  Since it is possible that archaeological remains may be adversely affected by this proposal, we recommend that the applicant complete an Archaeological Trial Trench Evaluation of the proposed development site prior to determination of any forthcoming planning application.  This will require provision by the applicant for:  A field evaluation, by appropriate techniques including trial trenching, to identify and locate any archaeological remains of significance, and propose suitable treatment to avoid or minimise damage by the development.  Further design, civil engineering or archaeological work may then be necessary to achieve this.  This information should be submitted to the Planning Inspectorate before any decision on a future planning application is taken, so that an informed decision can be made.  These recommendations conform to the advice provided in DCLG National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) Section 12, paras. 128, 129 & 135).  The Historic & Natural Environment Team (HNET), Leicestershire County Council, as advisors to the planning authority, will provide a formal Brief for the work and approve a Specification for the Evaluation at the request of the applicant.    Should you have any further queries please do not hesitate to contact us.  Yours sincerely,  Teresa Hawtin  Senior Planning Archaeologist  Leicestershire County Council

CommentOriginal: Dear Laura O'Brien,    Application Received Under S62A - Hospital Lane, Blaby - S62A/2014/0001  Access & Public Rights of Way  I have had an opportunity to look through the various plans and documents relating to this application and would make the following comments:-    Existing Public Rights of Way -    1 - The Framework Plan shows the line of Public Footpath Z54 incorrectly.  Please see the attached rights of way overlay plan.  This will need to be corrected to accord with the Definitive Map of Public Rights of Way.  There are also some minor discrepancies between the route of Bridleway Z53 as shown on the Framework Plan and the Definitive Line which may need to be addressed.    2    3 - The retention of both public rights of way on/close to their current routes through public open space  is welcomed as it is conforms with L.C.C./ 6Cs. Design Guidelines (Public Rights of Way & Development: Guidance notes for Developers, Designers & Planners).    All Weather Surfaces -     4 - Public Bridleway Z53 is already surfaced to a high standard and forms part of National Cycle Route NCN6.  However Footpath Z54 which links into to it from Blaby Village is currently a field footpath with no surface.  This footpath will form a strategic link to the new development for non-motorized users.    If the development proceeds and this footpath is not improved the increase in footfall generated by the proposed 220 new households would cause unacceptable damage to the footpath.    5 -  The footpath's character and useage would change significantly if the development went ahead, from semi-rural recreational field walking to suburban multi user (including cycle, wheel chair buggy and child-cycle) use.   It should therefore be provided with a full construction 2.5 to 3 metre wide tarmacadamed all-weather surface to 6Cs Design Guide Standards, in order to continue to be fit for purpose.    Extra Cycle Access -    6 - Consideration should also be given to upgrading Footpath Z54 to Cycletrack standards.  It would then serve as a strategic link into the National Cycleway Network.    General Comments -    7 - The retention of some of the existing access links to Bouskell Park and enhanced provision for cyclists and pedestrians throughout the proposed development as outlined in Section 5.10.4 of the Design & Access statement is to be welcomed.  It is clear that the applicants have given very careful consideration to pedestrian/cycle access within the development which is commendable.    Advisory Notes -     8 - If it is necessary to divert a public right of way to enable the development to take place then a formal diversion of the public path will need to be sought under the provisions of the Town & Country Planning Act 1990.  Normally such an application would be submitted to the Local Planning Authority which granted planning permission.  In the case of the above application it may be necessary for the application to be made to the Secretary of State.  (This will need to be verified)    9 - If it is necessary to close a right of way temporarily to allow construction to proceed in safety then an application will need to be made for a Temporary Traffic Regulation Order closing the path at least 8 weeks prior to commencement of works.  The application should be made to Leicestershire County Council as Highway Authority.  During closure the developer would be expected to provide a safe and convenient temporary alternative route, signed on site.    I trust the above information is of assistance.  Regards,  Piers Lindley     Piers Lindley  Senior Access & Development Officer (Rights of Way)  Leicestershire County Council

CommentOriginal: The development proposal hasn't changed since the pre-app stage, when I replied as follows to Laura O'Brien at PINS, giving some recommendations for planning conditions.   The ecology consultants  (Baker, April 2014) have updated the ecology surveys, but this hasn't affected my recommendations.    I've no further comments to those sent pre-app, and no requirements for any further survey work etc prior to determination.  Comments sent pre-app, 07 January 2014 14:19, to "laura.o'brien@pins.gsi.gov.uk"  The suite of ecology surveys (Baker Consultants, 2010, 2012 and 2013) are satisfactory, and at this stage no further surveys would be required to inform a planning application.   However, should three years elapse from the survey dates before an application is submitted (i.e. after spring 2016), it will be necessary to update the badger and great crested newt surveys.   As the ponds were assessed as "poor" in 2012, I don't feel there is a need for a GCN update survey any earlier.    Very few significant ecology features of more than local value were identified.   The species-rich hedgerow (which may meet our Local Wildlife Site criteria) is shown on the submitted framework plan as being protected.   Other woodlands and hedges will also be retained, with appropriate buffer zones adjacent to them.    A buffer zone is shown between the proposed development and the ecologically important Bouskell Park, and the adjacent Local Wildlife Site at the Cemetery is unlikely to be adversely affected by the proposal. There are opportunities for habitat creation associated with SUDs features and the large area of open space to the north.  Therefore, as long as the development is in accordance with the framework plan (DE_073-003) I have no objections to this proposal.  I would recommend conditions along the following lines:  1.       Development to be in accordance with the framework plan (DE_073-003);  2.       All landscape planting in the informal/natural open space and adjacent to the site boundaries to be of locally native species only;  3.       Buffer zones of at least 5 m of natural vegetation to be maintained alongside all retained hedgerows, woodlands, Bouskell Park and the cemetery, and other ecological features (the buffer zones must not be part of back gardens);  4.       Before development commences, a biodiversity management plan for all retained and created habitats  including SUDS, to be submitted and approved by the planning authority;  5.       The SUDS to be designed to maximise benefit to wildlife;  6.       Light spill onto retained hedgerows and woodlands and adjacent  to be minimised to a value of 1lux or lower at the edge of the habitats;  7.       Provision of bat boxes on mature trees and buildings adjacent to retained hedges/woodlands;  8.       Removal of vegetation outside the bird nesting season ;  9.       Badger and GCN update re-survey if development does not commence prior to spring 2016 .  Contact Sue Timms, County Ecologist sue.timms@leics.gov.uk 01163054108

Name: Leicestershire Police (Part 1)
CommentOriginal: Thanks for this and for notification of the application under ref s62A/2014/0001.  I am assuming that the contribution request we furnished at 8/1/14 as part of pre application consultation has been added to this file along with my email of the 15/4/14 in response to the developers views.    I have looked at the documents on the website and am concerned that the impact of the development on hard pressed local public services is not considered. In deed the only socio economic assessment [Regeneris] I can find is aimed to point out suggested beneficial impacts of the development. I am concerned that there appears to be little consideration of a balanced approach to socio economic impact in the application and I doubt the sustainability credentials of the proposal as a result. The inescapable impacts on Policing and community safety do not manifest in any of this documentation.  Turning to the draft s106 at the definition the sum indicated is not what is necessary but what the developer wants to pay. Whist the developer agrees that their development will negatively impact Policing to the extent that a contribution is necessary they seek to exclude our most costly infrastructure items from this. I have to say that what I have seen in relation to premises and CCTV is no justification to do this. The LPA needs to judge whether these items are essential to Police the development and my request and further information explains why this is. I do not understand how it can be asserted that premises are not fundamental to Policing as they are in the delivery of health and schooling. This is one of many large developments being pursued in our sub region and we just do not have the premises capacity to accommodate additional staff these are generating. It seems senseless to me that the developer accepts we will need additional staff, to equip them, enable adequate comms and IT infrastructure and vehicles to do their job and then deny them a base to work from.    In relation to CCTV you are asking for my comments on the proportionality of what we seek. I have identified a number of factors that bear on this. I need to say a bit more about through routing which is a constant on Hospital Lane as an alternative vehicle route to the Leicester City outer ring congested at many times of the day. The factors I am considering are    - size of the development, large in my view  - Location in terms of accessibility and opportunity, including adjoining uses and footpath as well as road links.  - nature of the development and local crime patterns  - deliverability, in terms of securing an amount which in itself will help trigger the investment.    With all these factors in mind I believe a CCTV contribution of £6426, 9% of what we seek, is proportionate from a development of 220 additional homes at this site. It would be disproportionate to ask for less bearing in mind these factors. On reflection I think I could have made the case to ask for full camera costs in this development. However it would be disproportionate to ask for more than we have. You have picked up on the point I made about the Bill Crane Way appeal where an Inspector was content that the development of 149 homes triggered the proportionate need for an additional ANPR camera and I have given you wording that assists this conclusion. I have the appellant’s submissions before me challenging the CCTV element of our request on location and accessibility grounds. Clearly that did not deter the Inspector at the Inquiry. I do not agree that consideration at appeals is in any way less than is necessary. I have given evidence and been challenged over  many hours on what we seek. This is far more probing and incisive than in the consideration of most Planning applications. I am more than happy to pursue such an approach through a hearing or an inquiry in front of an Inspector in this case. Please advise on next steps towards this.  In all the Planning appeals using our current approach there are contributions to CCTV. They are as follows    Bill Crane Way 149 houses £ 8722  Springwell 150 houses £4611  Moira 69 £4861  Rearsby 60 £2250  Barrow Upon Soar 250 £ 4722  Seine Lane 244 £4861  Hallbrook 111 £2966  Mountsorrel Lane 250 £17944    I can evidence other proportionate requests if you wish eg in Blaby or anywhere else in the Police area. We made 82 of these last year against all sizes of development and seeking to apply a proportionate approach based on the factors I have described.     On the last appeal a Link Road was included and because of increased accessibility to the appeal site and those surrounding an increased contribution was found proportionate.    I have not seen other requests but these may give you comfort as to the overall amount we seek being proportionate although I see the developer also challenges the size of the necessary Education contribution.    S106 content - In the definitions the cost per dwelling should be £347.40 and not £66.73. The trigger is acceptable on page 14. The clawback period, 5 years is acceptable. The agreement should require the Council to make the payment to Police on receipt. As it stands the agreement is unacceptable to Police and we look to the LPA to consider this and require these changes in order to make the development acceptable and sustainable and provide for the necessary Policing contribution.    Conclusion- LP have carefully considered the impacts of the development on Policing and have made a contribution request to provide a necessary mitigation of this. The development is unacceptable without this necessary contribution and Planning permission should not be granted. The application will lead to an unsustainable development imposing long term and negative impacts on local Policing and community safety for the residents of the site and the surrounding community. Police lodge a formal objection to the application as submitted and without the necessary Policing contribution and on these grounds.    I attach a further SOS appeal decision finding our request compliant in that case

Name: Leicestershire Police (Part 2 - email of 15th April)
CommentOriginal: I have a copy of Carol Clarke’s letter of the 3/4 in response to my request of the 8/1/14 offered in response to your request for pre application comments at that time. We do not know who owns this site or other requests made at this stage.    I have used the now accepted methodology we apply to all large planning applications and appeals in our area. The data changes in each request to take account of the details of each development and the locality of the development site. There are many legal agreements in place favouring Leicestershire Police and an increasing number of these using this approach. There are approximately 20 successful Planning appeals favouring Police. All the appeal decisions considering this approach, 7 number, found Police compliance. There have been 3 SOS decisions supporting Policing contributions including two using this approach. I attach a further SOS decision issued since I wrote to you, again for your reference. I note that the developer agrees that policing contributions are necessary based on our analysis of impacts and mitigations. I also note that there is as yet no matter of development viability  identified at this site.    Sadly in her telephone call Carol Clarke made no reference to the matters she has raised in relation to premises. Had she done so I may have been able to assist her with what she has provided to you. As it is however I am struggling to detect the point she is trying to make although it is focused on dismissing the additional premises requirement we will have as a result of her development. I have to say that the NPPF 204 tests apply to the particular development application on the particular site and now. It does not refer to any other site or application nor to any past position, related or unrelated. I believe I have provided all you need in order to consider compliance and our legal advice is that this is the case, the current approach being developed with leading Planning Counsel to ensure this.    As elsewhere I have provided up to date, proportionate, robust and objectively assessed needs based on the application and its site. Inspectors at appeal and in Local Plan Examination have accepted these attributes of our approach. Carol Clarke mentions the Core Strategy at Blaby. Police played a full role in this ensuring that adequate provision was made in the Councils infrastructure schedule and policies so that adequate Policing infrastructure is provided to support additional development proposed in the CS. The Core strategy was adopted at 2/13, a year ago, with this content applying to additional housing. I assume that the developer will suggest that this site can form part of this planned growth in which case it should conform to the CS Policies and IP. I refer to these in my request to demonstrate adequate local Policy support to meet additional Policing needs. If the development is additional to  planned growth I see no reason why these adopted policies should not apply anyway. At page 122 the CS infrastructure schedule includes Police equipment, communications, CCTV vehicles and premises to be met by developer contributions. Our request is Policy compliant locally and with NPPF. I am sorry that the developer’s reference to the Core Strategy does not consider this content.    In my request I look at how the locality of the development is currently Policed identifying the premises from which this is delivered, Blaby LPU at Braunston, Loughborough BCU and Force HQ Enderby also in Blaby. The developer accepts the staffing impact of her proposals and it must follow that adequate provision needs to be made to accommodate them and I detail that requirement based on existing policing of the locality of the development.    The reason we had to move out of the two police houses in Blaby town years ago was their age and condition and the fact that there was no capacity there for expansion to accommodate additional staff as a result of growth. The LPU function was moved to premises in Braunstone. We sold the old building using receipts in part to pay for the necessary refurbishment of Brauntsone in order to use it to capacity then. We still use this to capacity. We will extend this and other premises using pooled contributions from a number of developments but we do not know if and when permission will be granted and developments started. A contribution towards these expansions is appropriate and not  linked or determined by premises changes we have made in the past. My request is in relation to the position now when the new planning application is made. You have asked about comments on the subsequent planning application for our vacated premises. In the light of the preceding I can’t see the relevance of this to our request I am afraid. Please come back to me further if you feel the need.    There is reference to developer guidance which is out of date with CIL regs, the demise of C5/05 and NPPF. In any case that content does not determine what is necessary now. The interpretation of this by the developer is incorrect anyway- nobody was seeking to redevelop a Police station in active use.    There is no inconsistency in our approach as I have demonstrated and this particular request needs to be considered. In the 8 years that Police have sought contributions we have kept our practice up to date against all the legislative and policy changes that have been made over this time. Police carried out a service review two years ago reducing staffing in this work. As a result we have had to change our thresholds for intervention. This does not mean that small developments or even single additional houses will not impact Policing with the need for necessary mitigation. We just cannot resource requests at the levels the developer has indicated and we have said as much to the LPA. This does  not mean that what we seek is not necessary in relation to this application. CIL is the answer to this and many other recognised outstanding issues and difficulties with developer contributions however no local Council has implemented this, much to our concern, and indeed that of Inspectors at appeals and Examinations.    The interpretation of CIL Reg 123 is wrong. This has been the subject of advice we have taken from the CIL team in DCLG and the Governments Chief Planner. It is also the subject of further attention of police nationally because of the difficulties this hangover will cause at a later date to service providers where Councils have done nothing about CIL. In the meantime there is no restriction on the accumulation of pooled contributions from a number of developments towards infrastructures like premises or vehicles. Our request is not compromised by this as the developer tries to suggest.    This leaves the letter the Chief Constable sent to NWL District back in 2010. It describes our on going asset review which I also capture in my request and our efforts, now successful, to dispose of smaller premises that we owned. The same rational that drove these changes back then still drives the Force today. Even though we have rolled out a number of hub access points in premises owned by other agencies since then, we cannot maintain these when there are more pressing demands on our staff. Since 2010 88 access hubs have been established. Some have had to close since. In my request I describe the local situation in Blaby and the number of hubs established. Additional development brings additional pressure on these and recognising this the developer is content to contribute to additional equipment at a local hub. Unlike the additional premises need this is a relatively small contribution. As I  have said these are drop ins where we need additional equipment to meet public expectation. They are not the base for staff who assist at these and whether a hub arrangement exists or not will have no impact on our need to accommodate/base these staff.    Reflecting on all this I have to say that there is nothing here that causes me to doubt that what I have provided in my request adequately portrays the additional premises needs I have identified as a result of this development. We are confident that this is compliant. I would be very concerned to hear otherwise because of our tried and accepted approach which is generating what we need as a result of additional development across our area. It is meeting the NPPF priority to keep infrastructure provision in step with housing growth. I could not contemplate an exception in this case nor the impacts of this elsewhere in other Planning applications under consideration in the Police area.    Roadside ANPR is a networked resource across the Police district making a recognised contribution to detection, apprehension and the delivery of community safety. Our performance and assurance to the public depends on it. The resource is used and deployed to capacity meeting the demands of existing development. The proposal adds a new area and volume of development and the additional impact of this needs to be mitigated. This is a case accepted in all the other decisions I have referred to. It was a matter in the Bill Crane Way appeal. There a development considerably smaller than the one proposed paid for a camera in its entirety. That was because of the particular circumstances that prevailed there, a new development on a major access road to and from a settlement which of itself triggered the need for a contribution. I supplied this Inspectors decision back in January. The Inspector found  “ whilst the additional staff, accommodation, vehicles and equipment detailed by the Police could not be regarded as being for the exclusive use of the development, they would be necessary to provide for the effective policing of and to attend incidents on the site”  That is an important consideration and one that should be born in mind by the developer in this case. Further the impact of the development on policing and community safety will not be restricted to within the site as I confirm in my request. The occupiers of the site will be victims of crime and some will even be perpetrators but as such this experience will not be limited within the site boundary. They will benefit from Policing beyond this, in all its support functions and if they commit crime we will detect it off the site as well as on it. This is the environment in which CCTV should be viewed, not just the narrow confines of the site. Indeed this context extends to Policing and crime patters beyond the District itself in what is a subregionally provided and resourced service.    The variables of passing traffic, site generated traffic, the accessibility of the site to the major road network, through routes, local crime patterns, current camera locations, the size of the development, neighbouring development and deliverability all need to be considered. Judgement needs to be exercised and as the charged and accountable body for policing we have exercised this in relation to this case. We have done this with knowledge of the development, its location and its impact without additional mitigation. The developer suggests that rather than rely on this expertise and knowledge of the importance of these technologies to different sites and proposals and the dependence of Police and  residents on these, we should apply a blanket formula to determine CCTV contributions. Frankly this is senseless in an environment where we don’t know what growth is occurring where and when, whether PP will be granted, resultant impact on vehicle movements and crime patterns. We have to rely on our best judgement at the time of the application and in relation to the particular development. I do not see that the developer has considered any of this in proposing a formulaic approach as the only way to assess this.    Examining again the size and locality of the development the following were material in making our request.    - Hospital Lane is a main access road to and from Blaby town and that settlement is on the edge of the district close  to the boundary of Leicester City.  - There are no cameras on this route at this time.  - that route links to other settlements and the City experiencing particular crime problems.  - The development is large and indeed is likely to be the only significant expansion of this settlement in the foreseeable future. It has been considered as such locally and certainly in the mind of the LPA.  - Blaby town is one of two urban concentrations in the beat where most crime happens. Rural hinterlands are an escape and access route.  - total crime, burglary and theft are increasing in the beat with vehicle crime static. The development will add to this as I have evidenced.  - The pattern of crime related to the existing development of the settlement is dense involving a significant number of burglaries and vehicle related crime.  - In this context the new development itself will generate identified increases in Policing demand. It will particularly benefit from the location of a camera near to its main point of access and it is reasonable that it should contribute towards this.  - There are relatively few existing developments taking access from Hospital Lane in the vicinity, enhancing the particular benefit to the development.    Much of this also applies to the use of mobile CCTV and the case to expand this as a result of the impacts of the development. When the need arises we currently deploy these units from outside the district. There are particular characteristics in this settlement and the development will significantly increase its size. They are the local crime patterns and rates and the concentration of incidents in the town centre which adjoins the site. In a similar vein, and in addition, the pedestrian access through the park which connects the development to the shopping area/service centre. The development is unique in this respect as is the likelihood that there will be few if any others like it in this locality in the foreseeable future. Again a formula is suggested by the developer when judgement and experience  based on the particular characteristics of the development and its location need to be born in mind. Again this is a technology that will not be solely used in the site and a part contribution is therefore sought. That contribution is a relatively small amount proportionate to the size of the development.  These are the variables we have applied to exercise our judgement as to the addition impact of this development the subject of this application. They are related to the scale of the development, the kind of development and its particular location. Local and national planning policies are engaged. The contribution towards CCTV technologies is necessary as is the contribution to premises.    Please keep me posted on the progress of our request and the Planning application. We would normally expect to be able to present the Police case at Committee or appeal. How will your process accommodate this involvement ?
